entries.moduleTitle: Accelerating application building with Pega Blueprint
entries.title: Export and import
entries.text: You export the resulting Blueprint and import the file directly into Pega Platform (a new or existing application), jumpstarting a demo or project build-out by producing a functional application in minutes.

entries.moduleTitle: Accelerating application building with Pega Blueprint
entries.title: Who imports it
entries.text: The Lead System Architect (LSA) is responsible for importing the Blueprint file into the Pega Platform environment and uses the user stories created by Blueprint and BAs to configure functional and technical requirements.

entries.moduleTitle: Accelerating application building with Pega Blueprint
entries.title: What import creates (and the exception)
entries.text: On import, Pega creates the Blueprint's assets according to your configuration. ALL the assets are created in a Branch EXCEPT Access Roles.

entries.moduleTitle: Accelerating application building with Pega Blueprint
entries.title: PremBridge not required
entries.text: Pega GenAI PremBridge is NOT required to import Pega Blueprints into a new or existing application.

entries.title: Using Blueprint for an Industry App (Customer Service for Insurance)

entries.moduleTitle: Accelerating application building with Pega Blueprint
entries.title: Industry templates
entries.text: Blueprint can be used to create industry-specific applications — for example, a Customer Service for Insurance application — by starting from relevant best-practice templates and refining the proposed Case Types and workflows for the industry's needs.

entries.title: Capturing and presenting data
entries.text: Fields · Calculated values · Views

entries.title: Field
entries.text: A reusable UI component consisting of a NAME and a FIELD TYPE. Each field captures or presents one value associated with a Case. In Dev Studio a field is implemented as a property.

entries.title: Field Type
entries.text: Determines the format/validation of the data and the input control rendered to the user. Choosing the right type (instead of Text for everything) enforces a consistent, valid format across all Case Types and reduces errors.

entries.title: Single value vs. data relationship fields
entries.text: Two categories of Pega Field Types: SINGLE VALUE (basic) — captures ONE piece of data (e.g., text, integer, date) · DATA RELATIONSHIP (Embedded Data, Data reference, Case reference, Query) — connects a field to another data object or Case

entries.title: Calculated value field
entries.text: A field whose value is COMPUTED automatically from an expression/formula that references other fields, rather than entered by a user (e.g., Line total = Quantity × Price per unit). It keeps derived data accurate and consistent.

entries.title: Recalculation
entries.text: A calculated value can be configured to recalculate as the underlying data changes, so it always reflects current inputs. Calculated fields are typically presented read-only because the system maintains them.

entries.title: View
entries.text: A UI component that gathers data from a user OR displays data to a user, showing the fields and instructions needed for the current Step/Assignment. You add fields to Views to tailor the UI for each Step of the workflow.

entries.title: View types & editability
entries.text: Full Page View (read-only; one per Case/data object), Partial (read-only), List (relies on a data source; enable editing for create/edit/delete), and Form (editable; created per Step via Configure View). Default Form Views = Create and Edit.

entries.title: The Data Model
entries.text: Data modeling · Data records · Data Pages and the Visual Data Model · Integration Designer

entries.title: Data object (data type)
entries.text: A structure that groups related fields to describe a business entity (e.g., Customer with Name, Email, Phone). Reusable across all Case Types. In Dev Studio, a data object is called a data type and a field is a property.

entries.title: Why model data
entries.text: A well-designed Data Model promotes reuse, accuracy, consistency, and scalability. You model the data an application needs to complete work, then connect it to Case Types so the workflow has the right data at the right time.

entries.title: Sourcing data objects
entries.text: Data for a data object can be stored LOCALLY in the Pega database, or sourced from an EXTERNAL system of record (e.g., a client database or web service). Pega ships pre-configured objects (e.g., Address-Postal, Address-Email) to reuse or extend.

entries.title: Data Record
entries.text: The unique set of fields and values for one instance of a data object (e.g., one Customer = Ian / Mitchell / email / phone). Records live in a system of record — Pega DB or external.

entries.title: Value change vs. structure change
entries.text: Two types of data model changes with different implications: VALUE change (add a customer, update a phone number) — normal business operation; no process change needed · STRUCTURE change (adding/removing fields) — modifies the data object definition; requires careful planning

entries.title: pyGUID & local entry
entries.text: Local records can be added on the Records tab in the Pega-managed store and receive generated identifiers such as pyGUID. A record identifier is distinct from the Case workflow status and the data type definition.

entries.title: Data Pages and the Visual Data Model
Data Page
entries.text: The bridge between a data object and its data — retrieves from a source and CACHES it in Clipboard memory. Hides integration details so developers work with sourced data without knowing where it lives.

entries.title: Pega Live Data & default Data Pages
entries.text: Pega Live Data is the virtualization layer separating business logic from how/when data is accessed. Every data object includes three default Data Pages: a single read-only, a list read-only, and a single read-and-write. Case Types have two (both read-only).

entries.title: Visual Data Model
entries.text: A diagram showing the application's data objects and their relationships. Relationship indicators: one line = one-to-one; multiple lines on one side = one-to-many; multiple lines on both sides = many-to-many.

entries.title: Data objects and Integrations landing page
entries.text: The Integration Designer is the single place in App Studio to see the application's data objects, their Data Pages, the systems of record (SOR) that source them, which Case Types reference each object (Referenced By), and simulated data sources.

entries.title: Visual Data Model & Integration Map
entries.text: From the Integration Designer you open the Visual Data Model (objects and relationships) and the Integration Map (a diagram of data objects and the systems of record from which they are sourced).

entries.title: Creating a data relationship
entries.text: Data objects · Data relationships

entries.title: Data object
entries.text: A structure that groups related fields to model a single entity and establish common context (e.g., a Customer grouping First name, Last name, Email, Phone). Data objects are reusable across an application's Case Types.

entries.title: Extending a data object
entries.text: You can extend a data object by referencing another data object; the referenced object's fields become part of the referencing object. Any object can be referenced once or many times.

entries.title: Data relationship
entries.text: A container that associates related fields. Unlike a data object or field, it does NOT store data — it relates data-storing elements to the elements that need that data to resolve a Case (object↔Case, object↔object, or Case↔Case).

entries.title: Single record vs. list of records
entries.text: Two ways a data relationship references data: SINGLE RECORD — one related set of fields and values. · LIST OF RECORDS — multiple related records. A list Data Page uses pxResults; an embedded Page List uses its own property name and indexed entries.

entries.title: Embedded Data
entries.text: Use when information is collected from user input directly inside the Case. Data is stored WITH that Case instance (not shared from an external source), enforcing a common format (e.g., a patient's emergency contact entered in the Case).

entries.title: Data reference
entries.text: Use when you need to REUSE another data object from OUTSIDE the Case — data sourced from locally-stored Data Records or an external system of record (e.g., reference the facility where a medical appointment is booked).

entries.title: Case reference
entries.text: Use when you want to REUSE data from another CASE (e.g., a user selects from a list of Service Cases from the Service Case Type).

entries.title: Query
entries.text: Use for READ-ONLY access to information that is external to the Case; the Query Field Type allows PARAMETERS to query for specific data (e.g., return a medical professional's next appointment, or all appointments in a given time frame).

entries.title: Application user interface design
entries.text: Views (Constellation) · UI configuration in App Studio · Form views · Exploring fields · Model-driven UI controls · Portals and landing pages · Dynamic field behavior · Constellation form error handling

entries.title: View
entries.text: A reusable configuration of UI elements used to capture or display data for a Case. Constellation applications are built on a View-based UI architecture (the Constellation Ruleset), and Views are reusable across Case Types.

entries.title: Prescribed design system
entries.text: Constellation supplies reusable UI patterns and supported configuration choices. Its accessible defaults support implementation, but the finished application still needs accessibility testing.

entries.title: The four View types
entries.text: Full Page supplies Case or data-object context; Partial presents read-only information; List presents collections; Form supports task input and can include read-only content.

entries.title: Separation of Concerns
entries.text: The UI layer follows the Separation of Concerns principle — the application is divided into distinct parts, each addressing one concern — so front-end components connect cleanly to back-end APIs.

entries.title: Templates
entries.text: Generated Views use templates for layout and responsiveness. Template options depend on View type and location; test the resulting application with the intended users and devices.

entries.title: Full Page View
entries.text: Auto-added per new Case Type/data object; the three-pane visual framework representing a single Case. Edited on the UX tab. While authoring, the Preview shows only placeholder text — run a Case instance to preview with real data.

entries.title: Summary panel & Promoted Action
entries.text: The Summary panel sits upper-left and by default includes the Details View (showing Primary Fields) and Pulse View. A Promoted Action gives header access to a frequent Case-wide Action (e.g., Change Stage) — one per Case Type.

entries.title: Creating a Form View
entries.text: Two ways: on the Workflow tab (configuring a Step's View auto-creates a Form View) or on the UX tab's Other Views pane. Form Views use the Default template; Step-associated Views can also use the Hierarchical template.

entries.title: Layout
entries.text: Set 1–3 columns; two-column is best practice. Narrow inputs (Text single line, Currency) take one column; wider/any-height inputs (Rich Text Editor, Text area, Radio group, Checkbox, Booleans, Attachments) span two columns, keeping tabbing left-to-right.

entries.title: Field groups & multi-step vs hierarchical
entries.text: Three UI structuring concepts: FIELD GROUP — clusters related fields under one header; specific to the View (not reusable) · MULTI-STEP FORM — one Assignment split across MULTIPLE Views (linear; default for Create Stage) · HIERARCHICAL FORM — one Form View divided into Form-group tabs; useful when users can complete groups in any order

entries.title: Field settings
entries.text: Each field has a name and a Field Type that determines its format/validation and the control shown. You configure field settings (label, required, visibility, etc.) to tailor capture and presentation.

entries.title: Primary Fields
entries.text: Primary Fields identify important information and populate applicable standard Views, including Create, Edit, Details and List. A designation is not a required-field constraint; related data objects can supply their designated fields.

entries.title: Model-driven UI
entries.text: Field types and metadata determine the supported controls. Date fields use date input; Picklists support dropdown, search and radio presentation where appropriate. Model-driven does not mean every supported presentation is immutable.

entries.title: Patterns and consistency
entries.text: Because controls derive from the model via reusable patterns, the UI stays consistent and responsive across devices/channels, and adapts automatically when rules change. You can still customize a control's presentation where needed.

entries.title: Portal and task context
entries.text: A Portal is a web Channel. Configure its landing pages and navigation for its users; a task Form is a different interface within a Case. Responsive templates usually adapt the same UI to smaller screens.

entries.title: Presentation and processing
entries.text: Views present and collect information. Configure workflow processing with the appropriate Automations and Rules. Hiding a field does not authorize access, and client feedback does not replace server validation.

entries.title: User guidance
entries.text: Case status · Assignment instructions · Form instructions · Field settings and additional text · Case status property (legacy reference) · Constellation form error handling

entries.title: Case status
entries.text: Case status communicates progress. It uses Work-.pyStatusWork; configured Rules and notifications may refer to it, but the value does not by itself guarantee a particular notification.

entries.title: Status categories
entries.text: Four conventional Case status prefix categories: New — just created · Open — in progress · Pending — waiting on something or someone · Resolved — processing is complete, with no remaining open Assignments; examples include Resolved-Completed and Resolved-Rejected

entries.title: Setting status
entries.text: Configure status at meaningful Stages or Steps. A configured transition updates status; the final Stage’s resolution status applies after its Processes complete. Not every transition needs a different status.

entries.title: Guiding users: instructions, help text, and visual cues
Step (Assignment) instructions
entries.text: Text added to a Collect-information Step/Assignment that tells the user exactly what they must do to complete the Task. Instructions render at runtime on the assignment form, reducing confusion and errors.

entries.title: Contextual field text
entries.text: Additional text beside an input can clarify the expected value. Instruction text explains the task; neither replaces validation or authorization.

entries.title: Instruction overrides
entries.text: The Form can show the configured Step instructions, override them with task-specific text, or hide them. Choose guidance that helps the user complete the current Assignment.

entries.title: Routing Assignments to users
entries.text: Routing work · Work Queue role restrictions · Personas, operators and work access

entries.title: Routing
entries.text: Routing assigns responsibility for completing a Task to one or more users. It increases business efficiency by ensuring the most appropriate users receive the right work at the right time, orchestrating the workflow across teams.

entries.title: Worklist vs. Work Queue
entries.text: Two types of Assignment containers: WORKLIST — holds Assignments routed to a SPECIFIC user (operator) who owns the work · WORK QUEUE (work basket) — a SHARED queue for a team/Work Group; any qualified member can pull and complete the work

entries.title: Route to the current user
entries.text: Keep the Assignment with the user already working the Case — appropriate when the same person should continue.

entries.title: Route to a specific user
entries.text: Send the Assignment to a named operator's Worklist when one accountable individual must own the Task.

entries.title: Route to a Work Queue
entries.text: Send the Assignment to a shared Work Queue when any qualified member of a team can perform the work.

entries.title: Route using business logic
entries.text: Use configured business conditions to choose a user or Work Queue. A shared destination does not by itself select the least-loaded worker or enforce a skill policy.

entries.title: Separate destination from permission
entries.text: Work Groups organize shared work. Access Groups and Roles govern permissions. A Work Queue can require specified roles to process its Assignments; a Persona label alone is not a security boundary.

entries.title: Designing an approval Process
entries.text: Work approval · Cascading approvals · Reporting structure challenge (24.2) · Authority matrix challenge (24.2)

entries.title: Approval gate
entries.text: A user decision controls the approval path. Choose the reviewer and configure both outcomes.

entries.title: Default versus configured rejection
entries.text: Default rejection resolves the request as Resolved-Rejected. Revision requires an explicit destination; it is not implied by the word Reject.

entries.title: Outcome configuration
entries.text: Approval can continue work or select a Stage, with an optional status update. Rejection can resolve, continue, or select a Stage.

entries.title: Outside the application
entries.text: Enabled email or mobile approval lets the routed stakeholder decide outside the application. Check the recipient and enablement rather than assuming every Step sends these notifications.

entries.title: One decision or a series
entries.text: A single approval may use a named recipient, request-dependent routing, or a shared queue. Several required decisions need an explicit sequence or a cascade.

entries.title: Routing policy
entries.text: Choose between one particular reviewer and any eligible reviewer. Do not turn a shared Assignment into a claim that all queue members receive independent approvals.

entries.title: Cascade models
entries.text: Reporting structure follows manager relationships. Authority matrix supplies an ordered list and can include other departments. The next module explores both.

entries.title: Cascading approvals
entries.text: Cascading approvals · Work approval · Reporting structure challenge (24.2) · Authority matrix challenge (24.2)

entries.title: Ordered series
entries.text: A cascade represents several required decisions in order. It is not an any-one broadcast or majority vote.

entries.title: Two models
entries.text: Reporting structure uses management relationships; authority matrix uses a populated approver list.

entries.title: Design questions
entries.text: Which people are required? In what order? Does the number of management levels vary? Does anyone sit outside the reporting line?

entries.title: Rejected outcome
entries.text: Configure rejection flow explicitly. Resolution and revision are different policies; neither majority override nor restart should be assumed.

entries.title: Reporting source
entries.text: At runtime the current-user context and selected Reporting Manager or Workgroup Manager source identify the reviewer. Do not assume the original creator is always the current user.

entries.title: Depth
entries.text: One requests the immediate manager; All uses the whole hierarchy; Custom uses When Rules to select the required depth. Depth is not a promise of arbitrary middle-tier skipping.

entries.title: Challenge configuration
entries.text: The linked v7 reporting-structure challenge uses Dev Studio, an Approve/Reject Step, Cascading and Reporting structure. Its When conditions select one or two levels; the walkthrough targets Platform 24.2.

entries.title: Approver data
entries.text: An authority matrix needs a data structure of approvers. A Decision table, Data Page, Activity or Data Transform can populate it; a table is one supported approach.

entries.title: Decision table example
entries.text: The linked v7 challenge configures a Page List and an approver property, then a Decision table that appends required recipients. Evaluate all rows allows multiple matching results.

entries.title: Other departments
entries.text: Use the matrix when required reviewers are outside the chosen management line. List ordering still matters; population rules are not a parallel voting mechanism.

entries.title: Completing work on time
entries.text: Service Level Agreements · Setting goals and deadlines · Enforcing SLAs challenge (24.2) · Passed deadline interval

entries.title: Service-Level Agreement (SLA)
entries.text: Establishes a work-completion deadline to enforce on-time performance. Can be defined on an ASSIGNMENT or the overall CASE, and uses MILESTONES (goal, then deadline) to mark expected turnaround times.

entries.title: Goal vs. Deadline
entries.text: Goal and deadline use the SLA’s configured start reference. Case-resolution configuration can refer to this Case, its parent or the top-level Case. GOAL — desired completion time, normally the earlier target; calculate from the configured start reference · DEADLINE — the longest time work MAY take before it is 'late'

entries.title: Escalation actions at milestones
entries.text: When a milestone is missed, the SLA can increase Urgency AND run an escalation: NOTIFY (assignee, manager, participants, or Case creator), REASSIGN to another user/queue, or RESOLVE the Case. Repeating post-deadline escalation is covered by the passed deadline interval.

entries.title: Three timed responses: worked example
entries.text: For a calendar-time policy, Goal at day 3 can notify; Deadline at day 7 can reassign; a passed deadline interval of three days with one event can resolve still-open work at day 10. Configure every action explicitly and account for processing delay and calendars. The post-deadline Rule configuration is covered in SA-M16.

entries.title: Urgency (Case vs. Assignment)
entries.text: Urgency is numeric priority with maximum 100: CASE Urgency — priority of the Case itself · ASSIGNMENT Urgency — initial value equals Case Urgency (default 10); Stage/Process-level SLA adjustments affect Case Urgency

entries.title: Setting and increasing Urgency
entries.text: Set the Case Type’s initial urgency in Settings. Updating a Case’s urgency supplies the new value for new Assignments, not existing ones. This does not prevent an existing Assignment’s own SLA from adjusting its urgency.

entries.title: Get Next Work
entries.text: Pega prioritizes work by Urgency. GET NEXT WORK hands users the highest-Urgency Assignment they can perform first, so high-priority work finishes on time. Design SLAs/Urgency so the right work outranks the rest.

entries.title: Where SLAs apply (and the Create Stage exception)
entries.text: SLAs apply to Case Types, Stages, Processes, and Collect-information/Approval Steps. EXCEPTION: the Create Stage cannot have a goal, deadline, or escalation — it collects data before Case processing begins.

entries.title: Configuring a goal & deadline
entries.text: Use the appropriate Case or lifecycle-element Goal & deadline configuration. Case resolution offers Custom SLA, Existing SLA or Never, and This/Parent/Top-level Case anchors. Do not assume every lifecycle panel exposes all Case-resolution options. The linked 24.2 challenge configures the Schedule repair Step; the supplemental topic now uses Pega Infinity Studio terminology.

entries.title: Configuring escalation actions
entries.text: Configure notification recipients and message at the relevant goal and deadline. The supplemental Case/Stage/Process instructions describe Creator and Participants. General SLA escalation also includes reassignment or resolution; available controls depend on the selected context.

entries.title: Escalating late work
entries.text: Passed deadline interval · SLA milestones and escalation · Escalating late work challenge (24.2)

entries.title: Passed deadline interval
entries.text: Defines further scheduled action for still-open work after its deadline. Repetition follows the configured event count or Assignment completion policy; it is not automatically unlimited.

entries.title: It repeats (unlike goal/deadline)
entries.text: Key distinction from goal and deadline intervals: Goal and Deadline fire ONCE only · Passed deadline interval can REPEAT — a FIXED NUMBER OF TIMES or UNTIL the Assignment is completed · On each repeat: can increase Urgency and trigger escalation Actions

entries.title: Configured only in Dev Studio
entries.text: Configure the passed deadline interval in Dev Studio on the SLA Rule. App Studio-created SLAs auto-generate an SLA Rule — goal/deadline come from App Studio, but the passed deadline interval must be added on the Rule.

entries.title: Challenge configuration (24.2)
entries.text: The linked v7 challenge opens the Review Step’s SLA in Dev Studio, limits passed deadline events to six, sets a 15-minute interval, adds +10 urgency and selects Notify Manager. After this customization, goals and deadlines are edited through the SLA Rule as well.

entries.title: Urgency maximum is 100
entries.text: Urgency is capped at 100. Once an Assignment reaches Urgency 100, Pega IGNORES further Urgency increments — but CONTINUES other escalation Actions. Example: if Urgency is already 100, Pega skips the increase yet still sends the notification.

entries.title: Escalation Actions (reused each interval)
entries.text: Actions triggered on every passed deadline interval (same as goal/deadline): Notify (assignee, manager, or participants) · Reassign (to another user or Work Queue) · Resolve the Case

entries.title: Sending emails during Case processing
entries.text: Email correspondence · Send email challenge (24.2)

entries.title: Three questions for correspondence
entries.text: Three questions to answer when configuring automated email: WITH WHOM — who receives the email (Recipient: a field value, user reference, or participant) · HOW — the message content (Correspondence template referencing Case data) · WHEN — when in the Case life cycle (Send Email automation Step placement)

entries.title: Recipient (Send to) options
entries.text: Send to a SPECIFIC email address (fragile if the address changes), or resolve at runtime from a FIELD value (e.g., Customer email field), a USER REFERENCE, or a PARTICIPANT. Runtime resolution is preferred.

entries.title: User reference (incl. Create/Update Operator)
entries.text: A field pointing to one specific user, defined in the Case Type data model. CREATE OPERATOR and UPDATE OPERATOR are user-reference fields automatically defined for every data type associated with the Case Type.

entries.title: Participants (Owner / Customer / Interested)
entries.text: Default Case participants (Pega resolves their email from participant info): OWNER — the user who created the Case · CUSTOMER — the person the Case is for · INTERESTED — tracks progress only; not responsible for any action

entries.title: Rich text editor
entries.text: Pega provides a RICH TEXT EDITOR to create formatted email and REUSE Case data — e.g., greet the customer by referencing the first-name and last-name fields captured in the Case.

entries.title: Correspondence templates
entries.text: You can reuse out-of-the-box CORRESPONDENCE TEMPLATES that include Case processing data such as the Case ID (.pyID) and Case status (.pyStatusWork), instead of composing every email from scratch.

entries.title: Send email automation
entries.text: Add Send email at the workflow point where correspondence is required. Reaching this Step initiates sending to the configured recipient. A read receipt or reply dependency needs a separate design; this description does not guarantee successful delivery.

entries.title: Case-level notifications
entries.text: Enable Case-level email notifications for Assignment routing to a Worklist. The routed user is the recipient. Distinguish this event from arbitrary Case status changes and shared Work Queue routing.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.text: Teams of users · Advanced queue configuration (version-specific reference)

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Work Groups and Work Queues

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Work Group
entries.text: A CROSS-FUNCTIONAL team — a manager plus a Work Queue — whose members share work regardless of their business unit. Note: an 'Operator' in Dev Studio is a 'User' in App Studio.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Shared team queue and default queue
entries.text: The introductory Teams of users topic describes one shared queue for the team. Configuration uses a Default Work Queue field. Follow the documented setup for your version; do not infer additional queue or permission configuration solely from this simplified team model.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Work Queue vs. Worklist
entries.text: Two Assignment container types: WORK QUEUE — a SHARED list for all operators in a Work Group · WORKLIST — holds only work assigned to ONE specific operator · An Assignment moves from the Work Queue to a Worklist when ready to be worked

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Operators and Work Groups
entries.text: An operator must belong to AT LEAST ONE Work Group and can belong to MORE THAN ONE. Work Group membership controls work sharing without changing the organizational hierarchy. Configure users in App Studio; Dev Studio offers advanced options.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Queue processing roles (advanced configuration)
entries.text: The linked configuration reference distinguishes access to a queue from processing work. If Roles are configured on that queue, processing requires at least one listed role. Team membership alone does not establish every permission.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Managers and Authorized Managers

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Work Group manager
entries.text: A Work Group names ONE operator as its PRIMARY manager. The system uses manager information for NOTIFICATION Tasks, APPROVAL Tasks, ROUTING Tasks, and ESCALATION. Managers assign, monitor, and report on the group's work using the Web Portal.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating and managing teams of users
entries.title: Authorized Managers (and their limits)
entries.text: Authorized Managers assist with assignment transfer. This management relationship alone does not grant approval authority or unrestricted processing access. They need not be members of the group. · The introductory source excludes approvals from these duties. · An authorized manager outside the group cannot complete its queued assignments under this lesson model.

entries.title: Team application development
entries.text: Identifying roles in a Pega project · Parallel development

entries.title: Delivery roles: PO, Project Manager, Scrum Master
entries.text: Three delivery management roles: PRODUCT OWNER — manages scope and prioritizes sprint requirements · PROJECT MANAGER — leads delivery, maintains governance, liaises with client leadership · SCRUM MASTER — runs Sprint ceremonies (Planning, Sizing, Backlog Refinement, Retrospectives) and removes impediments

entries.title: Build & quality roles: SA/SSA/LSA, QA, BA
entries.text: Three build and quality assurance roles: SYSTEM ARCHITECTS (SA/SSA/LSA) — configure the application; LSA imports Blueprint files · QUALITY ANALYSTS — verify requirements and write test scripts · BUSINESS ARCHITECT — translates business needs into workflows, Data Models, and user experiences

entries.title: Client & design roles: SME, UX, Solutions Consultant
entries.text: Three client-side and design roles: SUBJECT MATTER EXPERT — client operational expert who supplies requirements · UX DESIGNER — ensures design meets user needs and accessibility standards · SOLUTIONS CONSULTANT — engages client in sales, co-designs Blueprint, hands off to delivery team

entries.title: Roles and studios
entries.text: Each studio serves a different set of roles: APP STUDIO (no-code) — SAs, BAs, UX designers, solutions consultants, Project Managers, Scrum Masters · DEV STUDIO (advanced) — System Architects and Quality Analysts · PREDICTION STUDIO — data scientists · ADMIN STUDIO — business IT for system administration

entries.title: Workspace → Branch → Application
entries.text: Three parallel development scopes (changes promote outward): WORKSPACE — one developer's PRIVATE changes, isolated until shared · BRANCH — the TEAM's active changes in progress · APPLICATION — shared application configuration after integration; merging does not itself deploy a production release.

entries.title: Workspaces
entries.text: Private development space tied to one operator and one application. Changes stay isolated until shared to a Branch — avoiding rule conflicts. Each operator gets one Workspace by default; multiple are allowed. Enabled via the EnableWorkspace setting.

entries.title: Branches and Branch Rulesets
entries.text: A BRANCH is a container of Rulesets under active development. Branch Rulesets are based on (branched from) another Ruleset. Best practice: one Branch per feature so teams work in isolation — a finished feature merges independently.

entries.title: Merging into the main application
entries.text: A Branch merges into the main application only after the feature is complete, conflicts are resolved, and approval is granted. Pega automatically checks which Rules are new or updated before completing the merge.

entries.title: Guardrails
entries.text: Settings that flag elements not complying with Pega best practices. You must respond to warnings to keep the application efficient. The WEIGHTED SCORE metric reflects the number and severity of guardrail warnings on a Branch.

entries.title: The four Branch quality metrics
entries.text: Four metrics tracked per Branch before merging: (1) GUARDRAILS — weighted compliance score · (2) MERGE CONFLICTS — potential conflicts to investigate · (3) TEST COVERAGE & UNIT TESTS — rules covered % and pass rate % · (4) UNCOVERED RULES — Branch Rules not covered by any test

entries.title: Collaboration with users
entries.text: Collaboration tools

entries.title: Pulse
entries.text: Pega's built-in messaging system. Users post, view, and reply in the Pulse Activity Feed — directed to specific users, team members, or Case stakeholders. Example: a CSR posts once to update every Case participant on a claim's status.

entries.title: Accessing Pulse (developers vs. users)
entries.text: Pulse collaboration access differs by role: DEVELOPERS — click 'Toggle developer collaboration' in the App Studio header · USERS — access Pulse via a Pulse widget on their Case or Work Object

entries.title: Replies and email notifications
entries.text: Reply to a Pulse message with or without a comment. Users opt into email notifications for @-mentions, likes, replies in conversations they participated in, or posts to Cases they follow. Email replies appear as Pulse comments without login.

entries.title: Tags
entries.text: Descriptive words or phrases ASSOCIATED WITH A PULSE MESSAGE that categorize messages so users can quickly find information to resolve a Case. Add a tag by typing # followed by a word/phrase WITHOUT SPACES.

entries.title: The Tags widget
entries.text: Lists tags relevant to a Case. Each tag is a link — clicking it shows all Cases sharing that tag. Added to the Full Case Page (not the Navigation bar, where the Pulse widget lives).

entries.title: Modular architecture and enterprise reuse
entries.text: Modular reuse architecture · Studio interoperability and Reuse Library

entries.title: Modular enterprise reuse
entries.text: A software development approach that uses standardized, reusable components to build applications. Instead of starting from scratch, developers ASSEMBLE pre-built, tested modules to speed up development and maintain consistency across the enterprise.

entries.title: Benefits across the lifecycle
entries.text: Reusing shared modules helps at every project phase: Design: reduces planning time with ready-made components · Development: speeds builds and minimizes coding · Testing: limits defects/scope via pre-tested modules · Deployment: simplifies implementation with standardized components · Maintenance: shared components reduce duplicated maintenance; consuming versions, compatibility and release processes still require governance.

entries.title: The Five Guiding Principles of Reuse
Interoperable
entries.text: Use consistent building blocks across applications AND authoring environments (App Studio and Dev Studio).

entries.title: Updateable
entries.text: Individual components (UI, data layer, business logic) can be updated independently — no need to rebuild the entire application when one layer changes.

entries.title: Configurable
entries.text: Application behavior is defined by rules, not hard-coded — meaning business users or architects can adjust behavior without rewriting underlying code.

entries.title: Modular
entries.text: The architecture avoids large monolithic layers. Instead, each concern (presentation, logic, data) is a distinct, replaceable module that is easier to test and maintain.

entries.title: Governed
entries.text: Establish governance (for example, a Pega Center of Excellence) to manage, evolve, and ensure the quality of reusable assets.

entries.title: Situational Layer Cake
entries.text: A patented Pega architecture that balances two competing forces: REUSE (economies of scale and consistency) and VARIATION (different products, regions, regulatory needs). It avoids both 'spaghetti' single-app if-then-else and the sprawl of 50–100 near-identical apps.

entries.title: Enterprise Layer
entries.text: Core Pega Platform features and enterprise-wide reusable assets (e.g., a company-wide authentication module used across all applications).

entries.title: Division Layer
entries.text: Reusable components specific to a division (e.g., a claims-processing flow tailored for the insurance division but reused across its applications).

entries.title: Application Layer
entries.text: Application-specific implementations that leverage lower-layer assets (e.g., a customer-service app that uses shared authentication and claims components but adds its own workflows).

entries.title: Implementation Layer
entries.text: Customizations for specific deployment scenarios WITHOUT altering the base application (e.g., localizing the customer-service app for a region by adjusting language and regulatory rules).

entries.title: App Studio role
entries.text: A simplified, collaborative, inclusive authoring experience that lets a wide range of low-code practitioners understand, interpret, and author processes/applications. It hides complexity and raises Case Type literacy so stakeholders express requirements and feedback better.

entries.title: Dev Studio role
entries.text: Robust low-code features for experienced architects to configure integrations, complex decisions, security, and advanced features. Think of Dev Studio as where you CREATE reusable modules and MARK Rules as relevant records for assembly in App Studio.

entries.title: Relevant records
entries.text: The key to marking rules as reusable in App Studio, enabling Studio interoperability. They describe rules that refine the behavior, presentation, and definition of a Case Type or data type, built in Dev Studio and assembled in App Studio.

entries.title: Auto-marked in App Studio
entries.text: When you create Fields, Views, Processes, and user actions in App Studio, Pega automatically marks them as relevant records.

entries.title: Reuse Library
entries.text: A centralized repository in App Studio that contains all reusable assets in the enterprise, helping developers of all skill levels discover, understand, and use reusable components. Combined with strong governance, it accelerates development, improves quality, and boosts agility.

entries.title: Creating a Rule
entries.text: Rules and rule types · Rulesets · Rule creation · Classes and class hierarchy · Rule reuse through inheritance

entries.title: Rule
entries.text: The basic building block of a Pega application that defines its behavior. Each Rule is an instance of a Rule Type, which determines the type of behavior it models. Pega uses Rules to generate application code in the background.

entries.title: Rule Type
entries.text: A template for creating a Rule that models a specific behavior — for example, a Flow Rule models a Process, while other Rule Types model UI, automated Decisions, and more.

entries.title: Automated Rule creation in App Studio
entries.text: As you add Processes, define Steps, and configure Views in the Case Life Cycle, Pega creates and manages the underlying Rules (Flows, Tasks, UI) in the background, letting developers focus on business tasks.

entries.title: Versioning
entries.text: Create a new version whenever Case behavior must change. Pega keeps change history — you can review and undo. Each Rule describes specific behavior, so changes are isolated to that Rule only.

entries.title: Delegation
entries.text: Developers delegate a Rule to business users so they can update Case behavior as conditions change while the rest of the application stays unchanged (e.g., Accounting raises an auto-approval threshold from USD 25 to USD 50 without a change request).

entries.title: Reuse
entries.text: Developers reuse Rules whenever an application needs existing behavior, instead of reconfiguring it every time (e.g., reuse one policyholder-info UI form across auto, property, and marine claims).

entries.title: Parametrization
entries.text: To increase reusability, use parameters to drive a Rule's logic based on a passed value instead of hard-coded data — reducing code duplication and the time to implement Rule specializations.

entries.title: Ruleset
entries.text: A group that identifies, stores, and manages the set of Rules defining an application, packaged for distribution. Rulesets can be SHARED between applications to reuse the same Rules (like an album shared across playlists).

entries.title: Ruleset version
entries.text: An instance of a Ruleset collecting individual Rules. Create a NEW version to update contents (unlocked for edits); best practice is to LOCK older versions. Version format: major-minor-patch (two-digit each), starting at 01-01-01.

entries.title: Ruleset stack
entries.text: The application stack orders Rulesets for lookup. A listed entry covers versions down to the lowest minor and patch in the specified major version, not every earlier major version.

entries.title: Two paths to a Rule
entries.text: In App Studio, Rules are created FOR you as you build the Case Life Cycle, Views, and data. In Dev Studio, you can directly create and manage how a Rule is created and reused to maintain Rule integrity and reusability.

entries.title: New Record form fields (Dev Studio)
entries.text: Four fields that uniquely identify a rule: (1) Rule Type (function), (2) Ruleset (grouping), (3) Apply to (target class), (4) Label (display name). These four fields together enable Rule Resolution.

entries.title: Rule creation methods (what auto-fills)
entries.text: Five paths to the New Record form, each pre-filling context: Create menu: Rule Type, application context and Ruleset · App Explorer: adds the class context · Rule reference: also provides Label/identifier when the reference has a name · Save As: source context, with Identifier, Class or Ruleset changed · Records explorer: application context and Ruleset

entries.title: Specialization by copy (Save As)
entries.text: Copy an existing Rule into a different class or Ruleset to specialize its behavior, preserving the original while creating a variant. At least one of Identifier, Class, or Ruleset must differ from the source.

entries.title: Instance key (.pzInsKey)
entries.text: The source describes a generally four-part instance key: internal Rule Type, applies-to class, identifier and creation timestamp normalized to GMT. Some Rule Types add identifying elements. Do not confuse this key with the entire runtime Rule selection algorithm.

entries.title: Class
entries.text: A grouping of Rules by reuse scope. Three class types per application: Work class (Case processing rules), Data class (data model rules), Integration class (connector rules). Classes form the inheritance hierarchy Pega uses to resolve rules at runtime.

entries.title: Parent and child classes
entries.text: A class can contain other classes. A parent class contains another class; a child class is contained by another. A child class can reuse/inherit any Rules defined for its parent class.

entries.title: Class hierarchy
entries.text: Classes are layered most-specific to least-specific. At run time, Pega starts with the most-specific class and expands to more general ones. The class name shows position: TGB-IT-Work is a child of TGB-IT, a child of TGB.

entries.title: Pattern inheritance
entries.text: AUTOMATIC inheritance using the existing class-name structure (shared prefix) to determine which Rules are available for reuse. Promotes reuse based on BUSINESS suitability — aggregating Rules at higher levels for departments within that division.

entries.title: Directed inheritance
entries.text: Inheritance where the parent class is EXPLICITLY specified on the class Rule form (not automatic). Lets an application class inherit Rules from OUTSIDE the business class hierarchy (e.g., Work- or Data-). Promotes reuse based on FUNCTIONAL suitability.

entries.title: Resolution order & @baseclass
entries.text: Pega searches parent classes via pattern inheritance; if unsuccessful, uses the directed inheritance parent for another pattern search — repeating until reaching @baseclass. If still not found after @baseclass, Pega returns an error.

entries.title: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Relevant Records — Purpose and Marking

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Relevant record
entries.text: A rule marked to make it accessible to other developers from App Studio prompts. Marking exposes Dev Studio rules so App Studio developers can use them without navigating to Dev Studio.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Why designate relevant records
entries.text: Relevant designation makes developer-prepared Rules discoverable in supported App Studio configuration prompts. For an existing SLA selection, mark the Dev Studio Rule relevant for the appropriate class. This designation is not a deployment or authorization control.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Auto-marked vs. manually marked
entries.text: Relevant designation supports discovery and reuse, rather than mobile/offline packaging. AUTO-MARKED — App Studio-created fields, views and processes in a Case Type or data type are examples of automatically designated records. · MANUAL — For an eligible Dev Studio Rule, use Actions → Mark as relevant record. Verify guardrail compliance before recommending it for reuse.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Relevant Records — Scope and Visibility

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Where relevant records appear in App Studio
entries.text: Accessed in App Studio when: (1) adding a step to a process, (2) adding fields to a user view, or (3) applying a service level. The Fields and Views lists in the Case Designer are populated with relevant records.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Viewing relevant records in Dev Studio
entries.text: Configure → Application → Inventory → Relevant Records, then enter a class name. By default, ACTIVE records are shown. The 'Marked relevant at' column shows which class level set the designation.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Inactive relevant records
entries.text: Records no longer applicable can be marked INACTIVE to narrow the list without deleting the rule. Enable 'Show inactive relevant records' to view them. Use the Actions icon to toggle active/inactive per class.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Inherited relevant records
entries.text: An active designation can be inherited by subclasses. In the source example, Insurance-Claims passes its SLA designation to Insurance-Claims-Auto and Insurance-Claims-Home. Show inherited relevant records for the class reveals those entries; active/inactive state is managed for the selected class.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Which rules can be relevant records

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Eligible Rule types in the reviewed source
entries.text: Correspondence, Data transforms, Decision tables, Decision trees, Harness (Pages), Notification, Paragraphs, Process (Flows), Property, Proposition filters, Pulse Feed, Sections, Service Level Agreements, Strategy, User Action (Flow actions), Validate, View, When.

entries.moduleTitle: Promoting rule reuse with relevant records
entries.title: Proposition filter requirement
entries.text: For Proposition filter rules, ALL properties, strategies, and When rules used as filter conditions must ALSO be marked as relevant records for the primary context class (default: the Customer class).

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.text: Automation shapes

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: What Automations are

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Automation
entries.text: Automations simplify Case processing by providing configurable tasks, often performed by the system. Examples include email delivery, Case creation and data copying. The App Studio palette also lists Questionnaire, which asks a user for input; inspect each shape’s behavior rather than assuming every listed shape is purely system-side.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: How to add an Automation
entries.text: Two paths to add an Automation shape: Case Life Cycle view: select a Step → More → Automations · Process modeler: Add → Automations (then configure with parameters specific to its purpose)

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Automation vs. user Step
entries.text: Distinguish automatic actions from tasks that require people or pause processing: Collect information requires a person to supply data. · Run Data Transform executes configured logic without asking a person to re-enter it. · Questionnaire asks a user to complete questions; Wait pauses until its configured condition is fulfilled.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Automation shapes available in App Studio

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Stage navigation shapes
entries.text: Change to a Stage = move to a SPECIFIC Stage. Change to next Stage = advance automatically. Change to previous Stage = return to the previously visited Stage. Three distinct shapes — each behaves differently.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Case action shapes
entries.text: CREATE CASE creates one or more Cases from the current Case, not necessarily only children. UPDATE A CASE targets the current Case or child Cases and descendants. PERSIST CASE makes a temporary Case permanent. SEARCH DUPLICATE CASES checks configured duplicate conditions.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Document & content shapes
entries.text: ATTACH CONTENT associates a file, URL or note with a Case. CREATE PDF produces an attachment from a specified View; the reviewed topic notes that Constellation requires a workaround. GENERATE DOCUMENT handles Case documents and is a separate shape.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Communication shapes
entries.text: SEND EMAIL — formatted emails to custom recipients. SEND NOTIFICATION — notification over multiple Channels. PUSH NOTIFICATION — iOS/Android mobile alert for a pending Case action. POST TO PULSE — posts a message to the Pulse feed.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Data, AI and waiting tasks
entries.text: Key Automation shapes available in the Process modeler: Run Data Transform executes a selected Rule. · Connect Generative AI uses configured prompts and response structures; enable and configure AI in application settings. · Wait pauses processing for a configured condition. · Questionnaire collects answers from a user. Decision branching is a separate workflow concept, not an additional item in this topic’s Automation table.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Use cases and selection

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Send email — use case
entries.text: Send automated email correspondence to all relevant parties with no user interaction. Example: an online store emails a customer about new offers. You configure how the application determines the recipient and compose the email content.

entries.moduleTitle: Automation shapes in the Case Life Cycle
entries.title: Run Data Transform — use case
entries.text: Run a selected Data Transform rule at runtime to set/copy/initialize Case data. Example: at checkout, if the billing address equals the shipping address, a Data Transform copies it automatically instead of making the customer re-enter it.

entries.title: Automating workflow decisions
entries.text: Process modeling fundamentals

entries.title: Process
entries.text: A series of Steps expected to occur in a logical, sequential order. When you add a Process to a Case Type in the Case Life Cycle designer, the Steps are configured in the typical sequence to completion.

entries.title: Process diagram
entries.text: Pega's visual canvas for advanced flow control. Shapes include Assignments, Automations, Decisions, and Subprocesses. Use the Process diagram when the Case Life Cycle's stage/step view doesn't support the required branching or parallel logic.

entries.title: Accessing the Process diagram
entries.text: Click the CONFIGURE PROCESS icon located on the Process in the Case Life Cycle. This opens the PROCESS MODELER, where you add, edit, and remove shapes in the Process diagram to build configurations that deviate from the logical sequential order.

entries.title: Decision shape (orange diamond)
entries.text: Orange diamond that adds conditional branching or skipping to a Process. Advances the Case automatically based on one or more conditions — no user action required at this shape. Supports more than one outcome path.

entries.title: Automating vs human expertise
entries.text: Decision automation frees operators to focus on complex cases: AUTOMATE — straightforward decisions with clear rules (e.g., credit score below threshold → auto-deny) · HUMAN expertise — ambiguous cases needing judgment (e.g., low credit score but high salary and strong history → agent review)

entries.title: Decision flow variations
entries.text: (1) Cases move forward but may include ANOTHER STEP as needed — you choose when extra processing supports the Case. (2) Cases go to ANOTHER STAGE using the Change Stage shape; by skipping a Stage you support out-of-sequence processing.

entries.title: Flow Action
entries.text: Defines what a user can do at a specific Assignment Step — which form appears, which fields are shown, and what submit options are available. Controls user interaction within a Step, not the path between Steps.

entries.title: Associating a Flow Action
entries.text: Within a Process, you associate a Flow Action with a CONNECTOR (the arrow between shapes) or an ASSIGNMENT shape (a green rectangle in the Process diagram).

entries.title: Connector Action
entries.text: Completes the Assignment AND advances the Case to the next shape. A Connector Action is configured as a LINE shape (the connector) in the Process Modeler.

entries.title: Local Action
entries.text: Updates the Assignment but does NOT advance the Case to the next shape. A Local Action is configured in the PROPERTIES PANE of an Assignment shape in the Process Modeler.

entries.title: Calculating fields using Decision tables
entries.text: Decision tables

entries.title: Calculated values and the calculation network
Calculation / calculated field
entries.text: A calculation sets a field's value based on one or more other fields (e.g., Total = Quantity × Price). The calculated field is read-only — the system owns it. Calculations update automatically when any input field changes.

entries.title: Where calculated fields live
entries.text: Create the calculated field in the Data model of a CASE TYPE or DATA OBJECT, depending on the use case. Configuration includes field name, type (e.g., Currency), and the 'This is a calculated field (read-only)' option.

entries.title: Calculation network
entries.text: A calculated field can be the input to another calculation, creating a dependency chain. Pega resolves the chain in the correct order — downstream fields update automatically when upstream inputs change.

entries.title: The three App Studio calculation types
Functions
entries.text: Functions iterate over a data relationship (list) and aggregate values. Supported for Decimal, Currency, and Integer. App Studio provides Sum, Count, Average, Maximum, Minimum.

entries.title: Expressions
entries.text: An expression calculates a field value from a combination of fields, functions, and data relationships. Reference fields with the dot operator (.FieldName). Expressions are evaluated at runtime whenever their inputs change.

entries.title: Concatenation (text expressions)
entries.text: Assembles a string by joining field references and static text with '+'. Example: "Appraiser " + .AppraiserID + " appraised " + .ItemName + " at " + .AppraisedAmount + ".". Field references are replaced with live values at runtime.

entries.title: Decision tables
entries.text: A Decision table evaluates conditions to return an appropriate result — for example, select a discount percentage based on customer tier. Rows define conditions; the matching row's result is returned. Check 'Evaluate all rows' to return multiple matching results.

entries.title: Constellation caveat
entries.text: Only applications based on CONSTELLATION support the creation of CUSTOM decision tables directly in App Studio. In non-Constellation apps, the Dev Studio decision table (marked as a relevant record) is how you make the logic available to App Studio.

entries.title: Decision tables and trees
entries.text: Decision tables in Dev Studio · Decision trees · Decision tree or Decision table · Decision Rule conflicts

entries.title: Decision table
entries.text: Tests property values against conditions to return a result. All rows in a column evaluate the same property. App Studio calculated-field Decision tables are stored as Decision Table Rules in Dev Studio under the Work- class.

entries.title: Decision logic maintenance (Delegation)
entries.text: Organizations can delegate maintenance of Decision tables to stakeholders who manage a specific product line. Example: a logistics manager updates the expedited shipping threshold. To delegate: configure the Delegation options in the Results tab of the Decision table form.

entries.title: Evaluate all rows
entries.text: By default, a Decision table returns the first match (single result). Enable 'Evaluate all rows' to return ALL rows whose conditions are satisfied. Required when multiple matching results are valid (e.g., applying all eligible discounts).

entries.title: Direct flow processing with Decision tables
entries.text: Add a Decision shape in a flow pointing to a Decision Table. Each result value maps to a flow connector, directing the Case to a different path — keeping branching logic out of the flow diagram.

entries.title: Decision tree
entries.text: Handles logic that returns a result from test Conditions. Each branch evaluates a property/operator pair against a single value; a true comparison can lead to nested branches. Decision trees can test DIFFERENT properties and operators across branches.

entries.title: Condition branches and nesting
entries.text: Each branch has a value, operator, and action (result or sub-branch). Branches nest — a true result triggers deeper comparisons. Example: 'Student?' → Yes → 'Senior?' → Yes → '60+ account'; else → 'Standard account'.

entries.title: Where Decision trees can be referenced
entries.text: Decision trees (and Decision tables) can be referenced in: Flow Rules · Declare Expressions · Activities · Routers

entries.title: Choosing: Decision Tree vs. Decision Table
When to use a Decision table
entries.text: Use when all conditions evaluate against the SAME property/operator pair. The columnar structure makes it easy to read and maintain when all rows test the same field (e.g., 'Account type =' with different values).

entries.title: When to use a Decision tree
entries.text: Use when conditions evaluate against DIFFERENT properties or operators. The branching structure handles logic that cannot fit in a single column (e.g., one branch tests 'Revenue >', another tests 'Customer type =').

entries.title: Conflict tests (Show conflicts)
entries.text: Identifies rows or branches that can never execute (unreachable conditions). Run via 'Show conflicts' to catch logic gaps before deployment. A conflict means no input could ever satisfy that row's conditions.

entries.title: Completeness tests (Show completeness)
entries.text: Identifies missing conditions in a Decision table or missing branches in a Decision tree. 'Show completeness' can generate a LARGE number of rows for many-valued combinations; the user determines which suggested conditions are necessary.

entries.moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
entries.title: Purpose
entries.text: Define conditions to control whether a Process or Stage runs in a Case. A condition consists of a property, an operator, and a value — evaluated at runtime against Case data.

entries.moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
entries.title: Default Stage behavior: Never skipped
entries.text: By default, Stages are NEVER skipped. To make a Stage conditional, select it in the Case Life Cycle and configure a skip condition. When the condition = true, the Stage and ALL Processes within it are bypassed.

entries.moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
entries.title: Default Process behavior: Always starts
entries.text: By default, Processes ALWAYS start. To make a Process conditional, select the Process in the Case Life Cycle and configure a run condition. When the condition is not met, that specific Process is skipped.

entries.moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
entries.title: Multiple conditions — AND logic
entries.text: You can add more than one condition to a Stage or Process. ALL conditions must be true simultaneously. Example: 'File personal injury claim' Process runs only when 'Was a party injured' = Yes AND 'Expense total' > USD50.

entries.moduleTitle: Skipping a Process or a Stage
entries.title: Configuration location
entries.text: Both Stage and Process conditions are configured inline in the Case Life Cycle — select the Stage or Process to access its condition panel. No separate Rule form is required.

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.text: Optional Actions

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Optional Actions

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Optional Action vs. Optional Process
entries.text: Two types of user-initiated additions to a Case workflow: OPTIONAL ACTION — a single Step users can invoke at any time · OPTIONAL PROCESS — a series of Steps users can optionally trigger

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Case-wide vs. Stage-only
entries.text: Scope determines when the optional action is available: CASE-WIDE — available throughout the ENTIRE Case lifecycle · STAGE-ONLY — available only during a specified Stage

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Runtime access — Actions menu
entries.text: At runtime, optional Actions are accessible from the Actions menu in the Case. Users choose whether to invoke them during Case processing.

entries.moduleTitle: Adding optional Actions to a workflow
entries.title: Promoted Actions
entries.text: Optional Actions promoted to the Case Page for higher visibility — they appear as buttons on the Case summary rather than only in the Actions menu. Examples: 'Edit details', 'Update contact'. Gives users quicker access without opening the menu.

entries.title: Identifying duplicate Cases
entries.text: Duplicate search

entries.title: Search duplicate cases
entries.text: Automation Step that identifies potential duplicate Cases by comparing field values. A duplicate occurs when a submitted Case matches an existing one. Example: same insurance authorization received twice — once online, once by fax.

entries.title: Basic conditions — mandatory match
entries.text: Conditions that MUST match exactly for a Case to be flagged as a duplicate. If ANY basic condition fails to match, the Case is NOT flagged — regardless of how many other fields match.

entries.title: Weighted conditions — scored match
entries.text: Each weighted condition carries a numeric score. When basic conditions match, the system evaluates weighted conditions and totals the score. Cases with sufficiently high scores are presented as potential duplicates for user review.

entries.title: Resolving a duplicate
entries.text: When the user determines the current Case IS a duplicate, they resolve it with the status 'Resolved-Duplicate'. This closes the duplicate Case and keeps the original.

entries.title: Creating a child Case
entries.text: Child cases

entries.title: Top-level Case vs. Child Case
entries.text: Two Case relationship roles: TOP-LEVEL CASE — has NO parent but CAN become one (e.g., Accident Claim) · CHILD CASE — created within a parent Case (e.g., Vehicle Damage, Medical, Rental Car — each handled by different parties)

entries.title: When to use child Cases
entries.text: Use child Cases when work is performed by DIFFERENT PARTIES, follows DIFFERENT REPORTING OPTIONS, operates on DIFFERENT TIME FRAMES, or is COMMON TO MULTIPLE Case Types (reuse).

entries.title: Create Case Step
entries.text: Add a Create Case Automation Step to the Case Life Cycle to create a child Case. When executed, it creates a child Case of the specified Case Type. Dev Studio provides additional options, including contextual Case creation.

entries.title: Data propagation — Copy vs. Data reference
entries.text: How parent data is shared with child Cases: COPY DATA — snapshots parent data at child creation; child is NOT updated if parent changes later · DATA REFERENCE — child data stays synchronized with the parent; requires advanced configuration in Dev Studio

entries.title: Pausing and resuming Case processing
entries.text: Case workflow dependency

entries.title: Wait Step
entries.text: An automation shape that deliberately pauses Case processing and resumes it when defined conditions are met. Two Wait types: Case Dependency and Timer. Added to a Process in the Case Life Cycle like any other automation Step.

entries.title: Case Dependency — how it works
entries.text: Pauses a PARENT Case until a child Case dependency resolves. Add the Wait Step to the parent; when reached, it pauses until the child reaches the specified status. Requires a hierarchical parent-child Case relationship.

entries.title: Child Case status triggers
entries.text: Two valid triggers: 'To be resolved' or 'Resolved'. Configure whether to check the child's status at the moment the parent reaches the Wait Step, or only track status changes that occur after that point.

entries.title: Cancelling the wait
entries.text: You can allow users to cancel the wait conditions and continue processing the parent Case without waiting for the child to resolve.

entries.title: Timer — two configurations
entries.text: Pauses a Case until a time condition is met. Two options: (1) Set date/time interval — pause for a fixed duration (e.g., 24 hours). (2) Reference date/time — pause until a specific date/time stored in a Case field is reached.

entries.title: Timer use cases
entries.text: Common Wait shape scenarios: Fixed interval: pause 24 hours for photo upload before review · Reference date: pause until end-of-day for fund valuation · Regulatory: pause exactly 72 hours before final review

entries.title: Wait Step vs. User Action Delay
Critical distinction
entries.text: A Wait Step is a DELIBERATELY configured automation that pauses Case processing. A user action delay is when Case processing stalls because a user has not completed an Assignment — NOT a Wait Step. These are completely different concepts.

entries.title: User action delay examples
entries.text: A Case that appears paused because a user hasn't acted on an Assignment or submitted required data. NOT a configured Wait Step — just the natural flow of waiting for human action. Examples: awaiting manager approval, or uploading photos.

entries.title: Creating and setting application variables
entries.text: Configuration Sets

entries.title: Configuration settings
entries.text: A unified, low-code framework for customizing application behavior parameters without Rule overrides. Configuration settings minimize the need for custom Rule changes, making applications easier to maintain, upgrade, and deploy — shortening time-to-market and reducing bugs.

entries.title: Configuration Set
entries.text: A named group of Configuration settings for a specific feature or Case Type, created in App Studio. Rules (classes, Data Pages, properties) are auto-generated in Dev Studio. Name stored as pyLabel of a class Rule (max 64 chars).

entries.title: DSS → Configuration settings (key migration note)
entries.text: In previous Pega Platform releases, Dynamic System Settings (DSS) provided dynamic behavior functionality. Configuration settings REPLACE DSS — they provide enhanced functionality and simpler maintenance.

entries.title: Where to access
entries.text: App Studio → Settings tab → Configurations landing page. Configuration Sets allow runtime customization by users without switching to a design-time environment (App Studio or Dev Studio).

entries.title: Role-based access
entries.text: Three access roles for Configuration Sets and settings: Administrators (PegaRULES:SysAdm4): Read/Write/Delete on both Configuration Sets and settings · Managers (PegaRULES:WorkMgr4): Read/Write/Delete on Sets, Read-only on individual settings · Users (PegaRULES:User4): Read-only on both

entries.title: Deployment
entries.text: Configuration Sets are defined in the Pega-Configuration class structure and included in the deployment file generated by product Rules. Configuration settings are included only when the 'Include associated data' checkbox is selected during product file creation.

entries.title: Condition Builder reference
entries.text: Reference Configuration settings throughout the application using the Condition Builder. The Condition Builder provides a menu to select a Configuration Set, then the specific setting within it. Allows business logic to react dynamically to setting values without hardcoding.

entries.title: Runtime customization example
entries.text: Show additional guidance text to new users via a Configuration setting (value = true). Once experienced, update the setting to false — guidance text is hidden. No Rule change, no redeployment required.

entries.title: Validating data against business logic
entries.text: Data validation

entries.title: Why validate data?
entries.text: Valid data is required for error-free processing. Three requirements: (1) correct TYPE (e.g., number in 'Total units') · (2) restricted to POSSIBLE VALUES (e.g., valid loan type from a list) · (3) meets BUSINESS CONSTRAINTS (e.g., start date in the past)

entries.title: Field Type/control vs. Business logic validation
entries.text: Two layers of data validation: FIELD TYPE/CONTROL — handles FORMAT validation (e.g., a calendar ensures a valid date format) · BUSINESS LOGIC — handles BUSINESS RULE validation (e.g., 'start date cannot be in the past')

entries.title: Validation on a Form vs. Validation on a Stage
Validation on a FORM
entries.text: Triggered when the user submits the form. If invalid, an error displays inline and submission is blocked until corrected. Use when the user CAN immediately fix the issue (e.g., entered a future date → correct it and resubmit).

entries.title: Validation on a STAGE
entries.text: Triggered when the Case enters a Stage. If invalid, entry is blocked. Use when the user CANNOT immediately fix the issue themselves — the developer must configure a resolution path (e.g., return to prior Stage, close Case).

entries.title: Configuring business logic validation in App Studio
entries.text: Configure form and Stage validations in App Studio. Create conditions defining INVALID data values — when met, an error displays and blocks the user from proceeding. Configured in the Case Type Data Model or on the Step/Stage.

entries.title: Validating data in Dev Studio
entries.text: Data validation in Dev Studio

entries.title: App Studio — true/false comparisons only
entries.text: Validation Conditions compare one field against a constant or another field. Example: Income > 10,000? StartDate before EndDate? Anything beyond binary comparison requires Dev Studio.

entries.title: Validate Rule — Case-level, fires on form submit
entries.text: Ensures data meets Case conditions before it advances. Assigned to Flow Actions. In Dev Studio you can extend App Studio-created rules or create new ones in the Process category.

entries.title: Edit Validate Rule — property-level, Java, client-side
entries.text: Compares a property value to a defined pattern using Java code. Example: check whether a value consists of seven numbers with a space between the 3rd and 4th digits. Fires immediately on value change — before form submit.

entries.title: Two ways to apply an Edit Validate Rule
entries.text: Two application points, each with a different trigger: ① Advanced tab of the property rule form → 'Use Validate' field: fires on VALUE CHANGE (client-side) · ② Call it from a Validate Rule: fires on FORM SUBMIT (server-side) — preferred for coordinated validation logic

entries.title: Use Case 1 — Format validation by business logic
entries.text: When input must match a location-specific pattern (postal code, email, phone). Example: US ZIP code must be exactly 5 numerical digits. → Edit Validate Rule called FROM a Validate Rule (not applied directly to the property here).

entries.title: Use Case 2 — Different rules per input value
entries.text: When validation logic depends on user selection. Example: experienced investors can add margin trading (low risk); limited experience = high risk; retirement accounts prohibit margin regardless. Use Validate Rule + Input tab qualification on experience and account type.

entries.title: Use Case 3 — Operations beyond true/false
entries.text: Dev Studio's Validate Rule provides a library of Validation Functions with customized configuration fields. Examples: check if a date falls within the past 4 or 8 weeks; check if a specific attachment category is attached.

entries.title: Input Property — qualify by user-entered value
entries.text: Applies a different validation set per value the user selected. Example: Experience level = 'Extensive' → validate broker license; 'Limited' → validate suitability score.

entries.title: Proposed Work Status — qualify by Case Status
entries.text: Applies different thresholds per Case Status. Example: Pending-Qualification → credit score ≥ 600; Approved → credit score ≥ 725.

entries.title: Flow Action — qualify by the user's action
entries.text: Applies different validation per triggered action. Example: 'Onboard Employee' → start date must be in the future; 'Annual Review' → must be in the past.

entries.title: Stages — qualify by current Stage ★ also in App Studio
entries.text: Applies different validation per Stage. Example: Submission → estimated income OK; Approval → confirmed value required. Only qualifier available in BOTH Dev Studio and App Studio (as Stage-entry Validation).

entries.title: Application data manipulation
entries.text: Data Transforms · Default property values

entries.title: Data Transform — what it does
entries.text: Manipulates data in an application: copy, convert, or drive. It does NOT perform validation or calculation — it moves or transforms data.

entries.title: Copy — move a value
entries.text: Copies a field value into another field. Example: copy customer details from the checkout form into the shipping address fields.

entries.title: Convert — change data type
entries.text: Changes the data type of a value. Example: convert the string 'December 4, 2021' to the date value 12/04/2021. Data Transforms don't just copy — they convert too.

entries.title: Parent-child tip — reference over copy
entries.text: In parent-child Case relationships, REFERENCE data instead of copying it via Data Transform. Referencing keeps the child Case synchronized if data changes in the parent.

entries.title: Method 1 — Run Data Transform Automation
entries.text: Added as an Automation Step in the Case Life Cycle. Runs automatically at runtime — no user interaction required. A new Data Transform can be defined inline (e.g., 'Convert string to date').

entries.title: Method 2 — Pre-processing
entries.text: Configured on a Step's Pre/Post Processing tab. The Data Transform runs BEFORE the Step executes. Use case: populate fields before the form is displayed to the user.

entries.title: Method 3 — Post-processing
entries.text: The Data Transform runs AFTER the Step completes. Use case: clean up or convert data after the user submits a form.

entries.title: Data initialization page — where to find it
entries.text: App Studio → Case Type → Settings tab → Data initialization. This is where you configure default property values assigned when a Case is created.

entries.title: Example use cases
entries.text: ① Pre-populate user's First Name and Last Name from the OperatorID clipboard page. ② Set a date field to today's date. ③ Speed up iterative testing in development by pre-filling required fields.

entries.title: pyDefault and pySetFieldDefaults — when are they created?
