entries.text: Constellation SDKs connect Constellation orchestration to alternative design systems and supported frontend frameworks. They reduce work compared with hand-building every orchestration step, but a custom presentation still needs development, testing and upgrade maintenance.

entries.title: Choose the right mechanism
entries.text: The Constellation DX API is a model-driven REST interface exposing case data and view metadata. It uses OAuth 2.0. Preserve response eTag and send it as If-Match on updates to protect against stale writes. Handle conflicts by refreshing and reconciling; do not bypass concurrency checks.

entries.text: Welcome to the course — Prerequisites section · Before you start · Tricentis Support Hub — License Request · Demo Web Shop (SUT)

entries.title: Overview: What You Need Before Starting
Three Prerequisites
entries.text: To begin the AS1 course, ensure you have all three of the following: Tricentis Tosca On-Premises installed on your machine · A valid Tosca license (request via the Tricentis Support Hub) · Tricentis Automation Extension installed in Google Chrome

entries.title: Windows Only — macOS Limitation
entries.text: Tricentis Tosca On-Premises is a Windows-only application. It does NOT run natively on macOS. macOS users must run Tosca inside a Windows VM · Supported VMs: Parallels Desktop (paid), VMware Fusion (paid), Oracle VirtualBox (free) · The Chrome extension must also be installed inside the VM — not on the macOS host

entries.title: System Under Test (SUT)
entries.text: The course SUT is the Tricentis Demo Web Shop — hosted online, no local server setup required.

entries.title: Tricentis Support Hub
entries.text: Free training licenses are requested at support-hub.tricentis.com. You need a Tricentis account (free registration) to submit a ticket.

entries.title: Tosca keeps showing a license pop-up on launch?
entries.text: This usually means Tosca Commander isn't connected to a valid license source. If your organization uses a Cloud License Server (instead of, or in addition to, a local .lic file), connect Tosca directly to it.

entries.title: Step 3: Install the Tricentis Automation Extension
What It Does
entries.text: The Tricentis Automation Extension is a Chrome browser plugin that enables XScan to inspect and interact with web application elements. Without it, web automation is not possible.

entries.title: Certificate vs Badges: What is the difference?
entries.text: The Tricentis Academy offers a robust certification program recognising users' skillsets, capabilities, and project readiness. This program provides curated learning journeys intended to enable partners to build competence within specific testing roles. Each path is designed with self-paced online learning, consisting of carefully chosen courses covering skills necessary for success in each role.

entries.title: Section 1 - Getting started
entries.text: Welcome to the course · Lesson 01 - Introduction to Tosca · Lesson 02 - Navigate Tosca · Lesson 03 - Tosca Workspace Best Practices · Lesson 04 - Introduction to the SUT · Knowledge check

entries.title: Tricentis Tosca
entries.text: A Model-Based Test Automation platform that enables codeless end-to-end testing by scanning the SUT to generate reusable test models.

entries.title: Tosca Commander
entries.text: The central IDE of Tricentis Tosca. Contains 9 sections in total; this course focuses on four core sections: Modules — UI element models captured from the SUT · TestCases — ordered sequences of test steps · ExecutionLists — collections of TestCases to run · Requirements — business/technical requirements linked to tests

entries.title: System Under Test (SUT)
entries.text: The application being tested. In this course the SUT is the Tricentis Demo Web Shop at https://demowebshop.tricentis.com.

entries.title: Single-User Access Rule
entries.text: Access is granted to whoever has the local workspace file. No administrator role is required — only local file access matters.

entries.title: Multi-User Check-out / Check-in
entries.text: In a Multi-User workspace, objects must be checked out before editing. This locks them for other users until the editor checks them back in. Check Out — marks the object as in-use; locked (read-only) for all other users · Check In — saves edits to the shared repository and releases the lock

entries.title: Subset
entries.text: A file containing Tosca artifacts (Modules, TestCases, etc.) that can be exported from one workspace and imported into another — the primary mechanism for sharing test assets between projects.

entries.title: Tricentis Standard Subset
entries.text: A subset provided by Tricentis containing pre-built Standard Modules, predefined virtual folders, and standard reports. Import it into any workspace to use ready-made assets immediately — no SUT scanning required for these modules.

entries.title: 4-Eye Principle
entries.text: A quality-control workflow ensuring a second reviewer validates all work before it is finalized. In Work — tester is actively building/modifying the artifact · Ready for Approval — tester signals the work is complete and ready for review · Approved/Completed — reviewer confirms and closes the item

entries.title: Component Folder Structure
entries.text: Tricentis recommends three types of top-level Component folders in every repository: Templates and references — reusable naming templates and sample structures shared across all projects · Relevant for all projects — shared Libraries and Standard Modules used by every project · Per-project folder — one per project, containing: Requirements, TestCaseDesign, TestCases, Execution, and Module sub-sections

entries.title: Naming Conventions
entries.text: Apply consistent, descriptive names across all folders, modules, and test cases. Practical rule: choose the name first, then add a more granular description — not the other way around.

entries.title: Tricentis Automation Extension
entries.text: A Chrome browser extension required for Tosca to scan and interact with web applications. Must be installed and enabled before any web-based scanning or automation.

entries.title: SUT Navigation
entries.text: Before automating, manually explore the SUT to understand user flows and identify which elements need to be scanned. This step prevents coverage gaps.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 02 — Navigate the System Under Test (SUT)
Section 2 - Modules
entries.text: Lesson 05 - Introduction to Tricentis Model-Based Test Automation · Lesson 06 - Standard Modules in Tricentis Tosca · Lesson 07 - Introduction to XScan · Lesson 08 - Scan your SUT with XScan · Lesson 09 - Identify Controls by Properties in XScan · Lesson 10 - Identify Controls by Anchor in XScan

entries.title: Model-Based Test Automation
entries.text: A testing technique in which Models capture the technical information and expected behavior of the SUT. Business data is fed into these models to steer and test the system — no coding required.

entries.title: Advantages of MBTA
entries.text: Three key reasons to choose MBTA over scripted automation: Save effort — models are created by scanning the SUT, not written by hand · Readability — end-to-end tests are easy to read due to descriptive module and step names · Reduced maintenance — models are reusable; update once and all referencing TestCases benefit

entries.title: Module
entries.text: A representation of a SUT section (page, form, or panel) that Tosca can interact with. Contains one or more Controls, each mapping to an individual UI element.

entries.title: Control
entries.text: A single UI element within a Module — such as a button, input field, or dropdown. Each Control has identifying properties Tosca uses to locate it on the SUT.

entries.title: Module Attributes
entries.text: Properties describing the module itself: its name, the technology it targets (HTML, WPF, SAP GUI), and the Controls it contains.

entries.title: Steer
entries.text: When Tosca executes a TestCase, it 'steers' the Controls in the SUT — meaning it interacts with them exactly as a user would: clicking buttons, entering text, selecting from dropdowns. Steering is the act of automated interaction with a Control.

entries.title: Standard Modules
entries.text: Pre-built modules provided by Tricentis for common execution tasks — keyboard input, wait commands, file handling — that operate independently of the SUT.

entries.title: Tricentis Standard Subset
entries.text: The package distributed by Tricentis that contains Standard Modules. Import it into any workspace to immediately access utility modules without scanning.

entries.title: XScan
entries.text: Tosca's built-in scanning tool that inspects web application elements through the browser and captures their technical properties to create Modules.

entries.title: Launching XScan
entries.text: XScan is launched from Tosca Commander. The standard method taught in AS1: right-click a Module folder in the Modules section and select Scan >> Application. XScan opens alongside the browser ready to inspect the SUT.

entries.title: Module Naming Convention
entries.text: Within XScan, rename the Module using the pipe character as a separator: Application | Page. Example: 'WebShop | Log In Page'. This ensures consistent, readable Module names across the workspace.

entries.title: Wildcard (*) in Technical Properties
entries.text: In XScan Technical Properties, the Title field accepts the wildcard character *. Setting Title to 'Demo Web Shop*' tells Tosca to match any window whose title begins with 'Demo Web Shop' — ensuring the Module works correctly across multiple SUT pages (e.g., Demo Web Shop, Demo Web Shop. Books).

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 03 — Create Your First Module
The 5 XScan Identification Methods
entries.text: XScan provides 5 ways to identify a control. Properties is the default; the other 4 handle scenarios where properties alone are insufficient: Properties (default) — uses stable HTML attributes (ID, name, class) to directly match the control · Parent — uses the parent container element to scope the search; useful when a control's own properties are shared by multiple elements on the page · Anchor — uses a stable nearby element as a reference point; ideal for dynamic controls · Image — identifies the control by a visual screenshot match of its appearance · Index — identifies the control by its ordinal position within its parent container

entries.title: Anchor: Shortest Path vs. Coordinate
entries.text: When using Identify by Anchor, Tosca locates the target control via one of two strategies: Shortest Path — searches each DOM tree level for the target, starting from the anchor, going bottom to top up to the root element. Resolution-independent and robust. · Coordinate — finds the target by its exact on-screen coordinates relative to the anchor. Highly resolution-dependent — breaks if screen resolution changes.

entries.title: ControlGroup
entries.text: A named grouping of related Controls within a Module. ControlGroups organize logically related UI elements (e.g., all category navigation links) under one named group, making TestCases easier to build and maintain.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 04 — Identify by Anchor and Create ControlGroup
Section 3 - TestCases
entries.text: Lesson 11 - Introduction to TestCases · Lesson 12 - Create TestSteps · Lesson 13 - Populate your TestCase · Lesson 14 - Test Configuration Parameters · Lesson 15 - ActionModes · Lesson 16 - Run a Test · Lesson 17 - ActionMode Buffer · Lesson 18 - Dynamic Values · Lesson 19 - Libraries · Lesson 20 - Use the Libraries

entries.title: TestCase
entries.text: An ordered sequence of TestSteps that defines a complete test scenario. Stored in the TestCases section; references Modules for its steps.

entries.title: TestStep
entries.text: A single action or verification within a TestCase, created by referencing a Module or a specific Control. Each TestStep represents one interaction with the SUT.

entries.title: TestCaseFolder
entries.text: A container for organizing TestCases in a hierarchy. Can be nested. Best practice: organize by feature or business process. Inside a TestCase, TestSteps are further grouped using TestStepFolders (e.g., Precondition, Process, Postcondition).

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 06 — Open and Close the Application
Test Configuration Parameter (TCP)
entries.text: A reusable value defined at TestCase or folder level, referenced across multiple TestSteps. Centralizes test data so changes are made in one place.

entries.title: TCP Syntax (confirmed exam question)
entries.text: To reference a TCP in a TestStep value field, use exactly: {CP[NameOfTheTCP]} Outer curly braces { } are mandatory · CP prefix in square brackets [ ] is mandatory · Parameter name goes inside the square brackets

entries.title: Column Customization
entries.text: Right-click the header row in the TestCase view → select 'Column Chooser' → double-click a column to add it to the view.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 09 — Set Predefined Test Configuration Parameters
Hands-On: Exercise 11 — Set ActionMode Verify & Run Your TestCase
ModuleAttribute
entries.text: A representation of a Control (button, text field, label, etc.) selected during scanning. When a Module is dragged into a TestCase, each ModuleAttribute becomes a TestStepValue.

entries.title: TestStepValue
entries.text: The combination of an ActionMode, a Value, and a DataType for a specific Control inside a TestStep. Tells Tosca exactly what to do with that Control during execution.

entries.title: DataType
entries.text: Specifies the type of value being entered. The 5 DataTypes are: String, Date, Numeric, Boolean, Password. String — default; plain text · Numeric — use for numbers so that 10 and 10.00 are treated as equal · Date — use for date values · Boolean — use for True/False values · Password — masks the value; use for credentials

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 08 — Enter TestStepValues in Tosca
ScratchBook
entries.text: A built-in Tosca capability for trial runs of TestSteps and TestCases before final execution. Results are temporary and overwritten with each new ScratchBook run.

entries.title: Dynamic Values
entries.text: Expressions evaluated at runtime to generate values dynamically — current date, random text, calculated numbers. Written inside curly braces using Tosca's expression language. Syntax: {COMMAND[parameter1][parameter2]...}

entries.title: Buffer Syntax
entries.text: To recall a previously buffered value, use: {B[BufferName]} {B[PriceBlueJeans]} — recalls the value stored under that buffer name · Buffer name must match exactly (case-sensitive) the name given when the Buffer was set · XBuffer for dynamic parts: {XB[BufferName]} — reads and buffers only the dynamic portion of a string

entries.title: MATH Functions
entries.text: Perform calculations using static values or Buffer references. Syntax: {MATH[expression]} {MATH[{B[PriceBlueJeans]}*25]} — multiplies buffered price by 25 · {MATH[{B[SubTotal]}+10.00]} — adds 10.00 to the SubTotal buffer · Operators supported: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) · Tip: right-click Value field → 'Translate value' to test a MATH expression before running

entries.title: Random Values
entries.text: Generate unique random values at runtime to avoid test data collisions. {RND[7]} — 7-digit random integer (max 18 digits) · {RND[100][999]} — random integer between 100 and 999 · {RANDOMTEXT[10]} — random 10-character string (letters and numbers, max 1024) · {RANDOMREGEX["^[A-Z][a-z]+[0-9]{4}$"]} — random string matching a regex pattern

entries.title: Date / Time Expressions
entries.text: Structure: {FUNCTION[start][offset][format]} FUNCTION: DATE, TIME, DATETIME, DAY, MONTH, YEAR, MONTHFIRST, MONTHLAST · [start]: leave empty [ ] to use today's date as the reference · [offset]: d=days, w=weeks, M=months, y=years, h=hours, m=minutes, s=seconds — e.g. [-3y] = 3 years ago, [+4M] = 4 months ahead · [format]: MM=2-digit month, yyyy=4-digit year, dd=2-digit day, MMM=3-letter month abbreviation · Confirmed exam example: {MONTHLAST[][-3y][MMMyyyy]} = last day of month, 3 years ago, in format Jun2022 · Exercise 15 example: {DATE[][+4M][MM]} = expiration month +4 months as 2-digit; {DATE[][+3y][yyyy]} = expiration year +3 years as 4-digit

entries.title: Library
entries.text: A folder in the TestCases section containing reusable TestCase sequences. Other TestCases reference Library entries instead of duplicating steps.

entries.title: Reusable TestStepBlock (RTSB)
entries.text: An individual TestStep sequence stored inside a Library. Can be dragged from the Library into any TestCase.

entries.title: Reusable TestStepBlock Reference
entries.text: When an RTSB is dropped into a TestCase, it appears as a Reference with '_Reference' appended to its name (e.g., 'Precondition_Reference'). It remains linked to the Library — any change in the Library propagates to all TestCases using that reference. Drag RTSB from the Library folder, drop into the TestCase or TestStepFolder. · The dropped block is named [OriginalName]_Reference. · All TestCases using the same RTSB are updated simultaneously when the Library block changes. · Use this when you want a single source of truth (e.g., a shared Login flow).

entries.title: Resolve the Reference
entries.text: Replaces a Library reference inside a TestCase with an inline copy of the Library's steps — making the TestCase self-contained with no external dependencies. Right-click the RTSB Reference → 'Resolve Reference'. · Icon changes after resolving — the block is no longer linked to the Library. · After resolving, changes to the Library NO LONGER affect this TestCase. · Can be undone with Ctrl+Z ONLY before saving. After saving, the resolve is permanent. · Use when a specific TestCase needs a different version of the standard flow.

entries.title: Use the Libraries — Working with RTSB References
Hands-On: Exercise 17 — Create a TestCase from a Library
Section 4 - Advanced Module Actions
entries.text: Lesson 21 - Advanced Module Actions

entries.title: Rescan
entries.text: Re-scans an existing Module's Controls against the live SUT to update their technical properties — without deleting or recreating the Module.

entries.title: Value Range
entries.text: A property set on a Control within a Module that defines the list of acceptable values for that Control. Acts as a validation layer at the Module level.

entries.title: Value Range Syntax (confirmed exercise detail)
entries.text: When entering multiple values into a Value Range, separate them with semicolons and use NO spaces between values. Correct: AutomationDiscount2;PercentageTotal;PercentageShipping;FlatTotal · Wrong: AutomationDiscount2, PercentageTotal (commas + spaces) · Wrong: AutomationDiscount2; PercentageTotal (spaces after semicolons) · Separator = semicolon ( ; ) only. Spaces would be treated as part of the value.

entries.title: Module Merge
entries.text: Combines two separate Modules that represent the same SUT element into one authoritative Module. After merging, all TestSteps referencing either original module are updated automatically.

entries.title: Target Module vs. Source Module (key exam concept)
entries.text: In a merge, one Module is the Target and the other is the Source. Target Module = the one you KEEP. It survives the merge. · Source Module = the one that gets DELETED after its selected Attributes are copied into the Target. · If the wrong Module is set as Target, use the 'Switch Modules' option to swap them. · You choose which Attributes to bring from the Source into the Target. · Tosca automatically links Attributes that have identical properties in both Modules.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 18 — Apply Rescan, Value Range and Module Merge
Section 5 - Advanced TestCase Parameters
entries.text: Lesson 22 - Self-Defined Test Configuration Parameters · Lesson 23 - Business Parameters

entries.title: Self-Defined Test Configuration Parameter (TCP)
entries.text: A custom parameter defined by the tester at the TestCase or TestFolder level. Stores a reusable value referenced across multiple TestSteps using {CP[ParameterName]}.

entries.title: TCP Scope
entries.text: Where you define a TCP determines how widely it is accessible: TestFolder level — inherited by ALL TestCases within that folder · TestCase level — available to THAT TestCase only · Best practice: define at the highest appropriate level to maximize reuse

entries.title: TCP Syntax (confirmed exam question)
entries.text: Reference a TCP in a TestStep value field using exactly: {CP[NameOfTheTCP]} Outer curly braces { } — mandatory · CP in square brackets [ ] — mandatory prefix · Parameter name in square brackets — e.g., {CP[BaseURL]}

entries.title: Self-Defined TCP example (Exercise 19)
entries.text: Three TCPs defined on the TestCase, then referenced in TestSteps: Browser = Chrome — sets the browser for the run · DiscountName = AutomationDiscount2 — referenced as {CP[DiscountName]} in the 'Enter discount code' Input step · DiscountPercentage = 0.20 — referenced inside a MATH formula: {MATH[({B[SubTotal]}+10)*{CP[DiscountPercentage]}]} · TCPs combine freely with Buffers and MATH inside the same expression

entries.title: Wildcards
entries.text: A stand-in character for other characters, used to simplify a search or a data match. The asterisk * matches any sequence of characters. Example: Discount* matches 'Discount', 'Discount:', 'Discount Amount', etc. · Useful when a Control's exact label varies or contains extra characters. · Exercise 19 tip: if the 'Discount' option is missing from a dropdown, manually add a column and use the wildcard Discount* to match it.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 19 — Set Self-Defined Test Configuration Parameters
Business Parameters
entries.text: Parameters created on a Reusable TestStepBlock (RTSB) in a Library. They let you change the VALUES used by an RTSB Reference in a specific TestCase WITHOUT modifying the RTSB in the Library. They are the business-relevant elements of your TestSteps whose values you want to steer per TestCase.

entries.title: {PL} Parameter Link Syntax (confirmed exercise detail)
entries.text: Dragging a Business Parameter onto a TestStepValue field creates a Parameter Link: {PL[ParameterName]} PL = Parameter Link — connects the TestStepValue to the Business Parameter. · {PL[URL]}, {PL[Email]}, {PL[Password]} — the value is supplied at the RTSB Reference level in each TestCase. · Do NOT confuse with {CP[...]} (Test Configuration Parameter) — different prefix, different purpose.

entries.title: Section 6 - ExecutionLists
entries.text: Lesson 24 - ExecutionLists

entries.title: ExecutionList
entries.text: A structured list in the Execution section of Tosca Commander that runs TestCases and stores their results. Its key job is to execute TestCases AND keep a permanent record of every result.

entries.title: Execution hierarchy (ExecutionFolder → ExecutionList → ExecutionEntry)
entries.text: The Execution section is organized in three levels: ExecutionFolder — a container that groups ExecutionLists (e.g., 'Exercise 21 - Create an ExecutionList'). · ExecutionList — the actual runnable list (e.g., 'Web Shop'). This is what you Run. · ExecutionEntry — a single TestCase placed inside an ExecutionList. Dragging a TestCase in creates an ExecutionEntry. · ActualLog — the result record created inside the ExecutionList after a run, timestamped (e.g., 'created: 8/11/2021 11:28 AM').

entries.title: ExecutionList vs. ScratchBook — results persistence (confirmed exam point)
entries.text: The defining difference is what happens to the results: ExecutionList — stores ALL historic results permanently (via the ActualLog). You can consult past runs any time. · ScratchBook — results are TEMPORARY. Each new run overwrites the previous one; nothing is kept. · Use the ScratchBook for quick trial/debug runs; use an ExecutionList for formal, recorded execution.

entries.title: TestCase reuse (confirmed exam question)
entries.text: The same TestCase can be added to an ExecutionList an UNLIMITED number of times. Each entry runs independently — enabling the same test to run with different data sets or configurations.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 21 — Create and Execute ExecutionLists
Section 7 - Requirements
entries.text: Lesson 25 - Requirements · Lesson 26 - Weight Requirements · Lesson 27 - Link Requirements · Knowledge Check

entries.title: Requirements
entries.text: Criteria the system under test (SUT) is expected to fulfill. They map business requirements to checks that confirm the application works properly. Functional requirement — a functionality the SUT must carry out (e.g., 'the web shop must be able to process payments'). · Non-functional requirement — a quality/operational attribute rather than a specific behavior (e.g., security, reliability, performance, maintainability, scalability, usability).

entries.title: Requirement Weight
entries.text: A calculated risk score (integer 1–10) representing the priority and risk of a Requirement. Derived automatically by Tosca — not manually entered. Input 1: Frequency Class — how often the failure occurs if the requirement is unmet · Input 2: Damage Class — the severity of the impact if the requirement fails · Formula: exponential function of (Frequency Class, Damage Class) · Output: integer from 1 (lowest risk) to 10 (highest risk)

entries.title: Linking TestCases and ExecutionLists to Requirements
Linking TestCases
entries.text: Drag a COMPLETED TestCase onto an individual Requirement to create a link. This provides traceability: which tests cover which requirements. Link at the Requirement (atomic, bottom) level.

entries.title: Linking ExecutionLists
entries.text: Drag an ExecutionList onto a RequirementSet to associate its execution results with that set of requirements — enabling execution/coverage reporting across the whole set.

entries.title: Update Outdated Values
entries.text: After linking TestCases and ExecutionLists, right-click the RequirementSet and select 'Update Outdated Values' to refresh the calculated coverage and execution status. Without this, displayed values may be stale. Right-click the RequirementSet (e.g., 'Webshop Frontend') → 'Update Outdated Values'. · Recalculates coverage and pulls in the latest execution results from linked ExecutionLists. · Run it whenever links change or new results come in.

entries.title: Test Coverage
entries.text: Once TestCases are linked, Tosca shows requirement coverage — which requirements have linked tests (covered) and which do not (unverified).

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 22 — Link TestCases and ExecutionLists to Requirements
Section 8 - Additional Advanced Topics
entries.text: Lesson 28 - Working in the Multiuser Environment · Lesson 29 - WHILE, IF & DO Statements · Lesson 30 - Recovery Scenarios · Lesson 31 - CleanUp Scenarios · Lesson 32 - Dynamic Comparison · Lesson 33 - Parent Control · Lesson 34 - Dynamic ID · Lesson 35 - ExplicitName · Lesson 36 - TBox Set Buffer · Lesson 37 - ResultCount (RowCount & ColumnCount) · Lesson 38 - Repetition on Folder Level & ExplicitName on TestStepValue · Lesson 39 - ActionMode Constraint

entries.title: Multiuser Environment
entries.text: Multiple testers work against a shared Tosca repository. To prevent conflicts, objects are checked out/locked while one person edits them. A colored bar next to an object shows its lock status. A red bar next to an object = it is locked/checked out (not editable by you right now). · You CANNOT make any changes to a locked object. · If the locked object is a Module, you can STILL add/reference it in your own TestCases — using it does not require editing it. · A red bar does NOT mean 'no one is working on it' — the opposite: it is locked because someone holds it.

entries.title: Structure: Condition + Loop
entries.text: A WHILE/DO statement has two parts you fill in: a Condition and a Loop (Exercise 23). Condition — a Verify-type check that confirms a state (Exists==True, Visible==True, has a value, etc.). · Loop — the TestSteps Tosca repeats; it keeps running until the Condition is no longer met OR the max repetitions is reached. · Tip: use the Control Flow Diagram to see a visual representation of the statement.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 23 — Create a WHILE Statement
Key facts (Exercises 24 & 25)
entries.text: Details that show up on the exam: Recovery & CleanUp Scenarios do NOT work in the ScratchBook — only in the TestCase Section / TestCase / TestStep / TestStepValue level, or in a Reusable TestStepBlock. · Both are always contained within a Recovery Scenario Collection. · Recovery Scenario has a RetryLevel property (e.g., set to 'TestCase'). · Recovery settings live in Settings >> TBox >> Recovery (On dialog failure / On exception failure / On verification failure → set to 'Recover'). · A CleanUp Scenario can be set at the same levels as Recovery and does NOT require a Recovery Scenario to be present.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 24 — Create a Recovery Scenario
Hands-On: Exercise 25 — Create a CleanUp Scenario
Dynamic Comparison (XBuffer), Parent Control & Dynamic ID
Dynamic Comparison — XBuffer {XB}
entries.text: A way to verify a string that contains a DYNAMIC part. {XB} excludes the dynamic portion from the comparison and (optionally) buffers that portion for reuse. Use it for messages with auto-generated numbers, timestamps, etc. that change every run. Syntax: verify 'Order number: {XB[OrderNumber]}' with ActionMode Verify. · The static text ('Order number: ') is checked; the dynamic part is excluded from the match. · The excluded/dynamic value is stored in the buffer named inside the brackets (here: OrderNumber). · You can then reuse {B[OrderNumber]} later for verifications or to steer the app. · Tip: use the blue downward arrow in the Value cell to insert correct XBuffer syntax; set ActionMode to Verify when recording XBuffers.

entries.title: Parent Control (Identify by Parent)
entries.text: Identifies a UI element relative to its stable parent container. Used when scanning pages with REPEATING elements (e.g., a list of orders) where a child (order number, total, Details button) is not unique on its own but becomes identifiable once its parent DIV is specified. During XScan, select the parent DIV first, then the child controls within it. · Deselect unstable properties (e.g., InnerText) and use stable ones (e.g., OuterText = 'Order Number:*'). · Wildcards (*) handle the varying part of the text.

entries.title: Dynamic ID
entries.text: Handles elements whose ID attribute is generated at runtime (e.g., 'btn_7823', 'btn_4910'). Created via XScan using an identification method other than the literal ID — a pattern/partial match or identification by parent.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 27 — Identify by Parent and Create Dynamic ID Modules
ExplicitName, TBox Set Buffer, ResultCount & RowCount
ExplicitName
entries.text: A Configuration Parameter (named 'ExplicitName', Value = True) added to a ModuleAttribute. It lets Tosca steer the generated TestStepValues by INDEX and handle dynamic changes — so you can rename a TestStepValue (e.g., to '#1') and steer the repeating/dynamic control by its position. Added in the Module Attribute's Properties tab as Configuration Parameter ExplicitName = True. · Then in the TestCase you can rename the generated TestStepValue (e.g., 'Order Overview' → '#1'). · Steer by index handles dynamic repeating elements (works together with Parent Control / Dynamic ID).

entries.title: TBox Set Buffer
entries.text: A Standard Module that sets/resets a named buffer's value. Use it to initialize a buffer, store a timestamp, or perform a calculation and store the result. Add the Module as a TestStep, rename the TestStepValue '<Buffername>' to your buffer name, enter the value, ActionMode Input. Example: rename '<Buffername>' to 'NumberOfItems', value 3, ActionMode Input. · Can hold a MATH result: value {MATH[{B[CartItems]}-1]} to store a calculated number.

entries.title: ResultCount
entries.text: Counts the occurrences of a particular value in a table/list, independent of its position. Used in a Verify to assert how many matching items exist. Syntax in the Value cell: ResultCount=={B[NumberOfItems]} with ActionMode Verify. Example: verify a Digital Downloads list has the expected number of items: Item ResultCount=={B[NumberOfItems]} (Verify). · Can also buffer the count: ResultCount->CartItems with ActionMode Buffer, to reuse the number elsewhere.

entries.title: RowCount & ColumnCount
entries.text: Functions that count the TOTAL number of rows / columns containing data in a table — INCLUDING the header row/column. Used to steer through a whole table or capture its size. Syntax: in the table's value column, enter RowCount==RowNum (RowNum = buffer name), ActionMode Buffer. · The result INCLUDES the header — a 4-data-row table buffers RowNum = 5 (4 rows + 1 header). · ColumnCount works identically for columns. · Common pattern: buffer RowCount, then subtract the header with {MATH[{B[CartItems]}-1]} to get the real data-row count.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 29 — Use TBox Set Buffer and ResultCount
Repetition on Folder Level & ActionMode Constraint
Repetition on Folder Level
entries.text: Repeats the TestSteps inside a TestStepFolder a specified number of times, set in the FOLDER's Properties (Attribute 'Repetition'). The count can be static or a buffer (dynamic). This is how you repeat TestSteps in a TestCase — an alternative to a WHILE statement. Set on a TestStepFolder → Properties → Attribute 'Repetition'. · Value can be a buffer, e.g., {B[ActualCartNumber]}, to repeat a dynamic number of times. · Inside the loop, use the variable ${Repetition} (e.g., rename a table's <Row> to ${Repetition}) so each iteration acts on the next row. · Example: empty a shopping cart by repeating the 'remove row' steps once per item — without a WHILE statement.

entries.title: ActionMode Constraint
entries.text: Limits (constrains) the search within a table/list to identify ONE specific item, regardless of where it sits in the table. You set constraining values on one or more cells; Tosca finds the matching row, then acts on it (e.g., select its Remove checkbox). Set ActionMode Constraint on the cell(s) that uniquely identify the target row. · Example (Exercise 31): Product(s)='Music 2' (Constraint) + Price='*10.00*' (Constraint) → finds that exact row. · A combination of constraining cell values narrows down to the single intended item. · After the row is identified, another cell/action (e.g., Remove checkbox = True, Input) operates on it.

entries.title: The Big Picture — How Tosca Sections Connect (Mindmap)
The five Tosca Commander sections
entries.text: Each section owns one job; together they form the automation workflow. Modules — the technical map of the SUT, collected via XScan. To steer a control it must be uniquely identifiable (properties, anchor, parent). · TestCases — a sequence of actions (the path through the application) built from Modules. · Execution — runs TestCases/folders; organize with ExecutionLists; drag a TestCase onto an ExecutionList to create an ExecutionEntry; add Recovery Scenarios to keep runs going. · Requirements — plan test processes and monitor risk coverage (functional & non-functional); TestCases link here. · TestCaseDesign — NOT covered in AS1 (centralized test data; see the AS2 course).

entries.title: Syntax Cheat Sheet — Text Expressions & Random Values
General syntax
entries.text: All Tosca expressions follow: {COMMAND[Parameter1][Parameter2]...} — curly braces outside, square brackets for each parameter.

entries.title: Structure
entries.text: {EXPRESSION[BASEDATE][OFFSET][FORMAT]} — all variables are CASE SENSITIVE. Leave [BASEDATE] empty [] to use today's date. · Offset units: d=days, w=weeks, M=months (capital!), y=years, h=hours (1-12), H=hours (0-23), m=minutes, s=seconds. · Format codes: %d=1-digit day, dd=2-digit day, %M=1-digit month, MM=2-digit month, MMM=3-letter month, MMMM=full month name, yy=2-digit year, yyyy=4-digit year. · Basedate default formats: Date = dd.MM.yyyy, Time = hh:mm tt, DateTime = dd-MM-yyyy hh:mm tt.

entries.title: RowCount / ColumnCount
entries.text: Functions that count the TOTAL rows / columns containing data in a table — INCLUDING the header row/column. Syntax in the table's value cell: RowCount==RowNum (RowNum = buffer name), ActionMode Buffer. · Result INCLUDES the header: a table with 4 data rows buffers RowNum = 5. · ColumnCount works identically for columns. · For data rows only, subtract the header: {MATH[{B[RowNum]}-1]}.

entries.title: Reusable TestStepBlock (RTSB) Reference
entries.text: When you reuse a Library RTSB in a TestCase, it appears as a Reference and stays LINKED — any change in the Library propagates to every TestCase that uses it.

entries.title: Resolve the Reference
entries.text: Unlinks a specific referenced block from the Library so you can customize it in that one TestCase without affecting the others. Right-click the referenced TestStepBlock -> 'Resolve Reference' (the icon changes). · After resolving, Library changes NO LONGER affect this block. · Revert with Ctrl+Z / Undo ONLY before saving — after saving it is permanent.

entries.title: What Makes a Good TestCase — Best-Practice Job Aid
TestCase
entries.text: A good TestCase is complete, readable, and self-contained. Contains MULTIPLE TestSteps — an entire sequence through the application, rarely just one. · Marked with a WorkState: Planned, In Work, or Completed. · Once Completed, link it immediately to its Requirement AND its ExecutionList. · Contains NO IF statements; use Loops and Conditions only when necessary.

entries.title: TestStep Folders
entries.text: Organize TestSteps into clearly named folders. Recommended structure: Precondition, several Process folders, Postcondition. · Every TestCase should include a verification.

entries.title: Modules
entries.text: Reusable technical building blocks. A single Module creates multiple TestSteps and can be reused any number of times. · A Module contains MULTIPLE controls (never just one) — all controls needed to steer one page. · Identify controls using the most STABLE methods available.

entries.title: How to use this
entries.text: Match the on-screen error text to the table, read the likely cause, apply the fix. Grouped by theme for fast lookup.

entries.title: Tosca keeps showing a license pop-up on launch?
entries.text: This usually means Tosca Commander isn't connected to a valid license source. If your organization uses a Cloud License Server, connect Tosca directly to it: access the license configuration, go to the Setup tab, select Change connection, choose Connect to Cloud hosted License Server, then sign in with your Tricentis Support Hub credentials (enable Use default proxy if your organization requires a proxy).

entries.title: Section 1 - TestSheet Creation
entries.text: Lesson video 01 - TestSheet Creation · Lesson 01 - See and Try

entries.title: Scenario: Testing the Shirt Size Selector
TestSheet
entries.text: The basic framework of TestCase-Design. A TestSheet is a central, structured repository of test data — Attributes and Instances — that specifies every combination you need to test. Think of it as a high-level guide through one slice of your SUT. Double-click the TestSheet symbol in the Navigation pane to view its contents.

entries.title: Attributes
entries.text: Express a feature of a person or thing (e.g. a laptop's Attributes might be design or price; a person's might be hair color or height). Represented by a red square icon. An Attribute also acts as an organizational element for its child/sub-attributes.

entries.title: Instances
entries.text: The different variants of an Attribute (e.g. hair color Instances could be blond, brown, black). Represented by a flat white box with a capital "I". Instances have two roles: at the TestSheet level they represent individual TestCases; under an Attribute, they represent that Attribute's specific variant.

entries.title: ValidValues / StraightThrough
entries.text: The leftmost column of a TestSheet is called "ValidValues" — the most important, most frequently used, or easiest path with the least dependencies (similar to the "Happy Path" concept). In Tosca terminology this column is the StraightThrough.

entries.text: Lesson 02 - Templates

entries.title: Template
entries.text: Designed to contain all possible paths of a linked TestSheet. When the Template is modified to reflect a SUT change, those modifications automatically feed through to every TestCase generated from it — centralizing maintenance and making full risk coverage far more time-efficient.

Check Template
entries.text: Right-click the Template → Check Template to validate that all XL references actually resolve to something in the TestSheet. Important: this ONLY checks that the links exist — it does NOT check for functionality errors in TestSteps or formulas. The function highlights the TestStepValue containing the broken link, not the XL reference text itself.

entries.title: Scenario: A New SUT Feature to Verify
Verification Attribute
entries.text: A new type of Attribute — shown in green — that is NOT an input to the SUT. Instead, it holds a value Tosca compares against the SUT's actual output. If the two values match once entered into the TestCase, the verification succeeds; otherwise it fails.

entries.text: Lesson 05 - Conditions

entries.text: A RequirementSet is a hollow/outline orange triangle — a container that groups related Requirements (e.g. "WebShop Frontend"). Objective

entries.text: Welcome to the Course (API Deep Dive) · Introduction to Automating API test cases (video)

entries.title: Prerequisites for this course
entries.text: A basic understanding of APIs; completion of "Tricentis Tosca Fundamentals - Automating web application testing" (AS1); and access to, plus a valid license for, Tricentis Tosca. Basic understanding of APIs · Tricentis Tosca Fundamentals - Automating web application testing (AS1) · Access to and a valid license for Tricentis Tosca

entries.title: The API Scan is standalone
entries.text: The API Scan is also a standalone program (ApiScanStandalone.exe). No Tosca license is needed and no Tosca installation or testing knowledge is required to operate the API Scan by itself. This makes it easy to involve developers in the testing process: send them the .exe file, they scan the API, save the resulting messages, and send them back as a subset that can be manipulated and tested — without installing or activating the full Tosca package.

entries.title: Tosca keeps showing a license pop-up on launch?
entries.text: This usually means Tosca Commander isn't connected to a valid license source. Since every exercise in this course exports API Scan results into Tosca Commander, a working license connection is required even though the API Scan itself needs none. If your organization uses a Cloud License Server, connect Tosca directly to it.

entries.title: API
entries.text: Application Programming Interface — an interface created with the application in mind rather than the user. Where a UI is designed to be human-readable, an API is machine-readable: it speaks the language of the software directly.

entries.title: Getting Started - API & Webservice Theory
entries.text: Automation Specialist for API Theory Lesson (video) · Service Access Key generator

entries.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
entries.text: The messenger program used to interact with an application. Unlike a UI, which is designed to be human-readable, an API is machine-readable — it speaks the language of the software directly.

entries.title: Webservice
entries.text: A service offered by one electronic device to enable communication with other electronic devices via the World Wide Web. When a social media platform shows a map or an ad without writing that code itself, it has outsourced the job to a Webservice via an API request.

entries.title: SOAP vs. REST and HTTP Methods
SOAP and REST
entries.text: The two main Webservice implementation methods covered in this course. Both use the same underlying protocol, HTTP, but leverage it differently and support different message formats.

entries.title: XML (Extensible Markup Language)
entries.text: A markup language, much like HTML, that defines a set of rules for encoding documents in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable. XML is self-descriptive and designed to store and transport data, and it simplifies data sharing and platform changes.

entries.title: The Systems Under Test (SUTs) for This Course
Two SUTs, one per Webservice method
entries.text: This course needs two Systems Under Test — one for each Webservice implementation method being tested.

entries.title: Service Access Key
entries.text: A token required to authenticate against the Coffeeshop REST service, generated at http://webservice.toscacloud.com/training. The key creates a temporary (24-hour) profile pre-loaded with basic data that you can freely add to and edit without disrupting other users.

entries.title: Two ways to open the API Scan
entries.text: The API Scan can be started either from the ApiScanStandalone.exe file directly, or from inside Tricentis Tosca via the API Testing tab on the Home ribbon. This course always opens it from inside Tosca, since every exercise exports results into Tosca Commander.

entries.title: Operations, Messages, and the Payload

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 1 - Introduction to the API Scan
entries.title: Operations and Messages
entries.text: Operations contain Messages. A Message's content is only loaded the first time you click its Operation — this avoids the performance cost of generating content for every message up-front on a large, complex API.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 1 - Introduction to the API Scan
entries.title: Payload
entries.text: The area where you interact with and check responses. When a Message is first selected, the Payload shows a representation of what can be sent as a Request. Sending that default content usually returns an error — you must fill in appropriate data first. Some Requests (e.g. a GET) can have an empty Payload by design. Unneeded elements can be deleted from the Payload if they aren't relevant to what you're testing.

Lesson 2 - The Project Section
entries.text: Lesson 02 - The Project Section (video)

entries.title: The Home Menu's six options
entries.text: Save, Open, and Close (left-hand side) manipulate the API Scan project as a whole. Duplicate, Delete, and Rename (right-hand side) manipulate individual elements of the project, such as messages or operations.

entries.title: Duplicate
entries.text: Highlight a folder or message and click Duplicate to create a copy in the same root folder. The copy keeps the old name with a number appended (e.g. duplicating "Ex 2" creates "Ex 3").

entries.title: Delete
entries.text: Highlight an element and click Delete (or press the Delete key) to remove it from the project file.

entries.title: Rename
entries.text: Either highlight an element and click Rename in the Home Menu, or click the element and press F2. All three actions — duplicate, delete, rename — are also available from the right-click context menu on any element.

entries.title: Numerical-prefix naming convention
entries.text: The API Scan sorts folders, payloads, messages, and components alphabetically. Because of this, best practice is to rename elements with a numerical prefix matching the order they'll be used in the TestCase — e.g. "01 Get Address", "02 Add to Cart".

entries.title: Lesson 3 - API Scan Results
entries.text: Lesson 03 - API Scan Results (video)

entries.title: The Five Tabs of the Message Section
Lesson 4 - Tosca Export
entries.text: Lesson 04 - Tosca Export (video)

entries.title: One Message In, Two Modules and Two TestSteps Out
Request/Response pairing
entries.text: Every Message exported from the API Scan becomes TWO Modules and TWO TestSteps: one pair for the Request, one pair for the Response. This lets Tosca both steer the SUT (send the request) and set/verify dynamic parameters (read the response). The Modules hold the technical information needed to steer the system under test.

entries.title: Hands-On: Exercise 05 - Exporting from the API Scan to Tricentis Tosca
Lesson 5 - API Modules
entries.text: Lesson 05 - API Modules (video)

entries.title: API Modules and the Technical View
API Module
entries.text: Contains the technical information imported from the API Scan. Every exported Message produces two Modules (Request + Response) because the two views hold different technical information — even though they were linked together in the API Scan, they become fully independent once in Tosca.

entries.title: Technical View tab
entries.text: A tab on the Module — new compared to the Details and Test Configuration tabs you know from UI Modules — that mirrors the Message section of the API Scan exactly. This is where Business Parameters are created.

entries.title: Business Parameter
entries.text: A business-relevant element of a message — such as a name, ID, or address — added from the Technical View so a non-technical reader can understand what a TestStep does without looking at raw API code. When added, it acts as a ModuleAttribute that Tosca uses to execute the TestCase.

entries.title: Updating Modules When the API Changes
Update Button (API Home Menu)
entries.text: Updates changes made to the API Scan after it has been exported to Tricentis Tosca. It is the ribbon counterpart to editing a Business Parameter manually — either approach pushes a change through, but only the Update button does it for every reference to that element at once.

entries.title: Lesson 6 - API TestCases
entries.text: Lesson 06 - API TestCases (video)

entries.title: Request/Response naming
entries.text: Request Modules and TestCases keep the same name as the original Message in the API Scan. Tosca automatically appends "Response" to the Response Module/TestCase name.

entries.title: Value Range
entries.text: When multiple values exist for the same Business Parameter (e.g. multiple cities across multiple shops in a Response), highlighting them in the Payload and clicking Add populates the ValueRange column on the corresponding TestCase. This lets you pick any one of those real values from a drop-down in the Value column.

entries.title: Auto fill Values ("from Default")
entries.text: Clicking Auto fill Values on the ribbon, then "from Default", populates the Value field with the Module's default value. It works when either only TestSteps, or only TestStepValues, are selected — not when a TestCase or a mix of TestSteps/TestStepValues is selected.

entries.title: Values from Clipboard
entries.text: If an XML or JSON file already contains the parameters and values you need in a readable format, select the TestStepValues in Tosca, click "Values", then "from Clipboard" to populate them directly from whatever was copied to the clipboard.

entries.title: Lesson 7 - Building the TestCase
entries.text: Lesson 07 - Building the Test Case (video)

entries.title: Module ↔ TestStep synchronization
entries.text: As with UI automation, when a Module is updated in Tosca Commander, its linked TestStep — and by extension the whole TestCase — updates automatically. If you're unsure which Module a TestStep links to, select the TestStep and press Ctrl+J, or right-click it and choose "Jump to Module".

entries.title: Adding Modules to an API TestCase
entries.text: Like in UI TestCases, Modules can be added to an API TestCase either by dragging and dropping them from the Modules section, or with the Ctrl+T shortcut — both methods work identically to how you already add Modules in UI automation.

entries.title: Test Configuration Parameters (TCP) in API TestCases
entries.text: Just like in UI TestCases, add a Test Configuration Parameter — e.g. "Key" holding the Service Access Key — to every TestStepValue that needs it. This is far less laborious than updating the same literal value in every TestStep individually if the key ever changes, especially in long TestCases.

entries.text: Selecting a payload line and clicking Buffer creates and buffers a Business Parameter from that element — but what gets stored differs by direction. entries.text: Sometimes an API is fully specified — the business knows exactly what it needs to do, how, and for whom — but it isn't hosted anywhere yet. Rather than wait for hosting, the API Scan lets you manually create the message structure from the technical specification alone, so testing can begin immediately (shifting testing further left in the development cycle).

entries.title: Pretty Print
entries.text: Self-created SOAP payloads may not arrive formatted into separate, readable lines — the content still functions correctly either way, but it's hard for a human to read. Pretty Print reformats the payload into readable, indented lines without changing the message itself in any way.

Lesson 11 - XML Modules
entries.text: Lesson 11 - XML Modules (video)

entries.title: XML as a table-like data source
entries.text: An XML file has a table-like structure and is effectively scanned much like a database. This lesson uses AddressBook.xml, containing pre-populated contacts (Name, Company, Email, Telephone, Address) — representing, for example, an internal HR system's offline employee contact list that needs its add/remove/verify operations tested.

entries.title: No Technical View for XML Modules
entries.text: Unlike REST/SOAP Modules, an XML Module has no Technical View tab — instead, the XML elements are stored directly within the Module itself.

entries.title: Resource attribute
entries.text: Rather than manipulating the XML file directly on disk, Tosca Commander uses the Resource key to load the XML file temporarily into RAM. If a mistake happens during a test run, the original file on disk is never overwritten and no data is lost — the working copy lives only in memory until explicitly saved.

entries.title: Lesson 12 - XML Data
entries.text: Lesson 12 - XML Data (video)

entries.title: Inserting Data Into an XML File
Open/Create XML File and Save XML File
entries.text: Tricentis Standard Modules used for common XML steering operations across any XML file. Open/Create XML File loads the Resource from a given file path; Save XML File writes the in-memory Resource back out — either overwriting the original file (leave the file path empty) or creating a new file (specify a new name). Tosca can only save into an existing folder.

entries.title: Verifying Data in an XML File
Select → Constraint → Verify
entries.text: To check that inserted data landed correctly: Select on the outer container nodes (e.g. Contacts, Product) tells Tosca where to look. Constraint on a unique identifying field (e.g. an Id or Email) narrows the search down to exactly the one entry just created. Verify on every other field then checks the actual stored values against what you expect.

entries.title: Introduction

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Where TDS1 fits in the testing lifecycle

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Test Design Specialist (TDS1)
entries.text: This course prepares you to work in the two Tosca sections that sit at the front of the STLC: Requirements (colored yellow in Tosca Commander) and TestCase Design (colored red). Together they cover the analysis and planning phases — figuring out what needs to be tested and how much data variation is needed — before any physical TestCase is built.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Requirements phase
entries.text: Answers 'what needs to be tested and how risky is it if it breaks?'. Requirements are defined, structured, and risk-weighted so testers know where to focus first, and so progress can be tracked against them later.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: TestCase Design phase
entries.text: Answers 'what data combinations do I need to prove each Requirement works?'. Business behavior and test data are translated into a structured, combinable format — the TestSheet — before a single physical TestCase is built in the TestCase section (which was covered in the Automation Specialist courses).

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Why invest time up front in test design

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: The traditional imbalance
entries.text: On many projects, only a small fraction of testing time is spent specifying test cases (often done ad-hoc/intuitively), while the vast majority is spent in execution — and that execution effort repeats every regression cycle. Weak upfront design tends to produce redundant test cases that over-cover high-visibility requirements while under-covering others.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Tricentis' approach
entries.text: Shift more effort into the design phase: define Requirements, weight them by risk, and derive test data combinations systematically (covered across Lessons 1-10). The payoff is fewer but more precise test cases, each with a clear, isolated purpose — which also makes failures faster to diagnose, because a well-designed TestCase only fails for one reason.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Course roadmap

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Lesson 1 - Requirements
entries.text: Lesson 01 - Requirements (video)

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Building the Requirements structure

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Requirement
entries.text: A criterion the system under test is expected to fulfil — functional (e.g. 'a customer can pay with a Visa card') or non-functional (e.g. system security). Requirements are gathered from workshops with stakeholders, or from existing specs/BA documents.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Structuring principle
entries.text: Start from the highest-level functionality (e.g. Customer, Products, Order Process) and expand downward into sub-Requirements. Keep the tree shallow, non-redundant, and easy to read — depth for its own sake makes the structure harder to navigate, not more precise.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Basic Weighting

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Weight column
entries.text: Every Requirement defaults to a Weight of 1 (equal importance). Basic Weighting lets you assign any value from 0-10 per Requirement; Tricentis' recommended best practice is to keep it simple and use a 1-5 scale.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Top-down entry order
entries.text: Collapse all sub-Requirements first and weight the highest level — this tells you which broad area to start testing in. Then expand each Requirement and weight its Leaf Requirements — this tells you exactly which specific item to focus on inside that area.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Complex Weighting

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Why complex weighting exists
entries.text: A single linear scale often can't distinguish importance clearly enough (is this a 3 or a 4?). Complex Weighting instead asks two separate business questions per Requirement and lets Tosca calculate the Weight for you.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: The formula
entries.text: Weight = 2^(Frequency Class) × 2^(Damage Class). Both inputs are entered on a 0-10 scale (best practice: 1-5), and Tosca calculates the resulting Weight automatically — though it can be overridden manually. Because the formula is exponential (base 2 by default, adjustable on the RequirementSet's Properties tab), Requirements spread out more distinctly than a simple additive or linear scale would allow, which makes prioritization decisions clearer.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Using Requirements as a dashboard

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Contribution (%)
entries.text: Shows a Requirement's share of risk coverage across the whole RequirementSet. Values are multiplied by their parent's weight going up the tree, so Contribution (%) reflects how much this Requirement matters to the project as a whole — not just to its immediate siblings.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Relative Weight (%)
entries.text: Shows a Requirement's weight compared only to its siblings on the same level. Relative Weight values for elements on the same level always sum to 100%.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Downstream links
entries.text: Once weighted, Requirements link outward: TestSheets (TestCase Design) link to Requirements, TestCases link to Requirements, and ExecutionLists link to whole RequirementSets. The ExecutionState column then reflects executed-TestCase results weighted by risk — a risk-based coverage statement, usable as a management report.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Keeping Requirements up to date

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Auto-update behavior differs by Tosca version
entries.text: In Tosca 10.2 and earlier, Requirements recalculate automatically the instant a linked object changes. In Tosca 10.3 and later, auto-update is OFF by default — recalculating on every change can be slow in large repositories with many users and objects.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
entries.title: Manual refresh
entries.text: When a Requirement's data is stale, an exclamation mark appears next to the affected RequirementSet. Select it and press F6, or click 'Update Outdated Values' in the Ribbon, to recalculate.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca - Test Design Specialist Level 1 (TDS1)
