entries.title: Saving your work
Introduction
entries.text: Welcome to the Course / Course Overview

entries.title: Beyond the browser
entries.text: AS1 and AS2 taught automation of web applications through the XBrowser Engine. But real end-to-end business processes rarely stay inside a browser: an order confirmation arrives as an email, a report is generated as a PDF, reference data lives in an Excel workbook, a back-office step runs in a Windows desktop application, and an approval may happen on a phone. AE1 covers the engines Tosca uses to reach all of those.

entries.title: One tool, many engines
entries.text: Rather than bolting on a separate tool per technology, Tosca exposes each technology through a dedicated Engine that plugs into the shared TBox framework. The way you build a TestCase — Modules, TestSteps, TestStepValues, ActionModes — stays identical whether you are steering a web page, a spreadsheet cell, or a mobile button. That consistency is the point of the framework, and it's what the next module covers.

entries.title: What you will be able to do
Exercise prerequisite: create the AE1 workspace
Why a subset is used as a template
entries.text: Each project gets its own Workspace. Subsets are how Tosca artifacts — including the Tricentis Standard Modules — are imported and exported. The course ships a base subset so every learner starts from the same Module set instead of building it up by hand.

entries.title: Lesson → exercise → solution
entries.text: Each lesson pairs a video with one or more hands-on exercises, and most exercises have a solution video showing how it would be completed. The recommended order is: watch the lesson, attempt the exercise yourself, then compare against the solution video.

entries.title: Optional sections
entries.text: The Hands-on guides and the Vision AI Theory section are marked optional. The Final Exam draws no questions from optional sections — but Vision AI is still worth understanding, since it is where Tosca's control identification is heading.

entries.title: TBox Theory - Engines and Frameworks
entries.text: TBox Theory Lesson - Engines and Frameworks

entries.title: The problem a framework solves
entries.text: Every technology exposes its controls differently: a browser has a DOM, a Windows application has native window handles, an Excel workbook has cells and ranges, a mail server speaks a protocol. Without a framework, automating each would mean a different tool, a different scripting model, and a different skill set per technology — and no way to build one TestCase that crosses them.

entries.title: TBox
entries.text: The Tosca TBox framework is the .NET-based foundation that all Engines 3.0 are built on, for both GUI and non-GUI tests. It provides one common interface across every supported technology, so the differences between technologies are absorbed by the Engine rather than pushed up into your TestCases. TBox and its Engines 3.0 are part of the standard Tricentis Tosca installation — nothing extra to install for the core engines.

entries.title: What an Engine does
entries.text: An Engine is the technology-specific layer that knows how to find and manipulate controls in one kind of application. It translates the generic instruction coming from the TestCase — 'set this value', 'verify this value', 'click this' — into whatever that particular technology actually requires.

entries.title: GUI engines
entries.text: Steer something a human could see and click: a browser page, an Excel worksheet, a Windows dialog, a mobile screen. Identification is about locating a visible control.

entries.title: Non-GUI engines
entries.text: Steer backend systems with no visual component — the XML and JSON engines, API calls, protocol-level interactions. There is no screen to look at; the Engine works directly against the data or the service.

entries.title: XModules
entries.text: Engines 3.0 use XModules to steer test objects. An XModule is the Tosca object that represents a piece of the application under test, and it carries the information the Engine needs to find that object again at execution time. XModules can be structured hierarchically and referenced across many TestCases — the same reuse model you already know from web automation.

entries.title: How the Engine gets chosen
entries.text: You do not pick an Engine manually per TestStep. The Engine is determined by the Module: when you scan an application, Tosca creates Modules bound to the appropriate Engine for that technology, and every TestStep created from that Module is steered by it. This is why the same TestCase can mix a web TestStep and an Excel TestStep without any special handling — each TestStep inherits its Engine from its Module.

entries.title: Why the workflow never changes
entries.text: Because the Engine is hidden behind the Module, the mechanics you learned in AS1/AS2 carry over unchanged: drag a Module onto a TestCase to create a TestStep, fill in TestStepValues, set ActionMode to Input, Verify, Buffer or Select, and run. Learning a new Engine in AE1 is therefore mostly about learning what that technology exposes — which properties exist on an Excel cell, what an Anchor means in a PDF — not about learning a new way to build tests.

entries.title: Bonus: steering a specific table row
Two ways to reach one row: $ (by value) vs # (by index)
entries.text: A scanned table gives you a row-level TestStepValue that can be pointed at a specific row two different ways. The # notation targets a row by its ordinal position — the 3rd row, the 12th row — regardless of what data it holds. The $ notation instead targets the row whose cell matches a value you supply, so the TestStep finds 'the row where Order ID = 4021' rather than 'row number 7'. Index-based steering breaks the moment a row is inserted, deleted, or re-sorted; value-based steering survives it, which is why $ is generally the more resilient choice for tables whose row order can change between runs.

entries.title: HeaderRow
entries.text: A steering parameter that tells Tosca which row of the scanned table holds the column headers. Once set, later TestStepValues can address a column by its header text instead of a raw column number — 'the Total column' rather than 'column 4' — which keeps the TestCase readable and keeps it working if columns are reordered but not renamed.

entries.title: Constraint ActionMode
entries.text: Used to narrow a table TestStep down to one specific row before acting on a different cell in that same row — for example, constrain to the row where the Product column reads 'Laptop', then verify or buffer the Price cell in that row. Constraint is what makes $-style value matching usable across multi-column tables: you locate the row by one column's value and then operate on another.

entries.title: Bonus: operating Tosca outside Tosca Commander
TC Shell
entries.text: TC Shell is the command-line control of Tosca Commander itself — it lets you navigate a Workspace, read or modify a TestStepValue, and run an ExecutionList entirely from the command line, without the Tosca Commander UI ever opening. It has two modes: interactive, where you type commands one at a time and get the same range of functions the GUI offers; and script, where a batch of commands is read from a script data file with no opportunity to intervene — the mode built for running an extensive test portfolio unattended, for instance from a CI pipeline.

entries.title: Interactive mode: jumptonode and task
entries.text: You start by copying an object's NodePath from its Properties pane in Tosca Commander (Workspace closed before touching TC Shell). From a command prompt in the Tosca Commander install directory, TCShell.exe -workspace "<path to .tws>" -login "<user>" <password> opens the Workspace; jumptonode "<NodePath>" then moves the shell's focus to that TestStepValue or ExecutionList; and task lists every action available at that point — for a TestStepValue that includes Modify Value, for an ExecutionList it includes Run — selected by number or by name.

entries.title: Script mode: .tcs and .bat
entries.text: The same jumptonode / task commands, written into a plain-text .tcs script file instead of typed live, let TC Shell replay a whole sequence — update a TestStepValue, then jump to an ExecutionList and run it — with zero interaction. A short .bat file wrapping TCShell.exe -workspace <path> -login <user> <password> <path to the .tcs file> then turns that sequence into something a build server can double-click or call from a pipeline step.

entries.title: Tosca REST API: downloading an execution report
entries.text: Separately from TC Shell, a Tosca Server installation exposes a REST API that can, among other things, print an ExecutionList's report to a file without anyone opening Tosca Commander at all. It requires the Tricentis.Tosca.RestApiService Windows service to be running (disabled by default) and the service's config file to point WorkspaceBasePath at the folder holding the Workspaces it should serve. On the ExecutionEntries object being printed, the PrintOutputFormat property has to be set to ASKUSER first — otherwise the report endpoint has nothing to act on.

entries.title: Lesson 1 - Excel Engine
entries.text: Lesson 01 - Excel Engine · Excel Modules reference (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Two different ways to reach Excel
Excel Standard Modules (file-level, background)
entries.text: The TBox Excel Modules manipulate the workbook as a file, in the background. Excel's window never has to be visible and the user interface is never driven. This is the faster, more stable approach and it is what you use for the vast majority of Excel automation: reading reference data, writing results, verifying calculated values. You find these under Standard modules → TBox XEngines → Excel.

entries.title: Excel UI Engine 3.0 (application-level)
entries.text: The Excel UI Engine 3.0 scans and steers the Microsoft Excel user interface itself — the main application window, its dialogs, and the worksheets with embedded controls currently loaded by the application. Use it when the thing under test genuinely is the Excel UI: a dialog that must appear, a ribbon interaction, an embedded control a user would click.

entries.title: TBox Open Excel Workbook
entries.text: The mandatory first step of any Excel Standard Module sequence. It opens the workbook in the background and can handle password-protected files and read-only access. Nothing else in the Excel Module family works until the workbook has been opened.

entries.title: TBox Close Excel Workbook
entries.text: The required final step. Besides closing the workbook it controls whether and where changes are saved — you can save to a specified path and in a specified file format, which is how you produce an output file that differs from the input.

entries.title: TBox Define Excel Range
entries.text: Establishes a named range that later steps operate on. It needs the workbook, the worksheet, and the cell boundaries. Defining a range once and referring to it afterwards keeps a TestCase readable and avoids repeating cell coordinates in every step.

entries.title: TBox Excel Range Manipulation
entries.text: The workhorse Module. It reads and writes cell data, and it also reaches the technical properties of cells — formulas, formatting, colors, fonts, and comments. Because it supports verification as well as input, this is the Module that satisfies the course objective 'verify Microsoft Excel cell special properties': you are not just checking the displayed value, you are checking that the underlying formula, the fill colour, or the font is what it should be.

entries.title: TBox Clear Excel Range
entries.text: Removes content from a range — and selectively, not just the values: formatting, notes, comments, hyperlinks, or outlines can each be cleared. Useful for resetting a sheet between test runs.

entries.title: TBox Excel 1:1 File Compare
entries.text: Compares two Excel files across specified sheets, covering cell contents, formatting, and objects. The result can optionally be exported to a text file, which is what makes it usable as evidence in a test report rather than just a pass/fail flag. This is the standard answer to 'the report we generate must match the expected report'.

entries.title: TBox Run Excel Macro
entries.text: Executes an existing Microsoft Excel macro from a TestStep, with a configurable timeout. Note the word existing — this Module runs a macro that already lives in the workbook; it is not a way to write VBA from Tosca. The timeout matters because a long-running macro would otherwise hang the TestCase.

entries.title: Lesson 2 - PDF Engine
entries.text: Lesson 02 - PDF Engine · Scan PDF files (Tricentis docs) · Compare PDF files (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: The PDF Scan
entries.text: PDFs have no DOM and no accessible control tree — there is nothing to query for 'the invoice total field'. The PDF Scan solves this by letting you mark regions of the document as controls. Start it by right-clicking a Module folder and selecting Scan, or with the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+P, then choose the PDF file. The scan interface shows the document alongside the controls you are identifying.

entries.title: Anchor controls: the core concept of this lesson
Why anchors exist
entries.text: A control's absolute position on a PDF page is not stable. Add a line to an address block or let a table grow by one row and everything below it shifts. Identifying a control by fixed coordinates would break on the next document. An anchor control solves this by locating the target relative to another element instead of by absolute location.

entries.title: How it works at runtime
entries.text: At execution, the PDF Engine 3.0 searches the document for the anchor — the text or image you defined — and once it has found it, calculates where the target control must be in relation to it. So the target moves with its anchor, and a shifted layout no longer breaks identification.

entries.title: Exact match by default
entries.text: By default Tosca looks for an anchor that is an exact match for the text or image you defined. That is the strictest and most predictable setting, and it is what you want whenever the anchor text is genuinely constant.

entries.title: Lowering accuracy
entries.text: When exact matching causes identification problems — typically with scanned or image-based PDFs where character recognition is imperfect — a lower level of accuracy can be configured through the OCR settings. This is a deliberate trade: you gain tolerance to recognition noise and lose some certainty about which element was matched.

entries.title: PDF 1:1 Compare
entries.text: The PDF Engine 3.0 compares PDFs through the Module PDF 1:1 Compare, which is part of the Standard subset. It performs a visual comparison between a reference PDF and one or more target PDF files. The TestCase passes if the similarity between the files is above the accuracy you specify — so the threshold is yours to set, rather than requiring pixel-perfect identity.

entries.title: Combining compare with exclusions
entries.text: This is where the scan's exclusion capability pays off. Real generated documents contain fields that change every run — generation timestamps, document IDs, batch numbers. Scanning those regions and excluding them from the comparison lets you compare everything that should be stable while ignoring what is legitimately variable.

entries.title: Lesson 3 - Mail Engine
entries.text: Lesson 03 - Mail Engine · Mail Engine 3.0 (Tricentis docs) · Connect to Cloud Mail Server (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Mail as part of the business process
entries.text: Very few end-to-end processes finish inside the application. Register an account and a confirmation email arrives; place an order and an order confirmation follows; reset a password and the whole flow depends on a link that only exists in an inbox. If the test stops at the web page, the part the customer actually receives goes untested.

entries.title: Mail Engine 3.0
entries.text: The Tosca Mail Engine 3.0 automates tests against email. Like the other Engines 3.0 it is part of the standard Tricentis Tosca installation, and its Modules belong to the Standard subset — you find them under Standard modules → TBox XEngines → Mail.

entries.title: Connect to Mail Server
entries.text: A dedicated TestStep defines the connection to the mail server — host, protocol, credentials. Note the subtlety: this step defines the connection, but the actual connection is established during the sending or receiving step, not at the moment the Connect step runs. A Connect step that passes is therefore not by itself proof that the server is reachable.

entries.title: Connect to Exchange Server
entries.text: A separate Module dedicated to Microsoft Exchange, sitting alongside the generic Connect to Mail Server in the same folder. Where the target mailbox is on Exchange, this is the more direct route than configuring a generic connection.

entries.title: OAuth 2.0 for Exchange Online / Microsoft 365
entries.text: Microsoft has been deprecating basic authentication for SMTP and EWS, and Tosca supports OAuth 2.0 as the modern alternative. Tricentis documents a dedicated Connect to Cloud Mail Server Module for this. Hands-on finding: in the AE1 base subset, Connect to Exchange Server itself already exposes an Authentication Type selector (defaulting to 'Direct', i.e. basic username/password) plus App Id and Tenant Id fields — switching Authentication Type away from 'Direct' and supplying an Azure AD app registration's App Id and Tenant Id gives OAuth 2.0 against Exchange Online from that same Module, no separate Connect to Cloud Mail Server step required.

entries.title: Real-world setup notes: Gmail and corporate mailboxes
Gmail: exact server values that work
entries.text: Connect to Mail Server, configured for RECEIVING: Mail Server = imap.gmail.com, Port = 993, Enable Security = True, Protocol = IMAP. Configured for SENDING (a separate TestStep): Mail Server = smtp.gmail.com, Port = 587, Enable Security = True, Protocol = SMTP.

entries.title: Send Mail
entries.text: The Send Mail Module sends — or replies to — an email message via SMTP. Typical uses in a test are triggering an inbound process (a system that acts on incoming mail), or generating a message the test will later verify was received and correctly handled.

entries.title: Receive Mail Simple
entries.text: Checks whether you received one specific, single email. This is the right choice for the common case: 'after registering, did the confirmation email arrive?' One expected message, one check.

entries.title: Receive Mail Expert
entries.text: Checks whether specific emails — plural — were received. Use it when a single message is not the unit of interest: several notifications are expected, or a more elaborate set of criteria has to be evaluated across messages.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.text: Lesson 04 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine · Steering UIA 3.0 Controls (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Two engines for one platform

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Why Windows needs two options
entries.text: Windows desktop applications are not built on a single technology. Some are WinForms, some WPF, some are decades-old Win32 executables, some are hybrids. No single access mechanism reaches all of them cleanly, so Tosca offers two different ways into a Windows application and lets you pick the one that works for the application in front of you.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: UIA Engine 3.0
entries.text: Based on the Microsoft UI Automation framework — a framework Microsoft developed specifically so that applications built on different technologies could be steered as uniformly as possible. When the UIA Engine steers an application, controls are addressed exclusively through that UI Automation interface in the target application. Beyond application windows, the UIA Engine 3.0 can also test Windows desktop elements and the taskbar.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: WinX Engine
entries.text: WinX is used for Windows UI API tests — it interacts with the application through direct Windows API-level calls rather than through Microsoft's UI Automation abstraction. It is the alternative path for applications that the UIA interface does not expose well.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Making the choice at scan time

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Where the decision happens
entries.text: You do not choose the engine on a TestStep or a Module property — you choose it while scanning. After selecting the desktop application you want to scan, right-click the application's tile and pick either UIA or WinX from the context menu. Whichever you choose determines the kind of Modules produced: UIA Modules for UIA tests, WinX Modules for Windows UI API tests.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Consequences of the choice
entries.text: This is the same Module-binds-the-Engine principle from the TBox theory lesson, applied to Windows. Because the engine is baked into the Modules created by the scan, switching engines later is not a setting you flip — it means rescanning the application with the other option and rebuilding the affected Modules. Worth a moment's evaluation before committing to a large scan.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Working with the scanned controls

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 4 - WinX Engine and UIA Engine
entries.title: Nothing new above the Module
entries.text: Once the scan has produced Modules, everything above that level is the workflow you already know: drag a Module onto a TestCase to create a TestStep, fill in TestStepValues, choose an ActionMode of Input, Verify, Buffer or Select. Whether a UIA or WinX Engine is doing the steering underneath is invisible at that level — exactly the uniformity the TBox framework exists to provide.

entries.title: Lesson 5 - Self Healing
entries.text: Lesson 05 - Self Healing · Self-healing TestCases (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Controls change; tests break
entries.text: An application under active development changes its controls constantly — an id gets renamed, a class is restructured, a button moves into a different container. Nothing about the business behaviour changed, but the automation can no longer find the control and the TestCase fails. Investigating and repairing these false failures is one of the biggest ongoing maintenance costs in test automation.

entries.title: Self-healing Mode
entries.text: With Self-healing Mode enabled, a TestCase does not fail just because a control changed. When Tosca cannot find the control during execution, it looks for a similar control in the system under test; if it finds a suitable one, it uses that control instead and execution continues. The result is more stable test runs, less manual repair work, and a record of which controls have actually changed.

entries.title: Turning it on: the SelfHealing TCP
A test configuration parameter, not a checkbox
entries.text: Self-healing is activated by creating a test configuration parameter named SelfHealing. Because it is a TCP, it inherits the usual scoping rules — set it high in the folder structure to apply broadly, or on a specific TestCase to limit it.

entries.title: SelfHealingWeightThreshold
entries.text: An optional companion TCP used with the Weighted mode. It defaults to 0.75 and filters out property combinations that score below that threshold — a way to stop the algorithm from accepting weak matches. Raise it to be stricter about what counts as 'the same control'; lower it to tolerate more change.

entries.title: Where the technical data lives
entries.text: Self-Healing Properties are the technical attributes of a control that give Tosca something to match against when the primary identification fails. They sit on the Self-Healing Properties tab of the ModuleAttribute — one level deeper than the identification you normally work with.

entries.title: They are created for you
entries.text: Tosca adds these properties automatically when a Module is created through XScan, Tosca Rescan, Salesforce Scan, or the Tricentis Automation Recording Assistant. You do not have to author them by hand — though you can edit, delete, or add properties manually after scanning if the automatic set is not right.

entries.title: Spotting a self-healed run
entries.text: After execution, a self-healing icon appears on the affected ExecutionEntries, and the ExecutionLog's Detail column explains which objects were self-healed. This is how you distinguish 'passed cleanly' from 'passed, but a control had changed' — the pass alone does not tell you.

entries.title: Apply Self-Healing properties
entries.text: Healing is per-execution unless you persist it. Right-click the log and select 'Apply Self-Healing properties' from the context menu to write the healed identification back into the Module. Without this step, the same control has to be re-healed on every subsequent run.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.text: Lesson 06 - Install and Use Custom Controls · Custom controls (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: The problem: widgets that aren't standard controls

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: When an engine sees the wrong thing
entries.text: Standard identification works because the engine recognises a control as something it understands — a text box, a checkbox, a table. Complex or third-party UI widgets break that assumption. A custom date picker, a rich grid, or a bespoke component may be built from dozens of nested primitive elements, so the engine sees a pile of divs or panels rather than one meaningful control. You can sometimes still automate it, but the steering is fragile and the Module is unreadable.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: Custom controls
entries.text: A custom control wraps a complex UI widget so that Tosca presents it as one of its standard UI elements. Instead of the tester manipulating the widget's internal structure, the widget is exposed as the control it logically is — and can then be steered with the ordinary ActionModes like any other control. Custom controls are based on special, custom-made DLL files that refine how Tosca detects UI elements.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: Not something you author in Tosca Commander
entries.text: Custom controls are compiled DLLs, not project objects you create through the Tosca UI. Tricentis' own guidance is to contact your Tricentis representative to obtain custom controls — they are provided for known widget libraries rather than built ad hoc by the tester.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: Making them available
entries.text: Once obtained, the DLL has to be put where Tosca will load it, and Tosca has to be restarted for the control to be picked up. The mechanism differs by deployment: in Tosca Cloud an administrator uploads them under Configurations → Uploads → Custom controls, and they are distributed automatically through Launcher and integrated into all test runs. For an on-prem installation — which is what this course covers — the AE1 lesson walks through the placement and activation steps directly; follow the version-specific path shown there rather than assuming a location.

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: Using them and where they fit

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Install and Use Custom Controls
entries.title: After installation, nothing special
entries.text: Once a custom control is installed, you scan the application as usual. The difference is what comes back: the widget now appears as a recognised standard control in the Module rather than as a tangle of low-level elements. From there it is steered exactly like any other control — same TestSteps, same TestStepValues, same ActionModes.

entries.title: Lesson 7 - Standard Modules
entries.text: Lesson 07 - Standard Modules · File Operations (Tricentis docs) · Folder Operations (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Why file automation belongs in a test
Setup, teardown, and evidence
entries.text: Most non-trivial TestCases touch the file system somewhere. A test needs an input file placed in a watched folder before it starts; an export must be verified after it runs; yesterday's output has to be cleared so today's run is clean; a generated report needs archiving as evidence. Doing any of that by hand defeats the point of automation, and the Standard subset provides Modules for all of it — no scanning and no engine-specific work required.

entries.title: TBox Read/Create File
entries.text: The dual-purpose workhorse: it creates files and writes text content, and it also verifies or buffers text content from an existing file. Encoding is configurable — UTF-8, UTF-16 and ISO-8859-1 are supported, with an optional byte order mark setting. Buffering content out of a file is how you feed data read from disk into later TestSteps.

entries.title: TBox Append File
entries.text: Adds text to an existing file, with optional newline and encoding settings. Note its convenient behaviour: if the file does not exist, Append creates it. That makes it safe to use for accumulating a log across a run without a separate create step.

entries.title: TBox Copy File
entries.text: Duplicates a file into another directory. The target directory must already exist at run time — this Module will not create it for you, which is why a TBox Create Folder step often precedes it. Tricentis also notes the Module might not work if a security and password management tool is in play.

entries.title: TBox Move/Rename File
entries.text: Relocates a file, renames it, or both. As with Copy File, the target directory must pre-exist for a move to succeed.

entries.title: TBox Delete File
entries.text: Removes files from a directory and supports wildcard patterns. Critical behaviour to know: it returns a positive result even if the file does not exist. That makes it ideal as an idempotent cleanup step at the start of a run — but it means a passing Delete step is not evidence the file was ever there.

entries.title: TBox File Existence
entries.text: Verifies whether a file exists in a directory. It supports negation with '!' (assert a file is absent), wildcards with '*' (match a pattern rather than an exact name), and the WaitOn ActionMode — which is what you use when a file is produced asynchronously and the test must wait for it to appear rather than checking once and failing.

entries.title: TBox File Compare
entries.text: Compares the content of two files and can optionally generate a diff report. Where the second file has additional content, the Module highlights that in green in the report — useful when the question is not merely 'are these identical?' but 'what changed?'.

entries.title: TBox Image Compare
entries.text: Verifies image files (BMP, JPG, GIF) with a pixel-accurate comparison — an exact pixel match, not a similarity threshold. Note the contrast with PDF 1:1 Compare from Lesson 2, which passes when similarity exceeds an accuracy you specify. Image Compare is the stricter of the two.

entries.title: Matching actions to Engines: Excel, Database, Browser, and Expressions
Excel UI Engine 3.0
entries.text: Steers the MS Excel application itself — driving it the way a user would, through its own interface. Use it when the TestCase needs to interact with Excel as an application, not just its data.

entries.title: Excel Engine 3.0
entries.text: Steers MS Excel files directly — reading and writing cell data without driving the Excel application's UI. Faster and more stable than the UI Engine when you only need the file's data.

entries.title: Database Engine 3.0
entries.text: Queries and steers data sets held in one or more databases — the go-to Engine whenever a TestCase needs to read from or write to a database rather than a file or application.

entries.title: HTML modules
entries.text: Cover browser and document-level actions that sit above individual HTML controls — such as Execute JavaScript, Open a URL, and Close Browser. These act on the browser session itself, not on a specific button or field inside the page.

entries.title: TBox Evaluation Tool
entries.text: Compares numeric, string, and alphanumeric expressions. Found under Standard subset → TBox Automation Tools → Expression Evaluation — distinct from TBox File Compare, which compares file content rather than expressions. Each comparison is entered as an Expression TestStepValue with ActionMode Verify, for example '#{DATE[][][]}'>'#{DATE[][-1d][]}' to check today's date is later than yesterday's, or '{B[Text1]}'='{B[Text2]}' to check two buffered values are equal — one Module handles dates, buffers, and plain numeric or string comparisons alike.

entries.title: Resource vs. file
entries.text: An XML Resource is Tosca's in-memory working copy — Create XML Resource makes one without any file on disk. Open/Create XML file can either make a brand-new file or load an existing one as a Resource. Save XML file is the step that commits an in-memory Resource's changes back to disk.

entries.title: Bonus: the JSON Engine — reading a repeating array with one TestCase
Scanning a JSON file
entries.text: A JSON file is scanned like an API — Module folder → Scan → API → point the file picker at the .json file, then export it as an XML/JSON TestCase. The scan produces a Module whose ModuleAttributes mirror the file's structure, including one attribute per array entry: item#1, item#2, item#3, and so on for however many entries the sample file happened to have.

entries.title: The problem: the array's length isn't fixed
entries.text: A Module scanned from one sample file hard-codes exactly the entries that file had. If the real data returns 20 entries instead of 3, a TestCase built directly on item#1 / item#2 / item#3 simply never looks at the other 17. Reading 'however many entries are actually there' needs the Module and the TestCase to both stop assuming a fixed count.

entries.title: The wildcard attribute: item#1 → item*
entries.text: On the Module, delete every ModuleAttribute after the first array entry, keeping only item#1, then rename that surviving attribute's Name from item#1 to item* — turning one specific indexed entry into a wildcard that matches any entry in the array, at any index.

entries.title: ExplicitName = True
entries.text: A Configuration Parameter added on that same wildcarded attribute. Without it, Tosca's wildcard matching behaves generically; with ExplicitName set to True, the attribute is treated as matching the literal repeating node structure of the source file, which is what makes the wildcarded Module actually bind correctly against the real (variable-length) JSON at run time.

entries.title: Counting entries, then repeating over them
entries.text: A first TestStep drags the Module in with ActionMode Buffer on an expression like .ResultCount == someBuffer, capturing how many array entries are present in this run. That count then goes into the Repetition property of a TestStepFolder — set it to {B[someBuffer]} — which turns the folder into a loop that runs once per entry. Inside that repeating folder, the item* attribute is referenced as #{REPETITION}, a token that automatically advances to the next array index on every pass, and each field buffered inside the loop is named with the same token (e.g. firstName_{REPETITION}) so every entry's data lands in its own uniquely named buffer instead of overwriting the last one.

entries.title: Windows, Buffer, and Process Operations — matching actions to Modules
TBox Dialog
entries.text: Steers a Windows dialog box or browser confirmation popup — an 'Are you sure?' prompt, for instance — without ever scanning it. Because it is a Standard Module rather than something produced by a scan, the same TestStep works across different webpages and applications: set Caption to identify the dialog window (wildcards allowed, e.g. 'demowebshop*'), Label to the dialog's message text, and Button to the button to click, all with ActionMode Input. This is the answer whenever a confirmation popup would otherwise force an extra scan just to handle one button.

entries.title: Lesson 8 - Image Based Controls
entries.text: Lesson 08 - Image Based Controls · Identify controls by image: Image-Based Test Automation (Tricentis docs) · Identify controls by anchor (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Identifying by what it looks like
entries.text: Every identification method covered so far works on structure — properties, the control tree, the UI Automation interface. Image-based identification abandons structure entirely and identifies a control by one or more screenshots of it. Tosca finds the control by locating that image on screen at execution time.

entries.title: How to create one
entries.text: In XScan, select the control you want to identify, then in the Identification methods pane choose ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → IMAGE. You then supply the screenshot or screenshots that represent the control.

entries.title: Making image identification as reliable as it can be
Use more than one screenshot
entries.text: The single most useful technique in this lesson: supply more than one screenshot to identify a control, especially when the control does not always look the same. A button with hover, focused, and default states, or an icon that changes slightly by context, will fail against a single reference image but match reliably against a set covering its variations.

entries.title: What still breaks it
entries.text: Multiple screenshots handle variation the control was designed to have. They do not protect against changes to the environment: display scaling, resolution, colour scheme or theme, anti-aliasing differences between machines, or a redesign. This is why image-based controls are also the most machine-sensitive form of automation — a TestCase that passes on the author's laptop can fail on an execution agent with different display settings.

entries.title: The other Advanced Identification method: Anchor
Identify by anchor
entries.text: Sitting alongside IMAGE in the same pane is ANCHOR — select the control, then ADVANCED IDENTIFICATION → ANCHOR. Rather than matching appearance, this identifies the target control by its location in relation to another element, the anchor control. It is often the better answer when a control has no stable properties of its own but sits next to something that does.

entries.title: Where this sits in the escalation path
Lesson 9 - Mobile Engine
entries.text: Lesson 09 - Mobile Engine · Get started with mobile test automation (Tricentis docs) · Configure local or remote test automation (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: What TMA does for you
entries.text: Mobile automation traditionally means assembling a toolchain — Appium, Java components, environment variables, device drivers — before a single test can run. The Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA) provides simplified setup and configuration of iOS and Android devices so that none of that is your problem: you do not need to install Appium, Java components, or configure environment variables yourself.

entries.title: Mobile Engine 3.0
entries.text: The Engine that steers mobile applications, working through the Mobile Agent. As with every Engine 3.0, once Modules exist the TestCase-building workflow is the familiar one — the mobile-specific work is all in the connection and scanning setup.

entries.title: Local (TMA)
entries.text: Connects a device to the workstation running Tricentis Tosca — via USB cable, or to a simulator or emulator running on that same machine. This is the typical setup while developing tests, and what the course exercises use.

entries.title: Remote (TMA)
entries.text: A remotely installed Tricentis Mobile Agent connects to a remote device, emulator, or simulator. This is what you use when the device farm lives elsewhere — a shared lab, a CI environment, or cloud-hosted devices.

entries.title: Mobile Scan
entries.text: The Mobile Scan handles native, hybrid, and web applications on mobile. The sequence is: prepare the test environment, start the Mobile Scan and connect to your device, then add the mobile device, emulator, or simulator you want to scan against. From there, scanning produces Modules the same way it does for any other technology.

entries.title: Configuring the connection with TCPs
entries.text: The connection to a device, emulator, or simulator is established through test configuration parameters. This is the same TCP mechanism used elsewhere in Tosca — for the TestDataService endpoint, for SelfHealing — so the scoping rules you already know apply.

entries.title: Open Mobile App must come first
entries.text: Drag and drop the Open Mobile App Module onto the TestCase — and note the constraint: it must be the first TestStep of the TestCase. Nothing can be steered on the device until the application has been opened through this Module.

entries.title: Real-world setup notes: running TMA on a separate machine
Remote TMA must be started with --rest-address
entries.text: Launching TMA from the tray icon or Start Menu starts it for LOCAL use only. When Tosca and TMA run on different machines, start the agent from the command line with the --rest-address flag: tricentis-mobile-agent start --rest-address <IP>:<port>. On Windows the executable lives under C:\Program Files\Tricentis\Mobile Agent; on macOS inside /Applications/Tricentis Mobile Agent.app.

entries.title: Diagnosing device-side vs Tosca-side problems
entries.text: TMA exposes a REST endpoint you can query directly: http://<ip>:<port>/api/devices returns JSON with each device's udid, name, connected, busy and statusReady fields. If that shows connected:true and busy:false, the device side is healthy and the fault is on Tosca's side — which saves you from chasing firewall, proxy, and network theories.

entries.title: Emulators must run on the same machine as TMA
entries.text: Tricentis recommends Android Studio for emulators, and the emulator has to run on the machine running TMA. That constraint drives the whole topology: if Tosca Commander runs in a VM but the emulator runs on the host, then TMA belongs on the host alongside the emulator, and Tosca connects to it remotely.

entries.title: Vision AI (Optional)
entries.text: Vision AI - Theory (optional section) · Scan with Vision AI (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Seeing the UI the way a person does
entries.text: Conventional scanning reads an application's technical structure — element ids, class names, the control tree. Vision AI instead analyses the application's visual components, using two neural networks: one for finding controls and one for optical character recognition (OCR). It identifies what is on screen much as a human tester would: this looks like a text field, that is a button labelled 'Submit'.

entries.title: Recognising control types, not just pixels
entries.text: The crucial detail is that Vision AI detects control types and adjusts its steering mechanism to the classification it has made. Having decided a region is a dropdown, it steers it as a dropdown. This is what separates it from raw appearance matching.

entries.title: Vision AI vs the two methods you already know
Versus property-based scanning
entries.text: Property-based identification depends on technical attributes staying stable. Vision AI steers by visual components instead, which makes it resilient to UI changes that alter the underlying markup without changing what the user sees — a framework upgrade that renames every generated class, for example.

entries.title: Versus image-based controls (Lesson 8)
entries.text: This is the comparison that matters most. Image-based identification matches a screenshot — it knows nothing about what the control is, only what it looked like. Vision AI recognises individual control types and adjusts its behaviour accordingly, which is smarter steering than pixel matching or screenshot comparison. Where Lesson 8's method is a last resort accepting brittleness, Vision AI aims to be a genuine identification strategy.

entries.title: When automatic recognition is not enough
User Identified Controls (UIDCs)
entries.text: Vision AI does not always classify a control correctly on its own. When standard recognition falls short, controls can be configured manually, or you can create User Identified Controls — controls you define yourself so the AI knows how to treat them.

entries.title: Anchors, again
entries.text: UIDCs use anchor points — surrounding elements that guide the AI to locate the target correctly. The same relational idea you met in the PDF Engine lesson and in XScan's Advanced Identification appears here too: when an element is hard to pin down on its own, describe it by what sits around it.

entries.title: Grand Scenario - Demo Web Shop
entries.text: Grand Scenario - Demo Web Shop

entries.title: What the Grand Scenario is for
From isolated lessons to one business process
entries.text: Each preceding lesson exercised one engine on its own. The Grand Scenario is the capstone that puts them together: a complete Demo Web shop purchase, from logging in through ordering a book and paying on delivery, to downloading the PDF invoice and logging out. It is the exercise that shows why the engines matter — a real process crosses technologies, and the test has to cross them too.

entries.title: Why the scenario is split into three
entries.text: The TestCases folder for the Grand Scenario is organised into Precondition, Process, and Post condition. This separation is a test-design discipline, not a Tosca requirement: the Precondition establishes the state the real test needs, the Process is the behaviour actually under test, and the Post condition returns the system to a clean state so the next run starts from the same place.

entries.title: The 'Login to web shop' reusable block
entries.text: Logging in is needed by the Precondition and would be needed by any other scenario against the same shop. Rather than duplicating those steps, the scenario keeps a TestStepLibrary containing a reusable TestStep block named 'Login to web shop', made up of three steps: Open demo web shop, Click on log in link, and Provide log in details.

entries.title: Why this matters beyond tidiness
entries.text: A reusable block is maintained in one place. When the shop changes its login page, one block is updated and every TestCase referencing it is fixed at once — the same centralised-maintenance argument behind Classes in TDS1 and Libraries in the TestCase section. The Precondition TestCase then consists of the reused block plus its own 'Verify successful login' step.

entries.title: The Process TestCase, step by step
Three TestStep folders
entries.text: 'Order fiction book and pay on delivery' is itself divided into three TestStep folders, which keeps a long flow readable and makes a failure immediately locatable to a phase of the process.

entries.title: The two techniques that make it work
Buffering the order number
entries.text: The step 'Verify order and buffer order no' does two jobs at once: it verifies the order was created, and it buffers the order number the shop generated. That number cannot be known in advance — it only exists at runtime — so it is captured into a buffer and then used by the following steps to navigate to the correct order details page. This is the standard Tosca answer to 'the application generated a value and I need it later'.

entries.title: Crossing into the PDF Engine
entries.text: 'Download PDF Invoice' is where the scenario leaves the browser. The invoice produced by the checkout is a PDF, and verifying it is exactly the PDF Engine work from Lesson 2 — scanning the document, using anchors to locate values that shift with content, and comparing against a reference while excluding the volatile parts such as the order number and date.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: A deep dive, not a single lesson
entries.text: AE1's 'Automating beyond web applications' course touches Mobile Engine 3.0 in a single lesson — enough to open a Mobile Scan and build one TestCase. This course goes much deeper: installing and configuring TMA yourself, preparing both Android and iOS targets, understanding Local vs Remote topologies, scanning native/hybrid/web mobile apps, and working through the full catalog of mobile-specific Modules and gestures.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: One engine, three kinds of app
entries.text: Mobile Engine 3.0 automates native apps (built specifically for iOS/Android), hybrid apps (a native shell wrapping embedded web views, common in cross-platform frameworks like React Native or Ionic), and mobile web (a site opened in the device's browser). The same Mobile Scan handles all three — the difference shows up in how controls are captured, not in a different tool.

entries.text: Roughly half of this course is environment setup — installing TMA, preparing devices, wiring the connection — before a single Module gets scanned. That ordering matches reality: the large majority of 'mobile automation isn't working' problems in practice are setup and connection problems, not TestCase-authoring problems.

entries.title: The classic mobile toolchain
entries.text: Automating a mobile app with raw Appium normally means: installing Appium and its Node.js dependencies, installing Java, wiring up platform-specific drivers (UiAutomator2 for Android, XCUITest for iOS), managing environment variables and PATH entries, and writing test scripts in a supported language. None of that is Tosca-specific — it is the general cost of mobile test automation before you write a single test.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 1 - Mobile Engine 3.0 & the Tricentis Mobile Agent
entries.title: TMA removes the toolchain, not the underlying engine
entries.text: The Tricentis Mobile Agent (TMA) provides simplified setup and configuration of iOS and Android devices. You do not install Appium, Java components, or configure environment variables yourself — TMA bundles and manages that layer. Underneath, Mobile Engine 3.0 still drives sessions the same way Appium-based tools do (UiAutomator2 on Android, XCUITest on iOS); TMA is what hides that machinery behind a device list and a Start/Stop toggle.

Once Modules exist, the TestCase-building workflow is the familiar Tosca one — Modules, TestSteps, TestStepValues, ActionModes — identical in shape to XBrowser or any other Engine. The mobile-specific work lives in the connection and scanning setup, not in how TestCases are structured.

entries.text: TMA runs on the same machine as Tosca Commander, connected to a device via USB or to a simulator/emulator on that same machine. This is the simplest topology and the one most learners start with.

entries.text: TMA runs on a different machine than Tosca Commander — for example a Mac running TMA for iOS work, connected to over the network from a Windows machine running Tosca Commander. Remote is also how shared device farms and CI environments are typically wired.

entries.title: A separate installer from Tosca Commander
entries.text: TMA ships as its own installer, downloaded from the Tricentis Support Hub or Tosca Downloads area, and installed independently of Tosca Commander. It can live on the same machine as Tosca Commander (Local setup) or on a different machine entirely (Remote setup) — the installer itself is identical either way; only where you run it differs.

entries.title: Starting TMA: tray launch vs command line

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Tray / Start Menu launch — local use only
entries.text: Launching TMA from the system tray icon (or the Start Menu / Applications folder) starts the agent bound to the local machine. This is sufficient whenever Tosca Commander and TMA run on the same machine.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Command-line launch with --rest-address — required for remote use
entries.text: When Tosca Commander and TMA run on different machines, TMA must be started from the command line with the --rest-address flag, binding its REST API to a network-reachable address instead of localhost only: tricentis-mobile-agent start --rest-address <IP>:<port>.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Ports and firewalls

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Default port 8585
entries.text: TMA's default REST port is 8585. In a Local setup this rarely matters since traffic never leaves the machine. In a Remote setup, that port (or whichever custom port is chosen) must be reachable from the Tosca Commander machine — meaning any firewall between the two machines needs an explicit allow rule.

entries.title: The TMA console

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Device Management
entries.text: Once TMA is running, its console (reachable at http://<TMA-host>:<port> in a browser) lists every device, emulator, or simulator TMA can currently see, along with a status: Ready, Busy, or Offline. Confirming a device shows Ready here — before opening Tosca at all — isolates device-layer problems from anything Tosca-side.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Keeping TMA up to date

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Version alignment with Tosca
entries.text: TMA and Tosca Commander are versioned and released independently, but a very old TMA against a very new Tosca (or vice versa) can produce session-start failures that look like device problems. When something that used to work stops working after a Tosca upgrade, checking for a matching TMA update is a reasonable early step.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation

entries.title: Why these two values matter
entries.text: To open an already-installed Android app, Tosca's Open Mobile App Module needs AppPackage (the app's unique identifier, like a reverse-domain name) and AppActivity (the specific screen/entry point to launch). These are Android's own identifiers, unrelated to Tosca — the same values any Android automation tool would need.

entries.title: Why iOS needs a Mac

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: XCUITest is Xcode-only
entries.text: iOS automation runs on XCUITest, Apple's own UI testing framework, which is only accessible through Xcode — and Xcode only installs on macOS. There is no Windows or Linux equivalent, so TMA cannot drive an iOS device or simulator unless it is running on a Mac.

entries.title: Preparing a physical iOS device

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Using the iOS Simulator

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Simulator vs physical device
entries.text: The iOS Simulator, launched through Xcode, runs an iOS runtime on the Mac itself rather than on real hardware — no cable, no Developer Mode toggle, no Trust prompt. It's the fastest way to get started, but it cannot exercise hardware-dependent behaviour (camera, real biometrics, cellular, certain sensors) the way a physical device can.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: Identifiers: UDID and BundleID

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: UDID — identifying the device
entries.text: Every physical iOS device and every simulator instance has a UDID (Unique Device Identifier). For a physical device, it's visible in Xcode's Window → Devices and Simulators panel, or via the command line with xcrun xctrace list devices. Simulators are identified the same way, listed alongside physical devices in that same command's output.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.title: BundleID — identifying the app
entries.text: iOS apps are identified by a BundleID (a reverse-domain string like com.company.appname) — the iOS equivalent of Android's AppPackage. Unlike Android, iOS has no separate 'activity' concept to also supply; the BundleID alone is enough to tell Open Mobile App which installed app to open.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: The same TCP mechanism used elsewhere in Tosca
entries.text: The connection to a device, emulator, or simulator is established through test configuration parameters — the identical mechanism used for the TestDataService endpoint, for SelfHealing, and elsewhere in Tosca. The same scoping rules (Project → Configuration → environment overrides) apply here too.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Static vs Dynamic device allocation

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Static allocation
entries.text: The DeviceName TCP is pinned to one specific device's identifier (a udid, or a specific emulator id). Every run always targets that exact device — the right choice whenever a test needs to run consistently on a specific device, e.g. verifying a bug that only reproduces on one particular phone model or OS version.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Dynamic allocation
entries.text: DeviceName carries a wildcard rather than one fixed identifier, matching against criteria (e.g. any Android device meeting a Platform/OS filter) instead of a specific udid. TMA hands out whichever matching device is currently free. This favours throughput and parallelization across a device pool over consistency on one exact device.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Local (TMA)
entries.text: Device/emulator/simulator on the same machine as TMA, and TMA on the same machine as Tosca Commander. TMAServer typically points at http://localhost:8585/ or http://127.0.0.1:8585/.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Remote (TMA)
entries.text: TMA runs on a different machine than Tosca Commander — commonly used when Tosca Commander runs in a VM or on Windows but the device/emulator needs to be on a different physical machine (a Mac, for iOS; a native host, for an emulator a VM can't run).

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Diagnosing device-side vs Tosca-side

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 5 - Connecting Tosca to TMA: TCPs, Local vs Remote
entries.title: Query TMA's REST API directly
entries.text: A GET request to http://<TMA-host>:<port>/api/devices returns JSON describing every device TMA currently sees — udid, name, connected, busy, and statusReady fields. If that call shows connected:true and busy:false, the device side is proven healthy and the fault must be on Tosca's side — saving time that would otherwise go into chasing proxy, firewall, or network theories that don't apply.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: One wizard, three app types
entries.text: The Mobile Scan handles native, hybrid, and web applications on mobile through the same wizard. The high-level sequence is always: prepare the test environment, start the Mobile Scan and connect to your device, then add the mobile device, emulator, or simulator you want to scan against. From there, scanning produces Modules the same way it does for any other Engine.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation

entries.title: Configuring Capabilities

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: The wizard's three panes
entries.text: The Mobile Scan dialog is organised into three panes that get filled in top to bottom: Select connection (Add connection, or a saved Local/Remote connection), Select device (filterable by Platform and OS Version, showing tiles for each device/simulator TMA currently sees), and Select application (Add app, or pick an app already scanned before, like a Tricentis-provided sample app).

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Desired Capabilities
entries.text: Below device/app selection, Set capabilities opens a Capabilities dialog where individual Appium Desired Capabilities can be added — each is an appium:-prefixed key and a value, the same capability mechanism any Appium-based automation session configures, just exposed through Tosca's UI instead of code.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Capability Sets — reusable, named bundles
entries.text: Rather than re-entering the same capabilities on every scan, Add capability set saves a named group of Desired Capabilities (e.g. 'Close Permissions/Alerts') that can later be reapplied in one click via Select Capability Set — while Add capability still adds one-off, ungrouped entries to the current session.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Scanning a native app

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: What gets captured
entries.text: For a native app, each captured control is identified by native accessibility properties — resource-id (Android) or accessibility identifier (iOS), class/type, text/label, and position — the same properties a native Appium-based tool would report. Screens are typically organised into separate Modules mirroring the app's own screen structure.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Scanning a hybrid app

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Native shell, embedded webview
entries.text: A hybrid app wraps one or more web views inside a native shell. From the outside it looks and behaves like a native app, but part or all of its content is actually rendered as HTML/CSS/JS inside an embedded browser engine.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Context switching during scan
entries.text: The Mobile Scan needs to know whether it's currently looking at native chrome (the shell's own tab bar, native buttons) or webview content (the embedded HTML). Switching context during scanning is what lets the same scan capture both native controls surrounding the webview and the DOM-based controls inside it, using the appropriate identification strategy for each.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: Scanning mobile web

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 6 - Mobile Scan: Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: The device's own browser, scanned in its device context
entries.text: For mobile web, the Mobile Scan opens the target site inside the device's own mobile browser rather than a desktop XBrowser session. This captures the page with the actual mobile viewport, mobile-specific rendering, and touch-driven interaction model — closer to how a real user on that device experiences the site than a desktop browser scan resized to a phone width would be.

entries.title: Open Mobile App comes first, always

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: The mandatory first TestStep
entries.text: Drag and drop the Open Mobile App Module onto the TestCase — and note the hard constraint: it must be the first TestStep of the TestCase. Nothing can be steered on the device until the application has been opened through this Module.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: What Open Mobile App actually does
entries.text: It's more than a click-through step: Open Mobile App creates the mobile device session (via TMA) for the TestCase, and it can install the app on the device at the start of that session if an install source (a local .apk path, or the equivalent iOS install path) is configured — or, for an app already on the device, open it directly by its identifier: BundleID for iOS, or AppPackage/AppActivity for Android.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: Switch Mobile App
entries.text: For TestCases that move between apps mid-flow (e.g. testing a deep link handoff, or a share-sheet interaction that opens a different app), Switch Mobile App changes the active app context without needing a second Open Mobile App step.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation

entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: Send Text Input To Focused Control
entries.text: Enters text into whichever control currently has focus — typically used right after tapping a text field, mirroring how a real user would tap then type.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: Set Autohide Keyboard
entries.text: Controls whether the on-screen keyboard automatically dismisses after a text-entry step. Leaving the keyboard open when the next TestStep expects to interact with an element it's now covering is a common source of flaky steps — this setting exists specifically to manage that.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: Running with LiveView

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Lesson 7 - Building Your First Mobile TestCase
entries.title: Watching execution happen
entries.text: With the LiveView TCP set to True, executing a mobile TestCase shows the device's screen updating in near-real-time inside Tosca — genuinely useful while a TestCase is still being built and debugged, since a failed TestStep can be visually correlated with exactly what the device was showing at that moment.

entries.title: A dedicated Module for a transient component
entries.text: Android Snackbar steers the Android Snackbar component specifically — the brief, auto-dismissing message bar that appears at the bottom of the screen (e.g. 'Item deleted — Undo'). Because it disappears on its own after a short delay, generic control-steering can miss it entirely; this dedicated Module exists to interact with it reliably within its visible window.

entries.title: From 'an emulator exists' to 'TMA can drive it'
entries.text: The Getting Started course covers creating an AVD as one step among many. This course treats AVD creation and TMA integration as their own dedicated part — because in practice, a surprising share of 'automation isn't working' reports trace back to an AVD that boots and looks fine but was never actually wired up correctly for TMA to use.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 1: AVD Setup & TMA Integration
entries.title: Picking the system image on purpose
entries.text: The API level chosen here determines which Android behaviours the AVD exhibits — permission dialog styles, Developer Mode specifics, security defaults. Matching the system image to whatever real-world Android version the app under test actually targets (or needs to be verified against) avoids automating against a device that behaves differently from production.

entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 1: AVD Setup & TMA Integration
entries.title: Wiring DeviceName to the AVD
entries.text: Once the AVD shows Ready with its emulator-#### identifier, that exact string is what goes into the DeviceName TCP for a static, pinned connection to this specific AVD instance. The identifier is tied to the running emulator process — if the AVD is closed and relaunched, it is not guaranteed to receive the same port/identifier.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 2: Testing Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: What stays the same across all three
entries.text: Regardless of app type, every mobile TestCase starts with Open Mobile App, steers scanned Modules with the same TestStepValue/ActionMode mechanics as any other Tosca TestCase, and verifies outcomes with the same Buffer/Verify actions. The Getting Started course covered this shape once (Lesson 7); this part is about applying it three times, deliberately, against each app type's specific quirks.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 2: Testing Native, Hybrid & Web Apps
entries.title: What actually changes
entries.text: Native: control identification relies purely on platform accessibility properties. Hybrid: the TestCase must explicitly manage native/webview context switches mid-flow. Web: steering happens inside the device browser's DOM, closer to an XBrowser TestCase in spirit but running through the Mobile Engine.

entries.title: Context switches belong in the TestCase, not just the scan
entries.text: A hybrid TestCase needs the same native/webview context switching used during scanning to also happen during execution, at the right points in the TestStep sequence — steer the native shell's tab bar, switch to webview context to steer the embedded content, switch back to native context to steer whatever surrounds it next.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 3: Dynamic Device Allocation
entries.title: Where this picks up
entries.text: The Getting Started course introduced Static vs Dynamic device allocation as a concept — pin one device, or let TMA hand out any matching one. This part is about actually configuring the dynamic side: the wildcard syntax, the criteria that matter, and what changes operationally once a TestCase no longer targets one specific device.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 3: Dynamic Device Allocation
entries.title: Configuring the wildcard

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 3: Dynamic Device Allocation
entries.title: DeviceName as a criterion, not an identifier
entries.text: Instead of a specific udid or emulator-#### value, the DeviceName TCP is set to the literal wildcard TOSCA_DYNAMIC_DEVICE_SELECTION. TMA resolves that wildcard against its currently-known device pool at connection time — handing out whichever Ready, non-Busy device satisfies the remaining criteria (Platform, OS Version, device type).

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 3: Dynamic Device Allocation
entries.title: How TMA resolves a dynamic match

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 3: Dynamic Device Allocation
entries.title: Resolution at connection time
entries.text: When a TestCase with a dynamic DeviceName connects, TMA evaluates the pool of devices it currently sees, filters to those matching the criteria, and hands out one that's Ready and not Busy. Which specific device gets picked is not something a TestCase controls or should assume — the same TestCase run twice in a row can legitimately land on two different physical devices.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 4: Troubleshooting with TMA
entries.title: Why this deserves a dedicated part
entries.text: Mobile automation setup spans several independent layers — the device/emulator, TMA, the network path between TMA and Tosca, and Tosca's own TCP configuration. A failure at any one layer can produce a symptom that looks like it belongs to a different layer entirely (the recurring theme across this whole course). Troubleshooting effectively means having a fixed order to check those layers in, rather than guessing based on where the error message points.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 4: Troubleshooting with TMA
entries.title: Why go past the console
entries.text: The TMA console's device list gives a status summary; TMA's underlying logs give the actual detail behind a session that failed to start, including the raw driver-level (Appium/UiAutomator2/XCUITest) error that the Tosca-side error message often paraphrases or, as with the trailing-slash case, mischaracterizes entirely.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Automating Mobile Apps on TMA — Part 4: Troubleshooting with TMA
entries.title: Session ID as the log's lookup key
entries.text: Each session TMA creates carries a Session ID, and every log line produced by that session is tagged with it. A log file typically holds several runs one after another, so the Session ID is what lets you jump straight to the one execution under investigation instead of reading the whole file — it identifies a session in the log, nothing more; it isn't used to steer controls or edit TestCase data.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: What this course covers

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: Why image-based identification exists

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: The gap it fills
entries.text: Every identification strategy covered so far depends on the application exposing something addressable: a resource-id, an accessibility identifier, a DOM node. Some controls expose none of that. Canvas-rendered content, custom-drawn widgets, embedded video or map surfaces, chart libraries that paint pixels rather than build a view hierarchy. For those, no amount of scanning discipline produces a usable property set, because the properties genuinely are not there.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: What IBTA matches on
entries.text: Image-Based Test Automation identifies a control by comparing a stored reference image against what is currently rendered on screen, and acting at the location where it matches. The identity of the control is its appearance. Nothing else about it is being checked.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: What breaks an image match

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: Matching tolerance
entries.text: Image matching is not exact-pixel equality; a similarity threshold decides how close a region must be to count as a match. Loosening it absorbs small rendering differences but raises the chance of matching the wrong region, particularly in a UI with repeated visual elements such as a list of similar cards. Tightening it does the reverse. There is no setting that removes the trade-off, only one that moves it.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Image-Based Test Automation (IBTA)
entries.title: Choosing between image-based and property-based
