entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: Two jobs, one mechanism

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: Connection TCPs versus tuning TCPs
entries.text: The earlier courses used TCPs to answer a single question: which agent and which device. TMAServer, DeviceName, Type. Those are connection parameters, and a wrong value there means nothing runs at all. This course adds a second category: parameters that assume the connection already works and instead shape how the run behaves. A wrong value there does not stop the run. It makes it slower, less stable, or less informative, which is considerably harder to notice.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: Parameters that shape a run

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: Reset application and test independence
entries.text: Skipping the reset is tempting because it makes a run start faster, and it works fine while you are executing one TestCase at a time by hand. It stops working the moment TestCases run in sequence or in parallel, because each one inherits state from whatever ran before it. The symptom is a TestCase that passes alone and fails in a suite, which is one of the most time-consuming failure patterns to diagnose.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: Scoping, and why it starts mattering here

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Mobile-Specific TCPs for Execution Tuning
entries.title: The same TestCase, several environments
entries.text: TCPs follow Tosca's normal scoping rules, so a value set at Project level can be overridden by a Configuration and again per environment. While everything runs on one local emulator, this is invisible. It becomes the central mechanism the moment the same TestCases have to run against a local emulator during development and a shared device pool in CI, because only the configuration should differ between those two, never the TestCases.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Where Module properties sit

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Fix it once, not in every TestCase
entries.text: A Module describes a control: how to find it and how to interact with it. Every TestCase that steers that control inherits the description. So a property adjusted on the Module applies everywhere the control is used, while the same adjustment made inside a TestCase applies to that TestCase alone. When the same control misbehaves across several TestCases, the Module is the correct place to fix it, and fixing it in each TestCase instead is how a workaround gets copied twenty times.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Identification properties

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Choosing what identifies the control
entries.text: A scan captures several properties per control and selects some of them to identify it. That automatic selection is a starting point rather than a verdict. Properties that look stable in one scan can turn out to be dynamic in practice, such as text that is localised, an index that shifts when a list reorders, or a coordinate that moves with screen size. Editing which properties participate in identification is how a Module is made resilient without touching a single TestCase.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Steering properties and realistic interaction

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Module Properties for Realistic Interaction
entries.title: Why realistic matters on mobile
entries.text: A framework can often set a value directly on a control, which is fast and reliable and completely unlike what a user does. Mobile UIs frequently attach behaviour to the interaction itself rather than to the resulting value: validation that runs on blur, a picker that only commits on confirm, a list that lazy-loads as it scrolls, an animation that has to finish before the next control accepts input. Automation that sets values directly can bypass all of that, which produces a TestCase that passes while the user-facing flow is broken.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.text: Handling advanced mobile automation use cases with Tricentis Tosca Mobile · Appium Desired Capabilities (official Appium docs)

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: What a capability actually is

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Session-level configuration, not TestCase logic
entries.text: Desired Capabilities are passed when the automation session is created, so they configure the session rather than any individual step. Two consequences follow. A capability applies to everything in that session, and changing one means the session has to be recreated. This is why capabilities belong in configuration rather than being toggled mid-flow, and why a Capability Set is a sensible unit to name and reuse.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Grouping them by what they control

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Why grouping helps
entries.text: Capability lists are long and mostly irrelevant to any given project, so memorising them is wasted effort. Knowing which group a problem falls into is what makes the list navigable: a run interrupted by a popup, a TestCase polluted by leftover state, a session dying during a long wait, and text landing in the wrong place are four different categories, and each has its own small set of candidates.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: The cost nobody mentions

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Suppress broadly, verify deliberately
entries.text: The workable position is not to avoid these capabilities, because runs that stall on OS dialogs are worse. It is to accept that suppression is the default for the bulk of the suite while keeping at least one TestCase that deliberately does not suppress, so the dialog behaviour itself stays under test somewhere.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Capability Sets versus one-off entries

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Advanced Use Cases - Additional Appium Capabilities
entries.title: Naming a bundle you will reuse
entries.text: A Capability Set groups several capabilities under a name, such as a Close Permissions/Alerts set holding autoGrantPermissions and autoAcceptAlerts, and applies them in one action. A single Add capability entry configures one value for the session at hand. The distinction is reuse: anything the whole suite needs belongs in a named set, while something genuinely specific to one scenario does not.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Beyond the local machine

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Where this part picks up
entries.text: Everything up to this point runs one TestCase, from one Tosca Commander, against one TMA and one device. The advanced use cases are about what changes when that stops being true: many executions across many agents (Tosca Distributed Execution), or execution owned by a hosted platform instead of a workstation (Tosca Cloud).

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Tosca Distributed Execution (DEX)

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: TestEvents and ExecutionList configurations
entries.text: Distributed Execution does not work by hand-picking which TestCase goes to which machine. Executions are managed through TestEvents together with ExecutionList configurations — the TestEvent defines what should run, and the ExecutionList configuration defines how, while agents pick the work up from there. Assignment is configuration-driven, not manual.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Tosca Cloud

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Uploading an ExecutionList
entries.text: Tosca Commander can upload TestCases in bulk, and entire ExecutionLists, to Tosca Cloud. An uploaded ExecutionList becomes a Tosca Cloud playlist — playlists are Cloud's own execution unit, managed under Run → Playlists. The ExecutionList is not deleted, not restricted to local machines, and does not block other executions; it is converted into the equivalent Cloud object.

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: What this means for mobile specifically

entries.trackName: Tricentis Tosca Mobile - Getting Started with Mobile Test Automation
entries.moduleTitle: Handling Advanced Mobile Automation Use Cases
entries.title: Distribution raises the stakes on device configuration
entries.text: Once executions are distributed or cloud-triggered, nobody is watching a LiveView window when something goes wrong. A TestCase pinned to one static device blocks every other run needing that device, and a TestCase carrying device-specific assumptions fails unpredictably across a pool. Dynamic device allocation and disciplined capability filters stop being conveniences and become prerequisites.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Web Testing Getting Started (Codeless Test) (Tricentis docs) · Recording a Web Test (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Recording: the starting point of every test

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: The AUT browser
entries.text: Creating a test starts by navigating to the relevant website inside the Application Under Test (AUT) browser window and recording the series of actions you want tested — clicks, text entry, scrolling, navigation. Testim captures each action as a step.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Steps
entries.text: Each recorded action becomes a step, shown as a box in the test procedure with an icon in its upper-left corner indicating the action type (click, enter text, scroll, etc.). Steps run top-to-bottom in the order they were recorded, and can be reordered, edited, or deleted afterward.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Smart Locators: why the test doesn't break on every UI change

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Smart Locators
entries.text: When an element is selected during recording, Testim's algorithm analyzes potentially hundreds of attributes associated with that element and assigns weights to them to uniquely identify it. These weighted attributes are the element's Locators. Smart Locators also learn with each test run — if some attributes change, Testim falls back to other still-valid attributes instead of failing outright.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Saving a test and viewing results

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Saving
entries.text: A recorded test is saved into the project's Test Library, where it can be organized into folders, labeled, and re-run at any time — locally, from the editor, from the CLI, or on a schedule.

entries.moduleTitle: Creating your first codeless test in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Viewing results
entries.text: After a run, Testim reports pass/fail per step and per test, and surfaces the reason a step failed (e.g. element not found, element not visible) so you can diagnose without re-watching a full manual re-run.

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.text: Testim overview (Tricentis docs) · Running Tests Overview (Tricentis docs) · Validation (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: The Testim visual editor

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Visual, codeless-first editing
entries.text: Testim's visual test editor has features built directly into the UI so that customizing a test — reordering steps, editing properties, adding validations — does not require writing code, while still allowing custom JavaScript steps for advanced cases (covered later in this learning path).

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Base URL
entries.text: Each project/test has a base URL — the starting address the AUT browser opens before a recording or run begins. Getting the base URL right (and open) is a prerequisite for actions like Reassign and Improve on a target element, which need the AUT browser open at that URL to let you re-select an element.

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Running tests: editor vs. Test List

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Running from the editor
entries.text: Clicking Play in the editor's toolbar opens a new browser and runs the currently open test's actions against the AUT. This is the fastest feedback loop while actively building or editing a single test.

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Running from the Test List
entries.text: One or more tests can be selected in the Test List (Ctrl/Cmd-click for multiple) and run together with the Play button. Tests run this way execute locally, which is useful for quickly re-checking a batch of related tests without leaving the Test List view.

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: From actions to assertions: basic validations

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Why validations matter
entries.text: A recording by itself only proves the AUT can be clicked through without crashing — it does not verify the application behaved correctly. Validation steps turn a recording into a real test by asserting specific, expected outcomes.

entries.moduleTitle: Tricentis Testim Fundamentals − Creating Automated Tests
entries.title: Core validation types
entries.text: Validate element visible checks that an expected element is present on the page. Validate element text checks that a specific text value appears in a specified element (Testim supports Regex in the Expected Value field). Validate element not visible checks the opposite — that an element has disappeared, e.g. after closing a modal.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Editing Target Element Properties (Tricentis docs) · Shared Steps (Tricentis docs) · Steps (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: The target element and its Properties panel

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Target element
entries.text: The target element is the element that was selected in the AUT (Application Under Test) browser as the main element for a step. It is shown as a thumbnail image in the step's Properties panel, and it is fully editable after the step has been recorded.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Opening the Properties panel
entries.text: Hovering over any step in the test and clicking Show Properties opens the Properties panel on the right-hand side. From there, hovering over the target element thumbnail reveals four options: Highlight, Reassign, Improve, and View locators.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: The four Target Element options

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Highlight
entries.text: Opens the AUT browser with the target element momentarily highlighted in pink. It changes nothing — it exists purely so you can visually confirm, during editing, that the correct element is targeted for a step.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Reassign
entries.text: Replaces the target element with a completely different element from the AUT: the system removes and overrides all existing locators for that step. Use it when the original element no longer exists at all — for example, a blue 'Login' button was removed and replaced by an entirely different control.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Improve
entries.text: Used when the SAME target element still exists but the DOM around it changed. Testim compares the existing locators to newly collected ones and updates (merges into) them rather than overriding them — examining which selectors changed, which stayed the same, and which disappeared. Example: the 'Login' button is still the same button, but its text changed from 'login' to 'LOG-IN' and its color changed. Improve — not Reassign — is the correct choice here, because it is the same element, not a different one.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: View locators
entries.text: Opens the Locators panel, showing exactly how Testim's Smart Locators identify the target element and its parent elements. Testim's algorithm inspects potentially hundreds of attributes on an element, assigns each a weight, and uses the highest-weighted ones to find the element on future runs — so if some attributes change, the Smart Locator can still find the element using the others.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Specialized step properties

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Expected value
entries.text: The value Testim checks for when the step runs (used by Validate element text, Validate CSS property, Validate HTML attribute, Wait for element text). It's editable after the step is created, and — importantly — it isn't limited to a literal string: Parameters, regular expressions, and JavaScript expressions can all be used in the Expected value field.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Expected status (checkboxes / radio buttons)
entries.text: Used by Validate checkbox and Validate radio button to set whether the step expects Checked (the default) or Unchecked. These validations only work on native checkbox/radio input elements — a custom checkbox implementation that doesn't use an underlying native input isn't supported.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Add Prefix / Add Suffix / String type / Length
entries.text: Properties of a Generate random value step. Add Prefix/Suffix attach a fixed string to every generated value (e.g. prefix 'User' → User47, User65, User32). String type controls whether the generated value uses letters only, numbers only, or both. Length sets how long the generated value is.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Date format / Time difference / Use UTC
entries.text: Properties of a Generate date step. The default date format is 'YYYY-MM-DD', but it can be changed to any JS date format. Time difference offsets the generated date/time before or after the current browser time (or UTC). Use UTC switches the reference time zone from the browser's local time to UTC.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Extract Mode
entries.text: On an Add extract value step, Extract Mode controls what data type is pulled from the matched text — by default the entire string, but it can be narrowed to a number, a date, or a regular-expression match for just part of the text. Even when extracting a Number/Date/Regular-Exp, the resulting extracted value is still stored as a string.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Variable name and Variable scope
entries.text: Add extract value step, Get cookie, Generate random value, and Generate date steps all store their result in a variable — Variable name sets what that variable is called (subject to JavaScript naming rules: no spaces or special characters). Variable scope controls where it can be referenced: Local (within the same group, or the same test if declared at test level), Test (the default — across steps and groups in the same test), or Suite (across tests in the same test suite).

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Native events (Click step)
entries.text: A Click step can be configured, at the project level, to fire as a Native event (the browser's real, built-in click-handling pipeline — what happens on an actual mouse click or tap) or a Non-Native event (a synthetic/programmatic click dispatched via JavaScript, simulating the interaction). If a Click step reports as passed but the click visibly didn't do anything in the AUT, toggling the Native events checkbox is a standard troubleshooting step.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Pre-step delay (ms)
entries.text: Available on Validate element not visible and Wait for element not visible. By default there's no delay, but you can set one (in milliseconds) to first wait before checking that an element is absent — useful when you want to make sure an element doesn't suddenly appear a moment later, not just that it's absent right now.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Sleep duration
entries.text: The property of a Sleep step — how long (in ms) the test pauses before the next step. The default is 1 second (1,000 ms), and it's directly editable.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: +PARAMS
entries.text: Available on custom/API/network steps (Add custom action, Add API action, Add custom validation, Validate API, Add network validation, Add custom wait for). Clicking the + next to PARAMS lets you define HTML and JS parameters for the step, so it can be reused to test different scenarios without hardcoding the values in advance.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Auto complete
entries.text: While recording a test, Testim watches for a match against your existing Shared Groups and suggests them as the next steps — a pop-up labeled 'Auto record your steps' appears above the steps counter listing the matching suggestions. Clicking a suggestion has Testim automatically perform and save those steps in the test being recorded, instead of you re-recording a sequence you've already built elsewhere. If the matched group has parameters, you're prompted to name them and supply values before the steps are added. This feature is available on the professional plan.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Replace with a clone / See old revisions
entries.text: Replace with a clone detaches a step from a Shared Step so an edit affects only this one test, instead of every test using that shared step. See old revisions opens the list of automatically-saved prior versions of the test (change message, user, date) whenever a change is saved — including changes to a shared step — letting you inspect or revert to an earlier revision.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Reusable editing: groups and Shared Steps

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Groups
entries.text: Steps can be grouped together, and groups can be nested inside other groups. A group is identified in the test by a folder icon in its upper-left corner.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Shared Steps / Shared Group
entries.text: Selecting the Shared Group checkbox on a group makes it callable from other tests in the project — not just copy-pasted, but referenced, so a single edit to the shared group propagates to every test that uses it. This is the core mechanism for reusable, maintainable test authoring (e.g. a login sequence built once and reused everywhere).

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Shared Steps Library
entries.text: A dedicated library view listing every shared step, group, and folder in the project, with four columns: Name, Date Modified, Kind (shared step / group / folder, plus the underlying step type), and Used by (a clickable count of how many tests reference that item — clicking it navigates to the Test Library filtered to just those tests). The library can be filtered by category: Groups, Actions, Validations, and Wait for.

entries.moduleTitle: How to edit tests in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Labels
entries.text: A lightweight organizational tool applied to tests in the Test Library, letting you categorize and quickly find tests without moving them between folders. A test can carry multiple labels at once (e.g. 'smoke', 'checkout'), and the library can be filtered or searched by label — useful once a project's test count grows past what folders alone can keep navigable. (Covered in more depth, alongside folders and dependencies, in the 'Advanced test management' module.)

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Conditions (Tricentis docs) · Advanced Conditions Settings (Tricentis docs) · Parameters (Tricentis docs) · Wait for (Tricentis docs) · Search Within a Test (Tricentis docs) · Recovering a test that was not saved (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Conditions: running steps only when it makes sense

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Conditions
entries.text: Conditions can be applied to a step (run it or not) or to a loop (repeat it or not). If a condition is false, the default behavior is to skip the step immediately or end the loop immediately; if true, the step executes or the loop repeats immediately.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Condition types
entries.text: Testim supports several condition types, including Element (does an element exist/is it visible), Element text (does an element contain specific text), and Custom (a JavaScript expression you write yourself) — covering everything from simple presence checks to fully custom runtime logic.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Advanced condition settings — retry
entries.text: By default, a false condition immediately skips the step (or ends the loop). The 'retry' setting changes this: you specify a period in milliseconds during which Testim keeps re-checking the condition before giving up and moving on — useful for conditions tied to asynchronous UI states that need a moment to resolve.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Setting a Custom condition on a step
entries.text: To attach a Custom (JavaScript) condition to a step or shared step: open the step, click the gear icon to open its Properties, find 'When to run step' (or 'When to run this step'), and select Custom — this opens the field where the JavaScript condition expression is written.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Parameters: variable data instead of hardcoded values

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Parameters
entries.text: A parameter is a variable that can be used to pass information into a test step, letting the same step or group work with different data without needing separate, near-duplicate steps for each scenario.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Parameters on groups
entries.text: Groups can define their own parameters. If a group is shared across multiple tests, those parameters remain available to every calling test — each test just sets its own values for the parameters rather than duplicating the group's underlying steps.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Generating dynamic test data: random values and dates

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Generate random value
entries.text: Found under the predefined steps menu ('M' icon) → Actions → Generate random value. Produces a random string (letters, numbers, or both, via String type), with optional Add Prefix / Add Suffix and a configurable Length — used to avoid hardcoding a value that must be unique or unpredictable on every run, like a test username or email local-part.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Generate date
entries.text: Also under the predefined steps menu → Actions → Generate date. Produces a date value offset from the current browser time (or UTC), controlled by Time difference and Use UTC, with a configurable Date format (default 'YYYY-MM-DD', or any JS date format).

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Finding your way around: search and draft recovery

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Search within a test
entries.text: Typing at least three characters into a test's search field searches across the test's Step description, JS Code, Parameters, Base URL, the URL inside a Navigation Step or an Add API Action step, Test Data, and Condition — a broad sweep across nearly everything a step can contain, not just visible step names. The search is not case sensitive.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Recovering an unsaved test
entries.text: Changes to a test are auto-saved locally as a draft in the browser's cache every 30 seconds. If the browser closes, you log out, the page reloads, or anything else interrupts editing on the same computer, reopening the test shows a recovery dialog with two choices: Recover opens the draft with the unsaved changes intact; Dismiss discards the draft and opens the test in its last saved state instead. After recovering, it's recommended to click Save — the auto-recovery draft itself isn't meant to be relied on as permanent storage.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Wait For: condition-based waiting instead of fixed delays

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test customization in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Wait For step
entries.text: Rather than inserting an arbitrary fixed-time delay (which either wastes time or isn't long enough), a Wait For step pauses the test until a specific condition becomes true — for example, an element becoming visible — before continuing to the next step.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Keyboard Shortcut Step (Tricentis docs) · Parameter override rules (Tricentis docs) · Extract Value Step (Tricentis docs) · Wait for (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Keyboard Shortcut steps

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Add Keyboard Shortcut step
entries.text: Sends a specified keyboard shortcut combination (e.g. Ctrl+C) to the AUT during execution — added like other predefined Actions. It's cross-platform by design: a shortcut recorded on Windows (e.g. Ctrl+C) is automatically translated to its Mac equivalent (Cmd+C) at execution time, and vice versa.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Setting the shortcut in Properties
entries.text: In the step's Properties panel, under the Keyboard Shortcut section, placing the cursor in the Windows field and pressing the keys (all at once) auto-fills the equivalent in the Mac field — or the reverse, starting from the Mac field. Whichever platform the test actually runs on at execution time, Testim uses the corresponding field.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Unsupported combinations
entries.text: Not every possible key combination is supported. If you use a keyboard shortcut Testim doesn't recognize, it presents an 'unsupported keyboard shortcut' error rather than silently ignoring it, defaulting to something else, or blocking the whole test from running.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Parameters: flexible test step customization

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Why parameterize
entries.text: Parameters let a step or group be customized per use — passing in different information without knowing every value in advance — so the same underlying steps serve multiple scenarios instead of being copy-pasted with small edits each time.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Parameter override rules
entries.text: When both parameters and test data could supply a value for the same field, parameters take precedence over test data. Within Testim's layered override system specifically, config-file parameters override params-file parameters, and — within the config file — a beforeTest hook's values override a beforeSuite hook's values; params-file parameters, in turn, override the default test data/run data.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Extract Value: capturing data for later steps

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Extract Value step
entries.text: The Extract Mode of an Extract Value step determines the value and format of the contents captured into an extract variable — for example, pulling an order number or a generated OTP code off the page and storing it so a later step can use or validate it. Selecting the mode is done directly in the step's own Properties, not through code, and not through a project-level setting.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Wait for Events: synchronizing tests with the application

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Waiting for an event, not a fixed time
entries.text: Testim can wait for a specific event to occur before proceeding to the next step — an element becoming visible, specific text appearing, or a file finishing its download — rather than a plain, guessed time delay. This is the same condition-based-waiting principle covered for basic Wait For steps, applied to a broader set of real application events.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Wait for element visible / not visible
entries.text: Wait for element visible pauses until a target element appears; Wait for element not visible pauses until an element disappears (e.g. a loading spinner clearing). Both are added the same way as other predefined steps: hover the arrow, open Testim's predefined steps, pick the step, then select the target element.

entries.moduleTitle: Mastering advanced editing techniques in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Changing the element after the fact
entries.text: If the wrong element was targeted (or the element changed), the fix is the same as for any other step's target element: open the step's Properties and use Reassign to point it at a different element — not deleting and re-recording the step, and not just adjusting the wait duration (which doesn't fix a wrong target).

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Run multiple tests locally (Tricentis docs) · Scheduler - Web (Tricentis docs) · Secrets Manager (Tricentis docs) · Execution Runs Screen (Tricentis docs) · Test runs (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Running multiple tests locally and on a schedule

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Run multiple tests locally
entries.text: From Test List > Tests, selecting several tests and running them takes control of your mouse and runs the selected tests sequentially in your local Chrome browser (local runs are Chrome-only). Because Testim is actively driving the browser, you should not use your mouse or computer while the tests run. Locally-run tests are tracked and viewable afterward under Runs > Executions, tagged 'local-suite'.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Scheduler
entries.text: Lets you schedule tests to run on a predefined schedule (the test must carry a Label or belong to a Test Suite), with options for Where to run (which grid) and Branch. A schedule can be cloned, modified, and saved as a new schedule — reducing the effort and risk of manually recreating a similar configuration. The Scheduler is especially valuable for teams that don't have CI/CD tooling in place: it provides built-in, manually-defined scheduled execution without needing a Jenkins/GitHub Actions/Azure DevOps pipeline to trigger runs.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Incognito mode and the Configuration File

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Incognito mode (Testim IO)
entries.text: Running tests in Incognito mode starts each execution from a fresh browser state — no cookies, no local storage, nothing remembered from a prior run. This is the primary benefit: a clean, predictable starting point every time, rather than saved login states or stored cookies leaking between runs and masking real issues (like whether a login flow genuinely still works).

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Configuration File with the CLI
entries.text: A Configuration File passed to the CLI is the main mechanism for keeping sensitive values (credentials, tokens) out of the test itself. Rather than hardcoding a password into a step, hidden parameters and encrypted credentials can be supplied through the Configuration File (or a JSON Parameters File) at run time — Testim explicitly recommends against exposing sensitive information in plain text or version history, pointing instead to the Configuration File, Hidden Parameters, and the Secrets Manager.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Timeouts and retries

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test timeout
entries.text: A timeout period (in milliseconds) aborts a test run if it's exceeded. The default is 10 minutes, with a maximum of 3 hours — long enough for legitimately slow flows, but still a hard ceiling against a genuinely hung run.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Timeout retry
entries.text: By default, when a test fails specifically due to 'test reached timeout', Testim automatically re-executes it — up to 3 times — before marking it failed. This default can be disabled with the --disable-timeout-retry CLI flag when you want a timeout to fail immediately and be investigated rather than retried.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Failed-test retries
entries.text: Separately, failed-test retries can be configured to re-run any failed test repeatedly until it either passes or the max retry count is reached — a broader mechanism than the timeout-specific retry, aimed at absorbing general flakiness rather than one specific failure cause.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Diagnosing a failure and reading the Execution Runs view

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Diagnosing why a test failed
entries.text: Beyond just an error message, comparing the run's baseline (expected) screenshot against its result (actual) screenshot is one of the most direct ways to see exactly what went wrong visually — a layout shift, an unexpected error banner, a missing element — rather than immediately re-running blind or reading console logs in isolation.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Execution Runs view
entries.text: The runs graph gives an overview of the number of executions and tests per execution over time, plotting duration on one axis against time, and showing Concurrency (how many executions ran at the same time as a given one). Hovering an entry surfaces further details: Extension Version, Source (local vs. remote), CLI Version, Grid Name, and the Test Data (parameters) used for that run.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: The Test Runs view: statistics across past runs

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test Runs / Test statistics
entries.text: The Test Runs screen shows statistics on past runs — aggregated across all selected tests, and per-test (e.g. how many times a specific test passed/failed and its average test duration) — under the Test statistics section. Filters (status, time, execution/label) narrow what's shown, and clicking a specific run opens it in the Test Editor to drill into per-step screenshots and durations.

entries.moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Counted runs vs. Local Editor Runs
entries.text: Remote execution runs — suite runs, plan runs, scheduled runs, and label-triggered runs — are the 'counted' runs shown in the main Test Runs view. Tests run directly from the editor are tracked separately, in their own 'Local Editor Runs' tab, and are explicitly excluded from (not counted toward) the subscription-quota-relevant Test Runs statistics.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Test Status (Tricentis docs) · Shared Steps Library (Tricentis docs) · Revisions (Tricentis docs) · Test Plans - Web (Tricentis docs) · Test suites (Tricentis docs) · Locators: Auto Improve (Tricentis docs) · Testim Extension - Capture Video & Bug Scenario (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test Library: folders, labels, and test status

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Folders and labels
entries.text: Folders (create via + → New Folder) give tests a single-location home in the Test Library. Labels are applied/removed via Edit Labels (or right-click → Edit Labels) and, unlike folders, a test can carry several at once — better suited to cross-cutting groupings like 'smoke' or 'checkout'. Search the library with label:<name> to filter by a label.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test status
entries.text: Testim's built-in test statuses are Draft (not ready to be used yet — still in progress), Active (automatically applied to tests that ran in the last 30 days), Evaluating (ready, but stability still needs to be examined), and Quarantine (unstable — generating errors, waiting to be fixed). 'Failed' and 'Archived' are NOT Testim test statuses — 'Failed' describes a run's result, not the test's lifecycle status, and there is no 'Archived' status.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Shared Steps Library and Revisions

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Filtering the Shared Steps Library
entries.text: Clicking Advanced filters opens the Filter Shared Steps pane, letting you filter by step category (Groups, Actions, Validations, Wait for) — the same filtering pattern used elsewhere in Testim's library views, including surfacing steps that are otherwise hidden from the default view so they can be selected and unhidden.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Revisions
entries.text: Every time a test with changes is saved, the version before the change is automatically stored as a revision — no action is required to create one; it happens by itself on every save. After saving, a dialog optionally prompts for a change message describing the purpose of the change. The revision list (change message, user, date) lets you always look back and revert to an older revision.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test Plans and Test Suites

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test Plans - Web
entries.text: Test Plans model genuine environment setup/teardown around a run — preparing the environment before tests start, and cleaning up after. A Test Plan can be integrated with a CI tool by picking the specific CI tool your team uses and executing the test plan through that tool's pipeline, rather than being limited to local-only execution or manual copying of test cases.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Test Suites
entries.text: Test Suites group tests into a collection and let you control the order they run in — the two core benefits: organizing tests into collections, and running multiple tests in sequence in a defined order. (Order is only guaranteed for non-parallel runs — passing --parallel to a suite run no longer guarantees the sequence.) Test Suites do not automatically delete unused tests, and executing directly from CI tools is a separate CLI/CI-integration concern, not a Test Suite feature itself.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Locators: Auto Improve and Smart Locator confidence

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Locators: Auto Improve
entries.text: If a locator's score drops below 70%, Testim automatically attempts to improve that locator to enhance the test's stability. If the improvement succeeds, Testim replaces the degraded locator with the improved one and creates a test revision labeled 'Testim auto improve' — so the change is tracked, not silent.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Smart Locator confidence and changed attributes
entries.text: Smart Locators weight potentially hundreds of attributes per element. When an element's attributes change during a test run, the test can still pass — Smart Locators can typically still identify the element using its other, unchanged attributes — but the confidence score for that locator may decrease. A page-change warning is shown specifically when that confidence level varies by more than 20% compared to the originally recorded test.

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Bug Reporting with the Testim Extension

entries.moduleTitle: Advanced test management in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Capture Video & Bug Scenario
entries.text: The Testim (Chrome) Extension's Capture feature records a video of a bug scenario, generates a screenshot per step, and can publish it straight to a connected bug tracker (e.g. Jira, Trello). Before any of that is possible, the prerequisite is installing the Testim browser extension for Chrome — the capture/video functionality lives inside the extension, not the web editor itself.

entries.title: Validating Test Steps in Testim
entries.text: Validate CSS property (Tricentis docs) · Validating using custom code (Tricentis docs) · Extract Value Step (Tricentis docs)

entries.title: Validate CSS property
entries.text: Checks any CSS property of an element. Property name takes a valid CSS property for the selected element (e.g. color, display, font-weight); Expected value is what that property should equal. The expected value can be a hardcoded literal (wrapped in quotes, e.g. 'red') or a parameter (entered by name, without quotes) — the same pattern used across other validation types.

entries.title: Editing after creation
entries.text: The property name and/or expected value can be changed later without re-selecting the element. If the element itself needs to change, hover the target element thumbnail and click Reassign, then click the new element in the AUT window — the same Reassign mechanism used on any other step.

entries.title: Data-driven validation in a real flow
entries.text: A signup/login flow is a natural example of validating data-driven actions end to end: click Login triggers navigation, a Validate element text step confirms the resulting login text/heading displays correctly, a Generate random value or extraction step supplies a dynamically generated email, and a further validation confirms the password field was set/accepted as expected. Each generated or entered value gets its own validation, rather than only checking the final outcome.

entries.title: Custom validations for actions beyond the predefined menu
Custom validations and custom actions
entries.text: When a check or action has no equivalent in the predefined steps menu, Testim lets you write your own JavaScript — run either in the browser or outside it, in a Node.js context (a CLI validation/action) — to implement exactly the logic needed.

entries.title: Pass/fail contract for custom validations
entries.text: A custom validation step is meant to return a boolean: returning true makes the validation succeed, returning false makes it fail. This is the entire contract — whatever logic runs inside, only the final true/false return value determines the step's outcome.

entries.title: Extracting a user-defined value for custom checks
entries.text: The Extract Value step captures a value from the app (select the element to extract from; Testim creates the step and assigns that element) into a new parameter. That parameter can then be used inside a validation, a Set Text step, a custom step's code, or anywhere else a value is needed later — including as an input to a custom validation's own logic.

entries.title: Reading the step's status
entries.text: After a run, a passed validation step shows its icon (upper-left corner of the step) in green, with a confirming message in the Properties panel. A failed validation step shows that same icon in red, with a failure message in the Properties panel — the same visual pattern applies to custom validation steps as to any predefined validation.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.text: Data-driven testing (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Uploading and structuring test data

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Supported formats and limits
entries.text: Test data files can be uploaded in CSV, JSON, or Excel, each up to 2 MB. When uploaded via the Excel/CSV route specifically, each row of the file is converted into a single data set, with a maximum of 1200 rows.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Multiple ordered data sets
entries.text: A single file can define multiple ordered data sets, letting one test run repeatedly against a whole matrix of input combinations instead of a single hardcoded scenario.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Config File vs. Params File for data-driven CLI runs

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Config File overrides
entries.text: A Config File can override the Visual Editor's test data at either the execution level or a specific test level (via overrideTestData) — and it's also how an external data source (like a linked CSV file, or a database) is supplied instead of an uploaded file.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Params File
entries.text: A Params File (JSON) is execution-level only — it applies the same set of parameters across every test in the CLI run, rather than being scoped to one specific test the way a Config File's overrideTestData can be.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Where the multiple data sets actually run

entries.moduleTitle: Performing Data-driven Testing using Excel Files
entries.title: Editor run vs. CLI/Scheduler run
entries.text: Running the test from the Testim Visual Editor only executes the FIRST data set in the file, even if the Excel/CSV has several. Only when the test is run from the Testim CLI, the Scheduler, or a local suite run does it actually execute multiple times, in order, once per data set.

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Repeat Group Loops (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Loops in Testim: six repeat-group types

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Where a loop lives
entries.text: A loop is a setting on a group step (folder icon) — the group's contained steps are what gets repeated. The loop type is chosen from a radio-button list on that group, and the default is Don't repeat: the group's steps run exactly once, with no repetition at all.

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: For each item, in depth

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: 'For each item' loop
entries.text: Runs the same set of actions/validations against similar, repeating elements — the canonical use case being a table with multiple rows where every row needs the same check applied. Rather than writing one validation step per row, a single group of steps is looped. Configure it by selecting 'For each item', clicking the first repeating element, and optionally adjusting the item limit (default 99).

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: TESTIM_ITERATOR
entries.text: An out-of-the-box parameter that tracks the current loop iteration's value. Each time the loop runs, TESTIM_ITERATOR increases by one, letting steps inside the loop reference 'which iteration am I on' — for example, to build a row-specific selector or to log progress. This applies across loop types, not just For each item.

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Condition-based and fixed-count loops

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: While element / While element text is
entries.text: While element repeats the group only as long as a chosen element is (or isn't) present — set via the Visible/Not visible condition. While element text is is the same idea, but the condition is a text match against the element (Expected value field, with regex/JS support) rather than plain visibility. Both are configured by selecting the loop type, clicking the target element, then setting the condition.

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Loop for
entries.text: Runs the group a fixed number of times — either a literal number typed in directly, or a parameter holding a number, capped at a maximum of 99. Unlike For each item, this doesn't depend on matching elements on the page at all; it's a pure iteration count.

entries.moduleTitle: Using loops for multiple validations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Custom
entries.text: For loop conditions that don't fit any of the built-in types, Custom lets you define the condition as a JavaScript function — with optional JS/HTML parameters passed in, and its own timeout override separate from the test's general settings.

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Validate email (Tricentis docs) · Extract Value Step (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: What Testim's email service is

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Testim's own email service
entries.text: Testim generates email addresses exclusively through its own built-in email service — there's no option to plug in a third-party email provider for this. Two address types are available: a permanent address, created once from Settings → Email Service → Generate Email Address; and a temporary address, generated fresh on every run via a Generate email address step in the test itself (shown as 'Temporary' in its title).

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Validate email and Extract Value together
entries.text: Validate email fetches the content of a Testim inbox (for a permanent or temporary address) as an array of all messages in that mailbox — confirming a message arrived. Extract Value then pulls just the specific, stable content needed out of that message (a code, a link) into a variable for later steps to use.

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: When to use Testim's email service

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Direct email flows
entries.text: The obvious case: any flow where the AUT itself sends an email — signup confirmation, password reset, order confirmation — and the test needs to receive and act on that email's content.

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: SMS content routed through email
entries.text: The less obvious, but exactly what this module is about: many applications and SMS/OTP providers can be configured to forward SMS content (like a one-time verification code) to an email address instead of, or in addition to, a phone number. When the AUT or its SMS provider is set up that way, Testim doesn't need any separate SMS API integration — the SMS content simply arrives as a message in a Testim email inbox, and it's read and extracted using the exact same Validate email / Extract Value mechanism as a normal email.

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Extracting an SMS-forwarded value from a test

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: The extraction pattern
entries.text: Rather than asserting on an entire forwarded-SMS message body, the recommended pattern is to extract only the specific, stable value needed — an OTP code, a verification link, a short confirmation phrase — and save it to a Testim variable so a later step (entering the code into the AUT, for example) can use it directly.

entries.moduleTitle: Extracting SMS messages using email service in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Choosing permanent vs. temporary for this scenario
entries.text: A permanent address suits a recurring flow you test repeatedly (e.g. re-verifying the same test account's phone number). A temporary, freshly-generated address suits a scenario that needs a brand-new, never-before-used contact point on every run — such as testing that a new-user SMS-verification flow works for a genuinely new signup each time.

entries.moduleTitle: Generating coded test steps with CLI actions in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Generating coded test steps with CLI actions in Tricentis Testim
entries.text: Add CLI validations and actions (Tricentis docs) · Testim Copilot Coding Assistant (Tricentis docs)

entries.moduleTitle: Generating coded test steps with CLI actions in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: CLI actions vs. custom (browser) actions

entries.moduleTitle: Generating coded test steps with CLI actions in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: CLI actions and validations
entries.text: Custom Node.js scripts executed in the CLI environment (not inside the browser), initiated from inside a test the same way a standard custom action is. Because they run outside the browser sandbox, CLI actions/validations can do things a browser-side custom action cannot — like database validation and manipulation, or image and PDF validations.

entries.moduleTitle: Generating coded test steps with CLI actions in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Generate applies to CLI actions too
entries.text: The same Testim Copilot Coding Assistant used for regular custom steps also works inside a CLI action step: create the CLI action, click 'Write code with AI', and use the Generate command with a plain-text description of what the Node.js code should do (e.g. 'query this database table and return the row count'). The generated JavaScript appears in the chat pane, ready to use as the CLI action's implementation — the tester doesn't need to hand-write the Node.js from scratch.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Add API Action
entries.text: Used to get data returned from an API call — the data it retrieves can simply be used to check that something was returned (or extracted and used later), rather than asserting a specific value on the spot.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Validate API
entries.text: Used to validate data returned from an API call — usually validating data directly against the backend, asserting the response matches an expected value rather than just retrieving it.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Adding an API validation step
entries.text: Hover over the arrow where the step should go, click the predefined-steps icon ('M'), then choose Validations to add an API validation step to a test.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: URL and request method
entries.text: In the URL field, you select the desired HTTP request method and enter the root endpoint and path, then configure what should happen on failure — for example, throwing an error message following a failed validation.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Validating API responses against the UI
entries.text: The Validate API feature lets you validate API response values against what's shown in the UI — cross-checking backend data against rendered content, not just asserting the response in isolation. You can also configure whether to retry the request if it fails, or run the step's validations even when the status code itself is an error.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Send via web page

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Send via web page (checked = default)
entries.text: Keep this checked when the API call should also carry browser information such as cookies — they're sent automatically, useful for endpoints that require the same session as the UI.

entries.moduleTitle: Performing API testing in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Send via web page (unchecked)
entries.text: Deselect it to send the API call outside the browser context, so browser restrictions don't apply — for example, when the target API doesn't support CORS and would otherwise reject an in-browser request.

entries.title: Hooks: running a shared step/group before or after something

entries.moduleTitle: How to use Hooks in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Hook
entries.text: An object that runs an existing Shared Step or Shared Group before/after each step, or before/after an entire test. Once a hook is created, tests run as usual — the hook simply executes automatically as any other step would, at the point it's attached to.

entries.moduleTitle: How to use Hooks in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Before each step / After each step
entries.text: A 'before each step' handler runs before every single step in the test; an 'after each step' handler runs after every single step — this is what gives the effect of running something 'between' steps throughout the whole test, not just once at the start or end.

entries.moduleTitle: How to use Hooks in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Configuration File run hooks
entries.text: A separate, CLI/config-level mechanism: the Configuration File can define run hooks used to set up the application backend and define parameters before/after a single test or before/after all tests in a run — useful for environment-level setup/teardown that isn't tied to any one specific step.

entries.title: Debugging tests during runtime

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Stop, Pause, Step
entries.text: Rather than always running a test start to finish, Testim lets you Pause execution at any point, resume with Play, or run step-by-step to inspect state between actions. Breakpoints (manual, set by you, or virtual, created automatically when using step into/out/over or pause) mark exactly where execution should halt.

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Resuming from a breakpoint
entries.text: After a test pauses at a breakpoint, clicking the Play button ('Run Test') in the action menu resumes the test from that exact step — not from the beginning, and not skipping ahead. The breakpoint itself isn't removed just because execution passed through it.

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Running from a specific step
entries.text: You don't have to start from the very beginning to debug a later part of a test: hovering the arrow between two steps and clicking Play from here starts the run from the step right after that point — useful for quickly re-checking just the part of the test that's actually under investigation.

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Organizing and filtering with Result labels

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Result labels
entries.text: Free-text labels attached to a run — distinct from the Labels applied to tests in the Test Library. Result labels are commonly used to record things like which application environment was tested, which application version was tested, or which user/system executed the run (examples: 'nightly-scheduler', 'v1.42.34', 'Jenkins', 'Staging').

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Adding and filtering by result labels
entries.text: Result labels are added as part of a Scheduler's Advanced Options when setting up a scheduled run. Once runs carry labels, both the Suite Runs / Test Runs pages and the Filter Remote Runs pane let you filter directly by a result label — alongside filtering by execution type (Execution, Label, Plan, Scheduler), branch, or browser.

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Tagging failed runs with failure types

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Tagging a failure
entries.text: A failed run can be tagged with a failure-type reason, turning a raw 'failed' status into a categorized one — the same kind of categorization used by the Failure Types report covered in test-results modules (e.g. Element not found, Element not visible, JavaScript Error).

entries.moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Why tag failures
entries.text: Once failures are tagged, the failure-type filter can show only the runs tagged with a specific reason, and the Reports view's donut chart shows the percentage distribution of failure types (each tag's share of total runs, alongside its change vs. the previous period) — turning individual failures into a trend you can act on. Clicking a failure tag jumps straight to the Test Runs screen, pre-filtered to every run tagged with that type.

entries.title: Installation
entries.text: The Testim CLI is installed with npm: `npm i @testim/testim-cli`. It can then run commands either locally or remotely.

entries.moduleTitle: Leveraging the Command Line Interface (CLI) in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Why use the CLI at all
entries.text: The CLI is the mechanism behind everything the editor/Test List local run can't do: cross-browser execution, parallel execution, CI/CD integration, and branch-scoped or data-driven runs across every data set (not just the first, as an editor run does).

entries.moduleTitle: Leveraging the Command Line Interface (CLI) in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Configuration file
entries.text: A config file (e.g. testimConfig.js) is created and passed to the CLI runner as a parameter, pointing to its path if needed. It can define the project ID, token, labels selecting which tests to run, the Selenium grid to use, and base URL overrides.

entries.text: When running locally — from the editor or the Test List — tests can only run on Chrome. This is a hard constraint of local execution, not a configurable setting.

entries.title: Running on multiple browsers
entries.text: To actually run on Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge — simulating different desktop and mobile browsers in parallel — you need to use the CLI or Scheduler, not the plain editor. Execution can target Testim's own grid or any compatible Selenium grid.

entries.text: The grid to run against is set via the CLI's --test-config option, updating the grid parameter to point at Testim's grid or a compatible Selenium grid.

Exporting is also available from the Test List > Tests view. When there are more than 200 results, the CSV download still contains all of them, not just the first 200.

entries.moduleTitle: Integrating Tricentis Testim with Continuous Integration (CI) Tools
entries.title: The CLI as the integration point
entries.text: Tricentis built the Testim CLI, installable via npm, specifically so tests can be integrated with CI systems. Because it's a simple shell command, it can be invoked from all major CI tools that can run a shell command — the CLI is what makes the integration broadly tool-agnostic rather than requiring a bespoke plugin for every CI system.

entries.moduleTitle: Integrating Tricentis Testim with Continuous Integration (CI) Tools
entries.title: Named integrations
entries.text: Testim integrates with Jenkins and other third-party tools including GitHub, GitLab, and Azure DevOps — some with dedicated, deeper integrations (branch mirroring, pipeline triggers) beyond just 'the CLI can be called from anywhere'.

entries.moduleTitle: Integrating Tricentis Testim with Continuous Integration (CI) Tools
entries.title: Monitoring CI runs from Testim
entries.text: Once integrated, you can monitor test execution across builds from Testim and open the relevant test result with one click to diagnose a failure, plus review historical pass/fail analytics filterable by time period.

entries.text: Integrating Testim with GitHub Actions means creating a GitHub Actions workflow that sets up Node.js and installs the Testim CLI, then runs it as a step in the workflow — the same CLI used for any other CI integration, just wired into GitHub's own workflow syntax.

entries.moduleTitle: Integrating Testim with Azure DevOps & GitHub Actions for streamlined test results
entries.title: GitHub integration (branches)
entries.text: Separately from Actions, Testim's GitHub integration mirrors version-control activity: branches created in GitHub are automatically created in Testim under the same name, and merging branches in GitHub automatically merges the corresponding branches in Testim — keeping test versions aligned with code versions without manual syncing.

entries.moduleTitle: Enhancing test workflows with integrations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Finding the integration
entries.text: Testim's integrations live under the Integration settings, where a Test Management section lists modules including TTM for Jira and Xray. Within TTM for Jira's module, you provide the required Jira API token and Jira domain information to connect the two systems.

entries.moduleTitle: Enhancing test workflows with integrations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Linking a test to a TTM for Jira test case
entries.text: Once connected, an existing Testim test can be linked (one-to-many) to a TTM for Jira test case — and a bulk create-and-map option lets you select multiple Testim tests and create their corresponding TTM for Jira test cases in one action, instead of mapping them individually.

entries.moduleTitle: Enhancing test workflows with integrations in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Viewing results in TTM for Jira
entries.text: After running a mapped test in Testim using a Remote Grid (not a local editor run), the result is automatically pushed to TTM for Jira and appears under that project's Test Execution tab — giving a single place to see both Testim's own results and TTM for Jira's execution history. The name and pass/fail status are the details pushed from Testim to TTM for Jira.

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: When a test is missing steps
entries.text: After running a test with debugging, you may find it's lacking some steps, or that some steps are outdated and need re-recording. Rather than re-recording the whole test from scratch, you can add steps manually or record just the missing portion through the AUT.

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Inserting recorded steps at a position
entries.text: Hover over the arrow between two existing steps where the new steps should go, click Start recording at this position, then record the additional actions on the AUT window — the new steps are inserted exactly where the arrow was, not appended to the end.

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Start Recording vs. Start recording at this position
entries.text: Testim actually offers two distinct entry points: the plain 'Start Recording'/Record button (available while execution is stopped) appends new steps to the END of the test, while 'Start recording at this position' — triggered from the arrow between two steps — inserts steps at that exact mid-test point instead.

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Setting up the AUT state before recording mid-test
entries.text: Before clicking 'Start recording at this position', first run the test up to that point (e.g. using a manual breakpoint) so the AUT is actually displaying the correct screen state — recording blind from the wrong state would capture the wrong actions. Once done, click Stop recording to finish.

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Combining recording with debugging

entries.moduleTitle: Recording new steps to resolve bugs in Tricentis Testim
entries.title: Isolating the exact cause
entries.text: Debugging tools — breakpoints and step-by-step execution — let you isolate the exact steps leading to an error and recreate the issue consistently, which is what tells you precisely where a missing or outdated step needs to be inserted, rather than guessing.
